chapters.title: Units and Measurements
points: **SI system** has 7 **base units**: **metre** (length), **kilogram** (mass), second (time), ampere (current), kelvin (temperature), candela (luminous intensity), mole (amount of substance).
**Significant figures**: all **certain digits** plus the first **uncertain digit**. In **multiplication/division**, the result keeps as many significant figures as the quantity with the least.
**Errors**: **absolute error** = |measured value - true value|; **relative error** = absolute error / true value; **percentage error** = relative error x 100.
**Dimensions** express a quantity in terms of **[M]**, **[L]**, **[T]** etc. Example: **force** = [M L T^-2], energy = [M L^2 T^-2], pressure = [M L^-1 T^-2].
**Dimensional analysis** checks an equation's **consistency** and converts units, but it cannot find **dimensionless constants** like 1/2 or 2pi.
**Least count**: **vernier callipers** LC = 1 MSD - 1 VSD (commonly 0.01 cm); **screw gauge** LC = pitch / number of circular scale divisions (commonly 0.001 cm).
**Parallax method** measures large distances: **D = b / theta**, where **b** is the baseline and theta the parallax angle in radians.

**Derived units** are combinations of **base units**, e.g. **newton** = kg m s^-2 for force and **joule** = kg m^2 s^-2 for energy; **1 parsec** = 3.08 x 10^16 m and **1 light year** = 9.46 x 10^15 m.
**Order of magnitude**: the power of 10 closest to a value; **accuracy** is closeness to the **true value** while **precision** is closeness of repeated measurements to each other.
**Zero error** in **vernier callipers** and **screw gauge** must be corrected for; **mean absolute error** is the arithmetic mean of the magnitudes of absolute errors in repeated readings.

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (a) The volume of a cube of side 1 cm is equal to _____ m^3.
The number of significant figures in 0.06900 is: (a) 5 (b) 4 (c) 2 (d) 3
questions.a: (b) 4. The zeros to the left of the first non-zero digit are not counted, but the trailing zeros are significant.

questions.q: The period of oscillation of a simple pendulum is assumed to depend on the length l and the acceleration due to gravity g. Derive the form of the period T by the method of dimensions.
questions.a: T = k x sqrt(l/g), where k is a dimensionless constant (actually 2pi). T is proportional to l^(1/2) g^(-1/2).

questions.q: Convert 1 kg m^2 s^-2 into g cm^2 s^-2.

The mass of a box measured by a grocer's balance is 2.300 kg. Two gold pieces of masses 20.15 g and 20.17 g are added to the box. What is (a) the total mass of the box, (b) the difference in the masses of the pieces to the correct significant figures?
questions.a: (a) Total mass = 2.300 + 0.02015 + 0.02017 = 2.34032 kg, reported as 2.340 kg to the correct significant figures (limited by 2.300 kg). (b) Difference = 20.17 - 20.15 = 0.02 g.

questions.q: Which of the following ratios express pressure? (a) Force/Area (b) Energy/Volume (c) Energy/Area (d) Force/Volume
questions.a: Force/Area and Energy/Volume both have dimensions [M L^-1 T^-2], the dimensions of pressure. Energy/Area is [M T^-2] and Force/Volume is [M L^-2 T^-2].

questions.q: Using dimensional analysis, convert 1 newton into dyne.
questions.a: Force has dimensions [M L T^-2]. 1 N in SI = 1 kg m s^-2; in CGS = (10^3 g)(10^2 cm) s^-2 = 10^5 g cm s^-2 = 10^5 dyne.

questions.q: The nearest star to our solar system is 4.29 light years away. How much is this distance in parsecs? How much parallax would this star show when viewed from two locations of the Earth six months apart?
questions.a: 1 parsec = 3.26 ly, so distance = 4.29/3.26 = 1.32 parsec. With baseline b = 2 AU = 3.0 x 10^11 m and distance D = 1.32 pc = 4.07 x 10^16 m, parallax angle theta = b/D = 7.4 x 10^-6 rad = about 1.52 arcseconds.

mcqs.q: Which of the following pairs of physical quantities have the same dimensions?
mcqs.why: Both torque and energy have dimensions [M L^2 T^-2].

mcqs.q: Which of the following quantities is dimensionless?
mcqs.why: Strain is a ratio of two lengths, so it has no dimensions and no unit.

mcqs.q: The dimensional formula of angular momentum is:
mcqs.why: L = r x p gives [L][M L T^-1] = [M L^2 T^-1].

mcqs.q: A light year is a unit of:
mcqs.why: 1 light year = distance travelled by light in one year = 9.46 x 10^15 m.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT an SI base unit?
mcqs.why: Newton is a derived unit (kg m s^-2); kelvin, candela and mole are base units.

mcqs.q: If the error in measuring the radius of a sphere is 2%, the error in the volume of the sphere will be:
mcqs.why: V proportional to r^3, so percentage error = 3 x 2% = 6%.

chapters.title: Motion in a Straight Line
points: **Displacement** is the shortest straight-line **change in position** (a **vector**); **distance** is the total path length (a **scalar**). Displacement can be zero or negative, distance cannot.
**Average velocity** = displacement / time; **instantaneous velocity** v = dx/dt. **Average speed** = total distance / total time.
**Acceleration** a = dv/dt; the **area** under a **velocity-time graph** gives displacement; the **slope** of a position-time graph gives velocity.
**Equations of uniformly accelerated motion**: **v = u + at**; **s = ut + (1/2)at^2**; **v^2 = u^2 + 2as**.
**Distance covered in the nth second**: **s_n = u + (a/2)(2n - 1)** for motion with **initial velocity** u and **uniform acceleration** a.
For **free fall** under **gravity**, a = **g = 9.8 m/s^2** downward; a body thrown up reaches **max height** h = u^2/(2g) in time t = u/g.
**Relative velocity** of A w.r.t. B is **v_AB = v_A - v_B** (in **one dimension** with signs).
**Position-time graph**: a **horizontal line** means the body is **at rest**; a **parabola** means **uniformly accelerated motion**; slope of a **velocity-time graph** gives acceleration.
**Instantaneous speed** is the magnitude of **instantaneous velocity**; for **uniform motion** average and instantaneous velocities are **equal** at every instant.

questions.q: Can the following be treated as point objects: (a) a railway carriage moving smoothly between two stations, (b) a spinning cricket ball that turns sharply on hitting the ground? Give reasons.
questions.a: (a) Yes - the size of the carriage is negligible compared with the distance between stations. (b) No - the ball's size is comparable with the distance over which it changes direction, and its spin matters.

questions.q: A ball is thrown vertically upwards with a velocity of 20 m/s from the top of a building 25 m above the ground. (a) How high does the ball rise above the ground? (b) How long before it hits the ground? (g = 9.8 m/s^2)
questions.a: (a) It rises u^2/(2g) = 400/19.6 = 20.4 m above the top, i.e. 45.4 m above the ground. (b) Solving 25 = -20t + 4.9t^2 gives t = about 5.1 s.

questions.q: A particle moves with x(t) = x0(1 - e^-gt), t >= 0, x0 > 0. Where does it start, and with what velocity?
questions.a: At t = 0, x = x0(1 - 1) = 0. Velocity v = dx/dt = x0 g e^-gt, so v(0) = x0 g. It starts at the origin with speed x0 g.

questions.q: A particle in one-dimensional motion has zero speed at an instant. Can it have non-zero acceleration at that instant? Give an example.
questions.a: Yes. A ball thrown vertically upward has zero velocity at its highest point, but the acceleration there is still g downward.

questions.q: A jet aeroplane travelling at a speed of 500 km/h ejects its combustion products at a speed of 1500 km/h relative to the jet plane. What is the speed of the products with respect to an observer on the ground?
questions.a: Speed relative to ground = 1500 - 500 = 1000 km/h in the backward direction (ejection is opposite to the plane's motion).

questions.q: A car moving with a speed of 126 km/h is brought to a stop in a distance of 200 m. Find the retardation of the car (assumed uniform) and the time taken to stop.

A three-wheeler starts from rest and rolls down a hill with a constant acceleration. It travels a distance of 400 m in 20 s. Find its acceleration. If its mass is 7 quintals, calculate the net force acting on it.

A woman starts from her home at 9.00 am, walks with a speed of 5 km/h on a straight road up to her office 2.5 km away, stays at the office up to 2.00 pm, and returns home by an auto with a speed of 25 km/h. At what times does she reach the office and return home?
questions.a: Time to office = 2.5/5 = 0.5 h, so she reaches at 9.30 am. Return time = 2.5/25 = 0.1 h = 6 min, so she returns at 2.06 pm.

mcqs.q: In one-dimensional motion, a particle:
options: Can have zero speed but non-zero acceleration
Must have acceleration in the direction of velocity
Cannot have acceleration opposite to velocity
Must move with constant velocity if speed is constant
mcqs.why: At the top of a vertical throw speed is zero but acceleration is g downward.

mcqs.q: The area under a velocity-time graph for a particle in one-dimensional motion gives:
mcqs.why: Area = integral v dt = displacement.

mcqs.q: A body is thrown vertically upwards. At its highest point:
options: Velocity and acceleration are both zero
Velocity is zero but acceleration is g downward
Velocity is maximum and acceleration is zero
Velocity and acceleration are both maximum
mcqs.why: Gravity acts throughout; velocity momentarily becomes zero at the top.

mcqs.q: If the position-time graph of a particle is a straight line parallel to the time axis, the particle is:
mcqs.why: Position does not change with time, so velocity is zero.

mcqs.q: Two trains, each 50 m long, are travelling in opposite directions with speeds 10 m/s and 15 m/s. The time of crossing is:
mcqs.why: Relative speed = 25 m/s; total length = 100 m; time = 100/25 = 4 s.

mcqs.q: A body starts from rest with constant acceleration. The distances covered by it in successive equal seconds are in the ratio:
mcqs.why: From rest s_n = (a/2)(2n-1), so successive seconds give distances in odd ratios 1:3:5...

chapters.title: Motion in a Plane
points: A **vector** has **magnitude** and **direction**. **Resultant** of two vectors: **R = sqrt(A^2 + B^2 + 2AB cos theta)**; direction tan phi = B sin theta / (A + B cos theta).
**Dot product** A. B = **AB cos theta** (scalar, used for **work**); **cross product** |A x B| = **AB sin theta** (vector, used for torque), direction by right-hand rule.
**Projectile motion**: **time of flight** T = 2u sin theta / g; **max height** H = u^2 sin^2 theta / (2g); **range** R = u^2 sin 2theta / g. Range is maximum at theta = 45 degrees.
**Uniform circular motion**: **centripetal acceleration** a = v^2/r = omega^2 r, directed towards the **centre**; **period** T = 2pi/omega.
For a **projectile**, **horizontal velocity** stays constant (no horizontal acceleration) while **vertical velocity** changes under **gravity**.
**Unit vectors** i, j, k have **magnitude 1** along x, y, z axes; any vector **A = A_x i + A_y j + A_z k** with |A| = sqrt(A_x^2 + A_y^2 + A_z^2).
**Resolution of a vector**: **A_x = A cos theta** and **A_y = A sin theta**; **equal vectors** have same magnitude and direction, **null vector** has zero magnitude and arbitrary direction.

**Scalar product** is zero for **perpendicular vectors** and **vector product** is zero for **parallel vectors**; **trajectory** of a projectile is a **parabola** y = x tan theta - gx^2/(2u^2 cos^2 theta).
**Relative velocity** in a plane is also **v_AB = v_A - v_B** vectorially; in **rain-man problems** the **apparent velocity** of rain is v_rain - v_man.

questions.q: State which of the following are scalars and which are vectors: volume, speed, density, acceleration, velocity, angular velocity.
questions.a: Scalars: volume, speed, density. Vectors: acceleration, velocity, displacement, angular velocity.

questions.q: A cyclist rides at 27 km/h and, approaching a circular turn of radius 80 m, brakes, reducing his speed at 0.50 m/s^2. Find the magnitude and direction of the net acceleration on the turn.
questions.a: v = 7.5 m/s. Centripetal acceleration = v^2/r = 0.70 m/s^2. Net acceleration = sqrt(0.70^2 + 0.50^2) = 0.86 m/s^2 at an angle tan^-1(0.7/0.5) = about 54.5 deg to the direction of velocity.

questions.q: 'The net acceleration of a particle in circular motion is always along the radius towards the centre.' True or false? Give a reason.
questions.a: False. It is true only for uniform circular motion. If the speed changes there is also a tangential component of acceleration.

questions.q: A fighter plane flies horizontally at 1.5 km altitude with speed 720 km/h, passing over an anti-aircraft gun. At what angle from the vertical should the gun (muzzle speed 600 m/s) be fired to hit the plane, and above what altitude would the plane be safe?
questions.a: (a) The shell must have the plane's horizontal speed: sin(theta) = 200/600, so theta = about 19.5 deg from the vertical. (b) The plane must fly higher than the shell's maximum height, about 16 km.

questions.q: Rain is falling vertically with a speed of 35 m/s. Winds start blowing after some time with a speed of 12 m/s from east to west. In which direction should a boy waiting at a bus stop hold his umbrella?
questions.a: The relative velocity of rain w.r.t. the boy has components 35 m/s down and 12 m/s towards east (opposite the wind). The umbrella should be held at tan^-1(12/35) = about 19 deg with the vertical, tilted towards the west (in the direction from which the rain appears to come).

questions.q: A cricket ball is thrown at a speed of 28 m/s at an angle of 30 degrees above the horizontal. Calculate (a) the maximum height, (b) the time taken to return to the same level, (c) the horizontal range.
questions.a: (a) H = u^2 sin^2 theta/(2g) = 28^2 x 0.25/19.6 = 10 m. (b) T = 2u sin theta/g = 2 x 28 x 0.5/9.8 = 2.9 s. (c) R = u^2 sin 2theta/g = 784 x sin 60 deg/9.8 = about 69 m (using sin60=0.866, R=69.3 m). NCERT value with g=9.8 is about 69 m.

questions.q: An aircraft executes a horizontal loop of radius 1.00 km with a steady speed of 900 km/h. Compare its centripetal acceleration with the acceleration due to gravity.
A vector has a magnitude of 14 units and lies along the direction of the vector 2i + 3j + 6k. Find the components of the vector.
questions.a: Unit vector along 2i+3j+6k is (2i+3j+6k)/sqrt(4+9+36) = (2i+3j+6k)/7. Multiplying by 14 gives 4i + 6j + 12k, so the components are 4, 6 and 12.

mcqs.q: A car is moving on a circular level road. When it turns, the necessary centripetal force is provided by:
mcqs.why: On a level road only friction can act towards the centre.

mcqs.q: For a projectile, the range is maximum when the angle of projection is:
mcqs.why: R proportional to sin 2theta, maximum when 2theta = 90 degrees.

mcqs.q: The dot product of two vectors is zero when the vectors are:
mcqs.why: A.B = AB cos theta = 0 when theta = 90 degrees.

mcqs.q: A particle moves in a circle with uniform speed. Its acceleration is:
mcqs.why: Uniform circular motion has centripetal acceleration v^2/r towards the centre.

mcqs.q: Two projectiles projected with the same speed at angles 30 degrees and 60 degrees have ranges that are:
mcqs.why: sin 2theta is the same for theta and 90-theta (complementary angles give equal range).

mcqs.q: A vector is unchanged when it is:
options: Slid parallel to itself (translated without rotation)
mcqs.why: A free vector depends only on magnitude and direction, not on position.

chapters.title: Laws of Motion
points: **Newton's first law**: a body resists change in its state of **rest** or **uniform motion** (**law of inertia**). **Inertia** increases with mass.
**Newton's second law**: **F = dp/dt = ma**. **Momentum** p = mv. **Impulse** = F x t = change in momentum.
**Newton's third law**: **action and reaction** are equal, opposite, and act on **different bodies**, so they never cancel each other.
**Conservation of linear momentum**: in the absence of **external force**, **total momentum** of a system stays constant (used in collisions and recoil).
**Friction**: **static friction** is self-adjusting up to **f_max = mu_s N**; **kinetic friction** f_k = mu_k N, with mu_k < mu_s. Friction opposes relative motion or its tendency.
**Centripetal force** needed for circular motion: **F = mv^2/r**. On a **banked road** the safe speed without friction is **v = sqrt(rg tan theta)**.

**Weight in a lift**: **apparent weight** increases when the lift accelerates up (**R = m(g + a)**) and decreases when it accelerates down (**R = m(g - a)**); in free fall the person feels weightless.
**Free-body diagram** isolates one body with **all external forces**; **tension** in a **massless, inextensible string** is uniform throughout if the pulley is frictionless.
**Maximum speed** on a **level circular road** is **v_max = sqrt(mu_s r g)**; **limiting friction** depends on the **nature of surfaces** and normal reaction, not on area of contact.

questions.q: Give the magnitude and direction of the net force acting on a stone of mass 0.1 kg just after it is dropped from a window.
questions.a: Only gravity acts: F = mg = 0.1 x 10 = 1 N vertically downward.

questions.q: A constant retarding force of 50 N is applied to a body of mass 20 kg moving initially with a speed of 15 m/s. How long does the body take to stop?
questions.a: Retardation a = F/m = 50/20 = 2.5 m/s^2. Time t = v/a = 15/2.5 = 6 s.

questions.q: A body of mass 5 kg is acted upon by two perpendicular forces 8 N and 6 N. Give the magnitude and direction of its acceleration.
questions.a: Net force = sqrt(8^2 + 6^2) = 10 N, so acceleration = 10/5 = 2 m/s^2, at an angle tan^-1(6/8) = about 36.9 deg to the 8 N force.

questions.q: A shell of mass 0.020 kg is fired by a gun of mass 100 kg. If the muzzle speed of the shell is 80 m/s, what is the recoil speed of the gun?
questions.a: By momentum conservation: 100 x V = 0.020 x 80 = 1.6, so V = 1.6 x 10^-2 m/s in the opposite direction.

questions.q: A man of mass 70 kg stands on a weighing scale in a lift. Find the scale reading when the lift (a) moves upward with a uniform speed of 10 m/s, (b) moves down with a uniform acceleration of 5 m/s^2, (c) moves up with a uniform acceleration of 5 m/s^2, (d) falls freely. Take g = 10 m/s^2.
questions.a: Reading = R/g in kg. (a) R = mg = 700 N, reading 70 kg. (b) R = m(g-a) = 350 N, reading 35 kg. (c) R = m(g+a) = 1050 N, reading 105 kg. (d) R = 0, reading zero (weightlessness).

questions.q: Two masses 8 kg and 12 kg are connected at the two ends of a light inextensible string that passes over a frictionless pulley. Find the acceleration of the masses and the tension in the string when the masses are released.
questions.a: a = (12-8)g/(12+8) = 4 x 9.8/20 = 1.96 m/s^2. Tension T = 2m1m2g/(m1+m2) = 2 x 8 x 12 x 9.8/20 = about 94 N (using the standard Atwood formula; with g=9.8, T = 94.1 N).

questions.q: A mass of 4 kg rests on a horizontal plane. The plane is gradually inclined until at an angle theta = 15 degrees with the horizontal, the mass just begins to slide. What is the coefficient of static friction between the block and the surface?
questions.a: At the point of slipping, tan theta = mu_s, so mu_s = tan 15 deg = about 0.27.

questions.q: A monkey of mass 40 kg climbs on a rope which can stand a maximum tension of 600 N. In which of the following cases will the rope break: (a) climbs up with an acceleration of 6 m/s^2, (b) climbs down with an acceleration of 4 m/s^2, (c) climbs up with a uniform speed of 5 m/s, (d) falls down the rope nearly freely under gravity? Take g = 10 m/s^2.
questions.a: Tension T = m(g+a) upwards, m(g-a) downwards. (a) T = 40 x 16 = 640 N > 600 N, rope breaks. (b) T = 40 x 6 = 240 N, safe. (c) T = 400 N, safe. (d) T = 0, safe. Only case (a) breaks the rope.

mcqs.q: A car moving on a banked road can negotiate a curve safely without friction when its speed is:
mcqs.why: Balancing components on a banked road gives v^2 = rg tan theta.

mcqs.q: Impulse of a force is equal to:
mcqs.why: Impulse = F x t = delta p by Newton's second law.

mcqs.q: A body of mass 2 kg is moving with velocity 10 m/s. Its momentum is:
mcqs.why: p = mv = 2 x 10 = 20 kg m/s.

mcqs.q: Action and reaction forces never cancel each other because they act on:
mcqs.why: Newton's third-law pair acts on two different bodies.

mcqs.q: The coefficient of static friction between a block and a surface is 0.4. The maximum acceleration of the block placed on a truck so that it does not slip (g = 10 m/s^2) is:
mcqs.why: Maximum friction provides a_max = mu_s g = 0.4 x 10 = 4 m/s^2.

mcqs.q: Conservation of linear momentum holds for a system when:
options: No external force acts on the system
mcqs.why: Total momentum changes only due to net external impulse.

chapters.title: Work, Energy and Power
points: **Work** W = **F. s = Fs cos theta**. Work is a **scalar**; it is zero if force or displacement is zero or if they are **perpendicular**.
**Work-energy theorem**: **net work** done on a body = change in its **kinetic energy**, W = (1/2)mv^2 - (1/2)mu^2.
**Kinetic energy** K = **(1/2)mv^2 = p^2/(2m)**. Doubling **speed** makes K **four times**.
**Potential energy**: gravitational **U = mgh** near Earth's surface; **spring potential energy** = (1/2)kx^2; **spring force** F = -kx (Hooke's law).
**Conservative forces** (gravity, spring) do work **independent of path**; for them **mechanical energy** (K + U) is conserved when no other force does work.
**Power** P = **W/t = F. v**. **1 horsepower** = 746 W.
**Collisions**: in **elastic collisions** both **momentum and KE** are conserved; in **perfectly inelastic collisions** bodies stick together and KE loss is maximum (momentum still conserved).
**Variable force** work is the **area under the F-x graph**, W = integral F dx; **work done by friction** is **path dependent** and always negative for kinetic friction.
**Potential energy curve**: **equilibrium** occurs where **dU/dx = 0**; it is **stable** at a minimum of U and **unstable** at a maximum of U.

questions.q: State carefully whether the following quantities are positive or negative: (a) work done by a man in lifting a bucket out of a well, (b) work done by gravity in that case, (c) work done by friction on a body sliding down an incline, (d) work done by the resistive force of air on a vibrating pendulum.
questions.a: (a) Positive (force and displacement both upward). (b) Negative (gravity acts downward, displacement upward). (c) Negative (friction opposes motion). (d) Negative (air resistance opposes the velocity).

questions.q: A body of mass 2 kg initially at rest moves under an applied horizontal force of 7 N on a table with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.1. In 10 s, compute (a) work done by the applied force, (b) work done by friction, (c) work done by the net force, (d) change in kinetic energy.
questions.a: Net acceleration = (7 - 0.1x2x9.8)/2 = 2.52 m/s^2; distance in 10 s = 126 m. (a) 7 x 126 = 882 J. (b) -1.96 x 126 = -247 J. (c) 882 - 247 = 635 J. (d) Change in KE = 635 J - verifying the work-energy theorem.

questions.q: A body is initially at rest and undergoes one-dimensional motion with constant acceleration. The power delivered to it at time t is proportional to: (i) t^1/2 (ii) t (iii) t^3/2 (iv) t^2
questions.a: (ii) t. Power P = F x v = (ma)(at) = ma^2 t, which is proportional to t.

questions.q: A body moves unidirectionally under the influence of a source of constant power. Its displacement in time t is proportional to: (i) t^1/2 (ii) t (iii) t^3/2 (iv) t^2
questions.a: (iii) t^3/2. Constant power gives v dv/dx = constant, leading to x proportional to t^3/2.

questions.q: A woman pushes a trunk on a railway platform which has a rough surface. She applies a force of 100 N over a distance of 10 m, thereafter she gets progressively tired and her applied force reduces linearly with distance to 50 N at a total distance of 20 m. Calculate the total work done by her over 20 m.
questions.a: Work = area under the F-x graph = area of rectangle (100 x 10) + area of trapezium with parallel sides 100 N and 50 N over 10 m = 1000 + (100+50)/2 x 10 = 1000 + 750 = 1750 J. (NCERT graph method gives 1750 J for the full 20 m.)

questions.q: A pump on the ground floor of a building can pump up water to fill a tank of volume 30 m^3 in 15 min. If the tank is 30 m above the ground and the efficiency of the pump is 30%, how much electric power is consumed by the pump?
questions.a: Output power = mgh/t = (30 x 10^3 x 9.8 x 30)/(15 x 60) = 8.82 x 10^6/900 = 9.8 kW. Input power = output/efficiency = 9.8/0.30 = about 32.7 kW.

questions.q: A body of mass 0.5 kg travels in a straight line with velocity v = 5 x^(3/2), where x is in metres. What is the work done by the net force during its displacement from x = 0 to x = 2 m?

Two inclined frictionless tracks, one gradual (A) and the other steep (B), meet at point A from where two stones are allowed to slide down from rest, one on each track. Will the stones reach the bottom at the same time and with the same speed? Explain.
questions.a: Both reach with the same speed, because speed at the bottom v = sqrt(2gh) depends only on the height (conservation of energy). They do not reach at the same time: acceleration along B is larger, so the stone on the steeper track B reaches earlier.

mcqs.q: A body is initially at rest and undergoes one-dimensional motion with constant acceleration. The power delivered to it at time t is proportional to:
mcqs.why: P = Fv = (ma)(at) = ma^2 t, proportional to t.

mcqs.q: The kinetic energy of a body is doubled by changing its momentum. The momentum becomes:
mcqs.why: K = p^2/(2m), so doubling K needs p multiplied by sqrt(2).

mcqs.q: Work done by a conservative force around a closed path is:
options: Equal to the change in KE
mcqs.why: For conservative forces work depends only on end points, so a closed loop gives zero.

mcqs.q: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the colliding bodies:
mcqs.why: Perfectly inelastic means maximum KE loss with the bodies moving together; momentum is still conserved.

mcqs.q: A spring is stretched by 5 cm. If the force constant is 800 N/m, the potential energy stored is:
Power is the scalar product of:
mcqs.why: Instantaneous power P = F . v.

chapters.title: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
points: **Centre of mass** of two particles: **x_cm = (m1x1 + m2x2)/(m1 + m2)**. **External force** moves the CM as if all mass were concentrated there: **F_ext = M a_cm**.
**Torque** tau = **r x F**, magnitude rF sin theta. **Angular momentum** L = r x p = I omega; **tau = dL/dt**.
**Moment of inertia** I = **sum m_i r_i^2**. **Ring**: MR^2; **disc**: (1/2)MR^2; **solid sphere**: (2/5)MR^2; **rod about centre**: ML^2/12 (all about central axes through CM).
**Rotational KE** = **(1/2) I omega^2**. Total KE of a **rolling body** = (1/2)Mv_cm^2 + (1/2)I_cm omega^2.
**Parallel axis theorem**: **I = I_cm + Md^2**. **Perpendicular axis theorem** (for a plane lamina): **I_z = I_x + I_y**.
**Angular momentum** is conserved when **net external torque** is zero (e.g. a spinning skater speeds up by pulling arms in).
**Rolling without slipping**: **v_cm = R omega**, **a_cm = R alpha**. A solid sphere rolls down an incline faster than a ring because more of its energy is translational.
**Radius of gyration** k is defined by **I = Mk^2**; **instantaneous axis of rotation** for pure rolling is the **point of contact**, which is momentarily at rest.
**Equations of rotational motion** for constant **angular acceleration** alpha: **omega = omega_0 + alpha t**, **theta = omega_0 t + (1/2)alpha t^2**, **omega^2 = omega_0^2 + 2 alpha theta**.

questions.q: Give the location of the centre of mass of (i) a sphere, (ii) a cylinder, (iii) a ring and (iv) a cube, each of uniform mass density. Does the centre of mass of a body necessarily lie inside the body?
questions.a: All four have their centre of mass at their geometric centre. No - e.g. the centre of mass of a ring lies at its centre, in empty space outside the material.

questions.q: A child sits stationary at one end of a long trolley moving uniformly with speed V on a smooth horizontal floor. If the child gets up and runs about on the trolley in any manner, what is the speed of the centre of mass of the (trolley + child) system?
questions.a: Still V. There is no net external horizontal force, so the velocity of the centre of mass of the system cannot change.

questions.q: A child stands at the centre of a turntable with arms outstretched, rotating at 40 rev/min. He folds his hands back, reducing his moment of inertia to 2/5 of its initial value. (a) What is his new angular speed? (b) Show that the new kinetic energy of rotation is more than the initial, and account for the increase.
questions.a: (a) By conservation of angular momentum: 40 x I = omega' x (2/5)I, so omega' = 100 rev/min. (b) KE scales as I x omega^2, so it becomes 2.5 times larger; the extra energy comes from the work done by the child's muscles in folding his arms.

questions.q: Why does a solid sphere have a smaller moment of inertia than a hollow cylinder of the same mass and radius, about an axis through their axes of symmetry?
questions.a: In the solid sphere the mass is distributed from the centre out to R, so the average r^2 is smaller; in the hollow cylinder all the mass is concentrated at distance R from the axis, giving a larger moment of inertia.

questions.q: A hollow cylinder of mass 3 kg and radius 40 cm is pulled by a horizontal force of 30 N applied at its centre. Find the angular acceleration and the linear acceleration of the cylinder, assuming it rolls without slipping (take the surface rough enough). For a hollow cylinder I = MR^2 about its axis; use the standard NCERT result for a force applied through the centre with friction acting.
questions.a: For rolling with a central force, a_cm = F/(M + I/R^2) = 30/(3 + 3) = 5 m/s^2 (since I/R^2 = M for a hollow cylinder). Angular acceleration alpha = a_cm/R = 5/0.40 = 12.5 rad/s^2.

questions.q: The angular speed of a motor wheel is increased from 1200 rpm to 3120 rpm in 16 seconds. (i) What is its angular acceleration, assuming it to be uniform? (ii) How many revolutions does the engine make during this time?
questions.a: omega_1 = 1200 x 2pi/60 = 125.7 rad/s, omega_2 = 3120 x 2pi/60 = 326.7 rad/s. (i) alpha = (326.7-125.7)/16 = about 12.6 rad/s^2. (ii) Average rev rate = (1200+3120)/2 = 2160 rpm for 16/60 min, so revolutions = 2160 x 16/60 = 576.

questions.q: A car weighs 1800 kg. The distance between its front and back axles is 1.8 m. Its centre of gravity is 1.05 m behind the front axle. Determine the force exerted by the level ground on each front wheel and each back wheel.
questions.a: Total weight = 1800 x 9.8 = 17640 N. Reaction at back axle x 1.8 = weight x 1.05 gives R_back_total = 17640 x 1.05/1.8 = 10290 N, so each back wheel = 5145 N. R_front_total = 17640 - 10290 = 7350 N, so each front wheel = 3675 N. (Distances as in NCERT Exercise.)

questions.q: A flywheel of an engine has kinetic energy of rotation 300 kJ when rotating at 600 revolutions per minute. Find its moment of inertia about its axis.

mcqs.q: The centre of mass of a system of particles does not depend upon:
options: Forces acting on the particles (internal arrangement motion)
mcqs.why: CM position is fixed by masses and positions only; forces affect its motion, not its definition.

mcqs.q: Angular momentum is conserved when:
options: Angular velocity is constant in magnitude only
mcqs.why: tau_ext = dL/dt, so L is constant when tau_ext = 0.

mcqs.q: The moment of inertia of a thin ring about an axis through its centre and perpendicular to its plane is:
mcqs.why: All mass of a ring is at distance R from the axis, so I = MR^2.

mcqs.q: A solid sphere rolling without slipping has translational KE : rotational KE in the ratio:
mcqs.why: Translational = (1/2)Mv^2, rotational = (1/2)(2/5 MR^2)(v/R)^2 = (1/5)Mv^2; ratio = 5:2.

mcqs.q: Torque is the rate of change of:
mcqs.why: tau = dL/dt, analogous to F = dp/dt.

mcqs.q: Two identical solid spheres roll down inclines of the same height but different angles. At the bottom they will have:
mcqs.why: By energy conservation v depends only on height and the shape factor, not on incline angle or mass.

chapters.title: Gravitation
points: **Newton's law of gravitation**: **F = G m1 m2 / r^2**, with **G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2**. The force is always **attractive**.
**Acceleration due to gravity**: **g = GM/R^2** at the surface. At **height h**: g' = g (R/(R+h))^2; at **depth d**: g' = g (1 - d/R). g decreases both ways.
**Gravitational potential energy** U = **-GMm/r** (zero at infinity). **Potential** V = -GM/r.
**Orbital velocity** of a satellite near Earth's surface **v_o = sqrt(gR)** = about 7.9 km/s. **Escape velocity** v_e = sqrt(2GM/R) = sqrt(2) x v_o = about 11.2 km/s.
**Kepler's laws**: planets move in **ellipses** with the Sun at one **focus**; **areal velocity** is constant; **T^2 is proportional to r^3** (T^2/r^3 = constant).
A **geostationary satellite** has **period 24 h**, orbits in the **equatorial plane** at about 35,800 km height, and appears fixed in the sky.
**Weightlessness** in an orbiting satellite is due to **free fall**: satellite and everything inside fall towards Earth with the same **acceleration g**.
**Gravitational field** E = **-GM/r^2** (force per unit mass); **escape velocity** from a planet depends on its **mass and radius** but not on the mass of the escaping object.
**Binding energy** of a satellite = **+GMm/(2r)**; total energy of an orbiting satellite is **E = -GMm/(2r)**, negative showing it is bound.

questions.q: Answer the following: (a) Can you shield a body from the gravitational influence of nearby matter by putting it inside a hollow sphere? (b) An astronaut in a small spaceship orbiting Earth cannot detect gravity. If the station were very large, could he detect gravity? (c) The Sun pulls Earth more strongly than the Moon does, yet the Moon's tidal effect is larger. Why?
questions.a: (a) No - gravity cannot be shielded by any material. (b) Yes - tidal (differential gravity) effects become detectable across a large station. (c) Tides depend on the difference of gravitational pull across Earth, which falls as 1/r^3; the Moon is much closer, so its tidal effect dominates.

questions.q: A rocket is fired from the Earth towards the Sun. At what distance from Earth's centre is the gravitational force on the rocket zero? (Mass of Sun = 2 x 10^30 kg, mass of Earth = 6 x 10^24 kg, Earth-Sun distance = 1.5 x 10^11 m.)
questions.a: At distance r from Earth: GMe/r^2 = GMs/(R - r)^2 gives (R - r)/r = sqrt(Ms/Me) = 577, so r = R/578 = about 2.6 x 10^8 m from Earth's centre.

questions.q: Both Earth and Moon are subject to the gravitational force of the Sun. As observed from the Sun, the orbit of the Moon: (a) will be elliptical, (b) will not be strictly elliptical because the total gravitational force on it is not central, (c) is not elliptical but will necessarily be a closed curve, (d) deviates considerably from being elliptical due to influence of other planets.
questions.a: (b) The total gravitational force on the Moon (Sun + Earth) is not central, so its orbit is not strictly elliptical.

questions.q: A Saturn year is 29.5 times the Earth year. How far is Saturn from the Sun if Earth is 1.50 x 10^8 km away from the Sun?
questions.a: By Kepler's third law: r_s = r_e x (29.5)^(2/3) = 1.50 x 10^8 x 9.55 = about 1.43 x 10^9 km.

questions.q: One planet is observed from Earth to have an orbital period twice as short as that of Earth around the Sun (i.e. half the Earth year). How small is its orbit compared with Earth's orbit (in AU)?
questions.a: By Kepler's third law r proportional to T^(2/3): r = 1 AU x (1/2)^(2/3) = (0.25)^(1/3) = about 0.63 AU.

questions.q: Io, a satellite of Jupiter, has an orbital period of 1.769 days and the radius of its orbit is 4.22 x 10^5 km. Show that the mass of Jupiter is about one-thousandth that of the Sun (mass of Sun = 2.0 x 10^30 kg).
What is the weight of a body at a height equal to half the radius of the Earth above the surface, if its weight on the surface is 63 N?
Suppose the Earth shrinks suddenly to half its present size, its mass remaining the same. What will be the effect on the value of g at the surface?
questions.a: g = GM/R^2. Halving R with M unchanged makes g four times larger: g_new = 4g.

mcqs.q: Kepler's third law states that for planets around the Sun:
mcqs.why: T^2/r^3 = constant for all planets in the solar system.

mcqs.q: Escape velocity on Earth is about 11.2 km/s. It depends on:
options: Direction of projection (for magnitude on a non-rotating Earth)
mcqs.why: v_e = sqrt(2GM/R) depends on the planet's M and R, not on the object's mass.

mcqs.q: A geostationary satellite must orbit:
options: In the equatorial plane with period 24 h
At any height with period 24 h
In the equatorial plane with period 12 h
mcqs.why: It must be equatorial, circular and with Earth's rotation period to appear fixed.

mcqs.q: The value of g at a depth d below Earth's surface (uniform density) is:
mcqs.why: Inside a uniform Earth only the inner sphere contributes, giving g proportional to (R-d).

mcqs.q: Weightlessness experienced by an astronaut in orbit is because:
options: There is no gravity in space
The astronaut and spacecraft fall together with acceleration g towards Earth
Gravity is exactly cancelled by centrifugal force in an inertial frame
mcqs.why: Both astronaut and craft are in free fall with the same acceleration, so normal reaction is zero.

mcqs.q: If the distance between two masses is doubled, the gravitational force between them becomes:
mcqs.why: F proportional to 1/r^2, so doubling r gives F/4.

chapters.title: Mechanical Properties of Solids
points: **Stress** = **restoring force / area** (N/m^2 or pascal). **Strain** = change in dimension / original dimension (**no unit**).
**Hooke's law**: within the **elastic limit**, stress is proportional to strain. **Young modulus** Y = longitudinal stress / longitudinal strain = (F/A) / (delta L / L).
**Bulk modulus** B = **-P / (delta V / V)** (negative sign because volume decreases as pressure increases). **Shear modulus** G = shear stress / shear strain.
**Poisson ratio** = **lateral strain / longitudinal strain** (typically 0.2-0.4 for metals; theoretical limits -1 to 0.5).
The **stress-strain curve**: **proportional limit**, **elastic limit**, **yield point**, **ultimate tensile strength**, **fracture point**. Area under it gives energy stored per unit volume.
**Elastic potential energy** stored in a stretched wire = **(1/2) x stress x strain x volume** = **(1/2) F x delta L**.
**Modulus of rigidity** eta is the ratio of **tangential stress** to **shearing strain**; a material with larger **Young modulus** is **stiffer** and needs larger stress for the same strain.

**Elasticity** is the property of regaining **original shape** after removal of **deforming force**; **steel is more elastic than rubber** because for the same stress, strain in steel is much smaller.
**Compressibility** is the reciprocal of **bulk modulus**, **k = 1/B**; **breaking stress** depends on the **material** only, not on the dimensions of the wire.

questions.q: A steel wire of length 4.7 m and cross-sectional area 3.0 x 10^-5 m^2 stretches by the same amount as a copper wire of length 3.5 m and area 4.0 x 10^-5 m^2 under the same load. What is the ratio of the Young's modulus of steel to that of copper?

The edge of an aluminium cube is 10 cm long. One face is fixed to a vertical wall and a mass of 100 kg is attached to the opposite face. The shear modulus of aluminium is 25 GPa. What is the vertical deflection of this face?
questions.a: Shear strain = F/(A x eta) = (100 x 10)/(0.01 x 25 x 10^9) = 4 x 10^-6. Deflection = strain x edge length = 4 x 10^-6 x 0.1 = 4 x 10^-7 m.

questions.q: Two identical steel cubes (mass 50 g, side 1 cm) collide head-on face to face, each with speed 10 cm/s. Find the maximum compression of each. (Young's modulus of steel Y = 2 x 10^11 N/m^2.)
questions.a: Initial KE = 2 x (1/2)mv^2 = 5 x 10^-4 J becomes elastic PE 2 x (1/2)K(delta L)^2 with K = YA/L = 2 x 10^11 x 0.01. Compression delta L = sqrt(5 x 10^-4/(2 x 10^11 x 0.1)) = about 1.58 x 10^-7 m.

questions.q: A copper piece with rectangular cross-section 15.2 mm x 19.1 mm is pulled in tension with a force of 44,500 N, producing only elastic deformation. Calculate the resulting strain. (Y_cu = 110 GPa.)
A steel cable with a radius of 1.5 cm supports a chairlift at a ski area. If the maximum stress is not to exceed 10^8 N/m^2, what is the maximum load the cable can support?
questions.a: Area = pi r^2 = 3.14 x (1.5 x 10^-2)^2 = 7.07 x 10^-4 m^2. Maximum load = stress x area = 10^8 x 7.07 x 10^-4 = about 7.1 x 10^4 N.

questions.q: Four identical hollow cylindrical columns of mild steel support a big structure of mass 50,000 kg. The inner and outer radii of each column are 30 cm and 60 cm respectively. Assuming the load distribution to be uniform, calculate the compressional strain of each column. (Y_steel = 2.0 x 10^11 N/m^2.)
questions.a: Area of one column = pi(0.60^2 - 0.30^2) = 0.848 m^2. Load per column = 12500 kg, stress = 12500 x 9.8/0.848 = 1.44 x 10^5 Pa. Strain = stress/Y = 1.44 x 10^5/2.0 x 10^11 = about 7.2 x 10^-7.

questions.q: A copper wire is stretched so that it suffers a strain of 0.50% within its elastic limit. Calculate the tensile stress produced in the wire. (Young's modulus of copper = 1.1 x 10^11 N/m^2.)
questions.a: Stress = Y x strain = 1.1 x 10^11 x 0.005 = 5.5 x 10^8 N/m^2.

questions.q: The increase in length of a wire on stretching is 0.025%. If its Poisson ratio is 0.4, find the percentage decrease in its diameter.
questions.a: Poisson ratio = lateral strain/longitudinal strain, so lateral strain = 0.4 x 0.025% = 0.010%. The diameter decreases by 0.010%.

mcqs.q: Young's modulus is defined as the ratio of:
mcqs.why: Y = longitudinal stress / longitudinal strain within the elastic limit.

mcqs.q: Which material is more elastic in the physics sense?
mcqs.why: For the same stress, steel suffers a much smaller strain, so it is more elastic.

mcqs.q: The SI unit of stress is:
mcqs.why: Stress = force/area, measured in N/m^2 = pascal.

mcqs.q: Poisson's ratio is the ratio of:
mcqs.why: Poisson ratio = lateral strain / longitudinal strain.

mcqs.q: For an ideal (perfectly) incompressible liquid, the bulk modulus is:
mcqs.why: Incompressible means delta V = 0 for finite pressure, so B = -P/(delta V/V) tends to infinity.

mcqs.q: Hooke's law is valid up to the:
mcqs.why: Stress is proportional to strain only up to the proportional/elastic limit.

chapters.title: Mechanical Properties of Fluids
points: **Pascal's law**: **pressure** applied to an **enclosed fluid** is transmitted equally in all directions (basis of the **hydraulic lift**: F2/F1 = A2/A1).
**Pressure at depth h** in a liquid: **P = P_atm + rho g h**. Pressure depends only on **depth and density**, not on the container's shape.
**Archimedes' principle**: **upthrust** = weight of liquid displaced = **rho_liquid x V_submerged x g**. A body floats when upthrust balances its weight.
**Equation of continuity** for incompressible flow: **A1v1 = A2v2** - fluid speeds up in **narrower sections**.
**Bernoulli's theorem** (for steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow): **P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant** along a streamline.
**Viscosity**: Newton's law **F = -eta A (dv/dx)**. **Stokes' law** for a sphere: F = 6 pi eta r v; **terminal velocity** v_t = 2r^2 (rho - sigma) g / (9 eta).
**Surface tension** S = **F/l** = energy per unit area. **Excess pressure** inside a liquid drop = **2S/R**; inside a soap bubble = **4S/R**. **Capillary rise** h = 2S cos theta / (rho g r).
**Reynolds number** Re = **rho v d / eta** decides flow type: **Re < 1000** streamline, **Re > 2000** turbulent; **Torricelli's law** gives speed of efflux **v = sqrt(2gh)**.
**Angle of contact** theta < 90 deg means liquid **wets** the solid (concave meniscus, capillary rise); theta > 90 deg means it **does not wet** it (convex meniscus, capillary depression).

questions.q: Streamline flow is more likely for liquids with: (a) high density (b) high viscosity (c) low density (d) low viscosity
questions.a: Both (b) and (c). High viscosity keeps the flow lines distinct, and low density keeps the Reynolds number (rvd/eta) low, both favouring streamline flow.

questions.q: Iceberg floats in water with part of it submerged. What fraction of the volume of the iceberg is submerged if the density of ice is 0.917 g/cm^3?
questions.a: Fraction submerged = density of ice / density of water = 0.917/1 = 0.917.

questions.q: Why is the blood pressure in humans greater at the feet than at the brain?
questions.a: Pressure in a fluid column is P = rho g h; the feet lie below the heart, so they carry the pressure of a taller column of blood than the brain does.

questions.q: A 50 kg girl wearing high heel shoes balances on a single heel. The heel is circular with diameter 1.0 cm. What is the pressure exerted by the heel on the horizontal floor?

In a test experiment on a model aeroplane in a wind tunnel, the flow speeds on the upper and lower surfaces of the wing are 70 m/s and 63 m/s respectively. If the wing has an area of 2.5 m^2, calculate the lift force. (Density of air = 1.3 kg/m^3.)
questions.a: Pressure difference = (1/2) rho (v1^2 - v2^2) = 0.5 x 1.3 x (4900 - 3969) = 0.65 x 931 = 605 Pa. Lift = delta P x A = 605 x 2.5 = about 1.51 x 10^3 N.

questions.q: A Torricellian barometer uses mercury of density 13.6 x 10^3 kg/m^3 giving a column of 76 cm. If mercury were replaced by wine of density 984 kg/m^3, what would be the height of the wine column for normal atmospheric pressure?
questions.a: h_wine = h_Hg x rho_Hg/rho_wine = 0.76 x 13600/984 = about 10.5 m.

questions.q: An office window has dimensions 3.4 m by 2.1 m. As a storm passes, the air pressure outside drops to 0.96 atm, while inside it stays at 1.0 atm. What is the net force pushing the window outward?
questions.a: Delta P = 0.04 x 1.013 x 10^5 = 4052 Pa. Area = 3.4 x 2.1 = 7.14 m^2. Force = 4052 x 7.14 = about 2.9 x 10^4 N outward.

questions.q: Water from a tap emerges vertically downward with an initial speed of 1.0 m/s. The cross-sectional area of the tap is 10^-4 m^2. At what distance below the tap does the cross-section reduce to half the original, assuming steady flow? (g = 10 m/s^2.)
questions.a: Halving the area doubles the speed to 2.0 m/s (continuity). From v^2 = u^2 + 2gh: 4 = 1 + 20h, so h = 3/20 = 0.15 m below the tap.

mcqs.q: Streamline flow is more likely for liquids with:
mcqs.why: High viscosity and low density keep Reynolds number low, favouring streamline flow.

mcqs.q: Bernoulli's theorem is based on conservation of:
mcqs.why: P + (1/2)rho v^2 + rho gh = constant is an energy-per-unit-volume statement.

mcqs.q: The excess pressure inside a soap bubble of radius R (surface tension S) is:
mcqs.why: A soap bubble has two surfaces, so excess pressure = 2 x (2S/R) = 4S/R.

mcqs.q: Terminal velocity of a small sphere falling through a viscous liquid is proportional to:
mcqs.why: v_t = 2r^2(rho - sigma)g/(9 eta), proportional to r^2.

mcqs.q: With increase in temperature, the viscosity of a liquid generally:
mcqs.why: Heating weakens intermolecular cohesion in liquids, lowering viscosity (opposite to gases).

mcqs.q: Capillary rise is larger when the tube radius is:
mcqs.why: h = 2S cos theta/(rho g r), inversely proportional to r.

chapters.title: Thermal Properties of Matter
points: **Temperature scales**: **T(K) = t(deg C) + 273.15**. Size of **1 degree** is the same on **Celsius and Kelvin** scales.

**Thermal expansion**: linear **delta L = alpha L delta T**; **area expansion** coefficient beta = 2 alpha; **volume expansion** gamma = 3 alpha. For gases at constant pressure, gamma = 1/273 per degree C (ideal).
**Specific heat capacity** c: **Q = m c delta T**. **Molar heat capacity** uses moles. Water has a very high specific heat (4186 J/kg K), hence its use as a coolant.
**Latent heat**: **Q = mL** (no temperature change during **phase change**). **Latent heat of fusion** of ice = 3.34 x 10^5 J/kg; of vaporisation of water = 22.6 x 10^5 J/kg.

**Heat transfer**: **conduction** (Q/t = kA delta T / d), **convection** (fluid movement), **radiation** (**Stefan-Boltzmann law** P = sigma A T^4; Kirchhoff's law - good absorbers are good emitters).
**Newton's law of cooling**: **rate of cooling** is proportional to the **excess temperature** of the body over surroundings (for small differences).
**Wien's displacement law**: **lambda_max x T = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K** - hotter bodies radiate at **shorter wavelengths**.
**Calorimetry principle**: **heat lost = heat gained** in an isolated system; **thermal conductivity** k is larger for **metals** (good conductors) and very small for insulators like wood and wool.
**Triple point of water** is **273.16 K** at 0.46 cm of Hg pressure — the **single temperature-pressure** point where ice, water and vapour coexist.

questions.q: The triple points of neon and carbon dioxide are 24.57 K and 216.55 K respectively. Express these temperatures on the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales.
questions.a: Neon: -248.58 deg C and -415.44 deg F. Carbon dioxide: -56.60 deg C and -69.88 deg F.

questions.q: Two absolute scales A and B have triple points of water defined to be 200 A and 350 B. What is the relation between T_A and T_B?

A brass wire 1.8 m long at 27 deg C is held taut with little tension between two rigid supports. If the wire is cooled to -39 deg C, what is the tension developed in the wire, if its diameter is 2.0 mm? (alpha_brass = 2.0 x 10^-5 per deg C, Y_brass = 0.91 x 10^11 Pa.)
questions.a: Thermal strain = alpha x delta T = 1.32 x 10^-3. Tension = Y x A x strain = 0.91 x 10^11 x pi x 10^-6 x 1.32 x 10^-3 = about 3.8 x 10^2 N.

questions.q: A body cools from 80 deg C to 50 deg C in 5 minutes. Calculate the time it takes to cool from 60 deg C to 30 deg C. The temperature of the surroundings is 20 deg C.
questions.a: By Newton's law of cooling, the rate constant K = (30/5)/(65 - 20) = 0.133 per min. Then (30/t) = K x (45 - 20), giving t = 9 minutes.

questions.q: A child running in a fever has a temperature of 101 deg F. What is this temperature on the Celsius scale? The normal human body temperature is 98.6 deg F - what is it in deg C?

A steel tape 1 m long is correctly calibrated for a temperature of 27.0 deg C. The length of a steel rod measured by this tape at 45.0 deg C is found to be 63.0 cm. What is the actual length of the rod at 45.0 deg C and at 27.0 deg C? (alpha_steel = 1.20 x 10^-5 per deg C.)
questions.a: The tape expands, so each cm division becomes longer by factor (1 + alpha x 18). Actual length at 45 deg C = 63.0 x (1 + 1.20 x 10^-5 x 18) = 63.0 x 1.000216 = about 63.01 cm. At 27 deg C the rod (same material) contracts by the same factor as the tape, so the reading stays 63.0 cm.

questions.q: Show that the coefficient of area expansion, beta, of a rectangular sheet of a solid is twice its coefficient of linear expansion, alpha.
questions.a: For a sheet of sides l and b heated by delta T: new area = l(1+alpha delta T) x b(1+alpha delta T) = lb(1 + 2 alpha delta T) to first order (neglecting alpha^2), so beta = 2 alpha.

questions.q: A cup of coffee cools from 90 deg C to 80 deg C in t minutes in a room at 25 deg C. How long will it take to cool from 70 deg C to 60 deg C in the same room?
questions.a: By Newton's law of cooling, rate proportional to mean excess temperature. First case mean excess = 85-25 = 60, rate = 10/t. Second case mean excess = 65-25 = 40, so 10/t' = (10/t) x (40/60), giving t' = 1.5 t minutes.

mcqs.q: The triple point of water on the Kelvin scale is:
mcqs.why: The triple point is defined as 273.16 K exactly in the NCERT treatment.

mcqs.q: For most solids, the coefficients of linear, area and volume expansion are in the ratio:
mcqs.why: beta = 2 alpha and gamma = 3 alpha, so alpha:beta:gamma = 1:2:3.

mcqs.q: Water is used as a coolant in car radiators mainly because it has:
mcqs.why: High specific heat (4186 J/kg K) lets water absorb large heat with small temperature rise.

mcqs.q: According to Wien's displacement law, as temperature increases, lambda_max:
mcqs.why: lambda_max x T = constant, so hotter bodies peak at shorter wavelengths.

mcqs.q: During a phase change at constant pressure, the temperature of the substance:
options: Remains constant until the change is complete
mcqs.why: Heat supplied becomes latent heat, changing the state without changing temperature.

mcqs.q: A good absorber of radiation is also a:
mcqs.why: Kirchhoff's law: emissive power is proportional to absorptive power at a given wavelength.

chapters.title: Thermodynamics
points: **Zeroth law**: if A and B are each in **thermal equilibrium** with C, they are in equilibrium with each other - this defines **temperature**.
**First law**: **delta Q = delta U + delta W** (heat supplied = increase in internal energy + work done BY the gas). Sign convention: work done by gas is positive.
**Isothermal process** (T constant): delta U = 0, **W = nRT ln(V2/V1)**. **Adiabatic process** (Q = 0): **PV^gamma = constant**, W = (P1V1 - P2V2)/(gamma - 1).
**Molar heat capacities**: **C_p - C_v = R**; **gamma = C_p/C_v** = 1.67 (monoatomic), 1.4 (diatomic), 1.33 (triatomic non-linear approx).
**Second law (Kelvin-Planck)**: no engine can convert **all heat into work**. **Carnot efficiency** eta = **1 - T_cold/T_hot** (temperatures in kelvin); it is the maximum possible.
**Refrigerator COP** = **Q_cold / W** = **T_cold / (T_hot - T_cold)** for a Carnot refrigerator.
**Internal energy** of an ideal gas depends only on **temperature**; for n moles of a gas with f degrees of freedom, **U = (f/2) nRT**.
**Cyclic process**: **delta U = 0** over a full cycle, so **Q_net = W_net** = **area enclosed** by the P-V diagram; **isobaric** means pressure constant, **isochoric** means volume constant (W = 0).
**Reversible process** is quasi-static and frictionless, an **idealisation**; **Carnot cycle** consists of two **isothermal** and two **adiabatic** steps and no real engine can exceed its efficiency.

questions.q: A geyser heats water flowing at the rate of 3.0 litres per minute from 27 deg C to 77 deg C. If the geyser operates on a gas burner, what is the rate of consumption of fuel if its heat of combustion is 4.0 x 10^4 J/g?
questions.a: Heat needed per minute = 3 x 4200 x 50 = 6.3 x 10^5 J. Fuel rate = 6.3 x 10^5/4.0 x 10^4 = about 16 g per minute.

questions.q: What amount of heat must be supplied to 2.0 x 10^-2 kg of nitrogen (at room temperature) to raise its temperature by 45 deg C at constant pressure? (Molecular mass of N2 = 28; R = 8.3 J/mol K.)
A refrigerator is to maintain eatables kept inside at 9 deg C. If the room temperature is 36 deg C, calculate the coefficient of performance.
A steam engine delivers 5.4 x 10^8 J of work per minute and services 3.6 x 10^9 J of heat per minute from its boiler. What is the efficiency of the engine? How much heat is wasted per minute?
questions.a: Efficiency = 5.4 x 10^8/3.6 x 10^9 = 0.15, i.e. 15%. Heat wasted = 3.6 x 10^9 - 5.4 x 10^8 = 3.06 x 10^9 J per minute.

questions.q: A room of volume 25 m^3 is heated from 20 deg C to 27 deg C at a constant pressure of 1 atm. How many moles of air escape from the room? (R = 8.3 J/mol K.)
questions.a: n = PV/(RT). Initially n1 = (1.013 x 10^5 x 25)/(8.3 x 293) = about 1042 mol. Finally n2 = (1.013 x 10^5 x 25)/(8.3 x 300) = about 1017 mol. Moles escaped = n1 - n2 = about 25 mol.

questions.q: An ideal gas at 300 K is compressed adiabatically to 1/32 of its initial volume. If gamma = 1.4, find its final temperature.
questions.a: For an adiabatic change TV^(gamma-1) = constant: T2 = T1 x (V1/V2)^(gamma-1) = 300 x (32)^(0.4) = 300 x 4 = 1200 K.

questions.q: During an adiabatic expansion of 2 moles of a gas, the internal energy of the gas is found to decrease by 100 J. What is the work done by the gas during the process?
questions.a: For an adiabatic process delta Q = 0, so by the first law 0 = delta U + W, giving W = -delta U = +100 J done by the gas.

questions.q: A Carnot engine has the hot reservoir at 500 K and the cold reservoir at 375 K. It takes in 600 kcal of heat per cycle from the hot reservoir. How much work does it deliver per cycle?
questions.a: Efficiency eta = 1 - 375/500 = 0.25. Work = eta x Q_hot = 0.25 x 600 = 150 kcal = 150 x 4186 = about 6.28 x 10^5 J per cycle.

mcqs.q: In an isothermal process for an ideal gas, the change in internal energy is:
options: Equal to heat absorbed plus work
mcqs.why: U of an ideal gas depends only on T, and T is constant in an isothermal process.

mcqs.q: For a monoatomic ideal gas, gamma = C_p/C_v is:
mcqs.why: f = 3 gives C_v = (3/2)R and C_p = (5/2)R, so gamma = 5/3 = 1.67.

mcqs.q: The efficiency of a Carnot engine depends on:
options: Temperatures of hot and cold reservoirs only
Amount of heat taken per cycle
mcqs.why: eta = 1 - T_cold/T_hot, independent of the working substance.

mcqs.q: In an adiabatic process:
options: Heat exchange with surroundings is zero
mcqs.why: Adiabatic means delta Q = 0 by definition; temperature generally changes.

mcqs.q: Over one complete cyclic process, the change in internal energy is:
options: Equal to net work done with opposite sign convention only
mcqs.why: U is a state function, so it returns to its initial value after a full cycle.

mcqs.q: C_p is greater than C_v for a gas because at constant pressure:
options: Part of the heat goes into doing external work of expansion
mcqs.why: At constant pressure the gas expands and does work, needing extra heat for the same temperature rise.

chapters.title: Kinetic Theory
points: **Ideal gas equation**: **PV = nRT = Nk_B T**. Pressure from kinetic theory: **P = (1/3) rho c_rms^2** = (2/3) x (KE per unit volume).
**rms speed** c_rms = **sqrt(3RT/M)** = sqrt(3k_B T/m). **Average KE** of one molecule = **(3/2) k_B T**; per mole = (3/2) RT.

**Degrees of freedom**: monoatomic gas **f = 3** (translational); diatomic at room temperature **f = 5** (3 translational + 2 rotational). **Equipartition**: each degree of freedom carries (1/2) k_B T per molecule.
**Law of equipartition** links **internal energy** U = (f/2) nRT and **heat capacities** C_v = (f/2) R, C_p = (f/2 + 1) R.
**Mean free path** lambda = **1 / (sqrt(2) pi d^2 N/V)**: increases when **density decreases** or molecule size decreases.
**Maxwell speed distribution**: **most probable speed** = sqrt(2RT/M), **average speed** = sqrt(8RT/(pi M)), **rms speed** = sqrt(3RT/M); rms is the largest of the three.
**Avogadro's law**: equal volumes of all gases at same **T and P** contain **equal number of molecules**; **Boltzmann constant** k_B = R/N_A = 1.38 x 10^-23 J/K.
**Dalton's law of partial pressures**: total pressure of a mixture = **sum of partial pressures**; rms speed is **inversely proportional** to **sqrt(molar mass)** at fixed temperature.

questions.q: Estimate the fraction of the molecular volume to the actual volume occupied by oxygen gas at STP. Take the diameter of an oxygen molecule to be 3 Angstrom.
questions.a: Molecular volume per mole = (4/3)pi(1.5 x 10^-10)^3 x N_A = about 8.5 x 10^-6 m^3. Molar volume at STP = 2.24 x 10^-2 m^3. Fraction = about 4 x 10^-4.

questions.q: At what temperature is the root mean square speed of an atom in an argon gas cylinder equal to the rms speed of a helium gas atom at -20 deg C? (Atomic mass of Ar = 39.9 u, of He = 4.0 u.)
questions.a: c_rms proportional to sqrt(T/M): T_Ar = 253 x (39.9/4.0) = about 2.52 x 10^3 K.

questions.q: A flask contains argon and chlorine in the ratio 2:1 by mass. The temperature of the mixture is 27 deg C. Obtain the ratio of (i) average kinetic energy per molecule, and (ii) root mean square speed of the molecules of the two gases. (Ar = 39.9 u, Cl2 = 70.9 u.)
questions.a: (i) 1:1 - average kinetic energy depends only on temperature. (ii) v_Ar/v_Cl = sqrt(70.9/39.9) = about 1.33.

questions.q: A cubic vessel (with faces horizontal and vertical) contains an ideal gas at NTP. The vessel is carried by a rocket moving at 500 m/s in the vertical direction. What is the pressure of the gas inside the vessel as observed from the ground?
questions.a: It remains the same. Motion of the vessel as a whole does not change the relative motion of the gas molecules with respect to the walls, which is what causes pressure.

questions.q: A cylinder of oxygen at 27 deg C has a volume of 30 litres and a pressure of 15 atm. When a part of the gas is used, the pressure drops to 11 atm and the temperature to 17 deg C. What mass of oxygen has been used? (Molar mass of O2 = 32 g/mol, R = 0.0821 L atm/mol K.)
questions.a: Initial moles = PV/(RT) = 15 x 30/(0.0821 x 300) = 18.27 mol (mass 585 g). Final moles = 11 x 30/(0.0821 x 290) = 13.86 mol (mass 444 g). Mass used = 585 - 444 = about 141 g.

questions.q: Estimate the average thermal energy of a helium atom at (i) room temperature 27 deg C, (ii) the temperature on the surface of the Sun, 6000 K, (iii) the temperature in the interior of the Sun, 10 million K.
Show that the molar volume of an ideal gas at STP is 22.4 litres.

In the diffusion of uranium isotopes, UF6 gas contains molecules with molar masses 349 g/mol (with U-235) and 352 g/mol (with U-238). Find the ratio of the rms speeds of the two types of molecules at the same temperature.
questions.a: c_rms proportional to 1/sqrt(M), so ratio (light/heavy) = sqrt(352/349) = about 1.0043. The lighter molecules move slightly faster and diffuse preferentially.

mcqs.q: The average kinetic energy of a gas molecule is proportional to:
mcqs.why: Average KE = (3/2) k_B T, directly proportional to T in kelvin.

mcqs.q: The rms speed of gas molecules is largest compared with:
options: It is greater than both average and most probable speeds
It is smaller than the most probable speed
All three speeds are always equal
mcqs.why: c_rms : c_avg : c_mp = sqrt(3) : sqrt(8/pi) : sqrt(2), so rms is the largest.

mcqs.q: For a diatomic gas at room temperature, the number of degrees of freedom (translational + rotational) is:
mcqs.why: 3 translational + 2 rotational = 5 (vibration neglected at room temperature).

mcqs.q: Mean free path of gas molecules increases when:
options: Temperature is lowered at constant volume only
mcqs.why: lambda = 1/(sqrt(2) pi d^2 n); fewer molecules per volume (lower density) means longer free path.

mcqs.q: Pressure exerted by an ideal gas is (in terms of mean square speed):
mcqs.why: Kinetic theory gives P = (1/3) rho <c^2> = (1/3) rho c_rms^2.

mcqs.q: At the same temperature, lighter gas molecules have:
options: The same rms speed as heavier molecules
mcqs.why: c_rms = sqrt(3RT/M); smaller molar mass M gives larger rms speed.

chapters.title: Oscillations
points: **SHM**: displacement **x = A sin(omega t + phi)**; **acceleration** a = -omega^2 x (always directed to mean position); **velocity** v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2).
**Time period** T = **2pi/omega**; **frequency** nu = 1/T. For a **spring-mass system** T = 2pi sqrt(m/k); for a **simple pendulum** T = 2pi sqrt(l/g).
**Energy in SHM**: **KE** = (1/2) m omega^2 (A^2 - x^2), **PE** = (1/2) m omega^2 x^2; total **E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2** stays constant (no friction).
**KE and PE are equal** at **x = A/sqrt(2)**. At the **mean position** KE is maximum and PE minimum; at extremes the reverse.
**Phase**: two oscillators with **phase difference 0** are **in phase**; pi means opposite phase. Phase difference = (2pi/lambda) x path difference in waves.

**Damped oscillations** lose **amplitude** gradually due to friction; **forced oscillations** take the driver's frequency; **resonance** occurs when driver frequency equals natural frequency, giving maximum amplitude.
**Angular frequency** omega = **2pi nu = 2pi/T**; **epoch** is the **initial phase** phi at t = 0; SHM requires **restoring force** F = -kx, proportional to displacement and opposite in sign.
**Seconds pendulum** has **T = 2 s** and length about **1 m** near Earth's surface; period of a pendulum is **independent of mass** and **amplitude** (for small oscillations).

questions.q: Which of the following represent periodic motion: (a) a swimmer completing one return trip from one bank of a river to the other and back, (b) a freely suspended bar magnet displaced from its N-S direction and released, (c) a hydrogen molecule rotating about its centre of mass, (d) an arrow released from a bow?
questions.a: (b) and (c). The magnet oscillates about its equilibrium direction and the molecule rotates periodically; the swimmer's trip and the arrow's flight are not repeated motions.

questions.q: Which of the following represent nearly SHM and which represent periodic but not SHM: (a) rotation of Earth about its axis, (b) motion of an oscillating mercury column in a U-tube, (c) motion of a ball bearing inside a smooth curved bowl released slightly above the lowest point, (d) general vibrations of a polyatomic molecule about its equilibrium position?
questions.a: Nearly SHM: (b) and (d) - the restoring force is nearly proportional to displacement. Periodic but not SHM: (a) and (c).

questions.q: A spring of force constant k is clamped rigidly at one end with a mass m at the free end; a force F stretches it. The same spring has both ends free with a mass m at each end, and each end is stretched by the same force F. (a) What is the maximum extension in the two cases? (b) If the mass(es) are released, what is the period of oscillation in each case?
questions.a: (a) F/k in both cases. (b) First case: T = 2pi sqrt(m/k). Second case: the reduced mass is m/2, so T = 2pi sqrt(m/2k).

questions.q: A spring balance has a scale that reads from 0 to 50 kg. The length of the scale is 20 cm. A body suspended from this balance, when displaced and released, oscillates with a period of 0.6 s. What is the weight of the body?
questions.a: k = (50 x 9.8)/0.2 = 2450 N/m. From T = 2pi sqrt(m/k): m = kT^2/4pi^2 = about 22.3 kg, so the weight is about 2.19 x 10^2 N.

questions.q: A particle oscillates in SHM according to x = 7 cos(0.5 pi t), with x in metres and t in seconds. Find the amplitude, period and frequency of the motion.
questions.a: Comparing with x = A cos(omega t): A = 7 m, omega = 0.5 pi rad/s. Period T = 2pi/omega = 4 s, frequency nu = 1/T = 0.25 Hz.

questions.q: A simple pendulum is mounted in a car. What is the period of oscillation of the pendulum if the car is moving down an inclined plane (angle alpha with the horizontal) without friction?
questions.a: Effective gravity along the plane geometry gives g_eff = g cos alpha, so T = 2pi sqrt(l/(g cos alpha)).

questions.q: The force constant of a spring is 800 N/m. It has an extension of 5 cm. Find the work done in stretching it further by 10 cm (i.e. from 5 cm to 15 cm extension).
Mercury is poured into a U-tube so that the column length is 30 cm in total. The mercury is displaced slightly and released. Find the period of oscillation. (g = 9.8 m/s^2.)
questions.a: For a liquid column in a U-tube, T = 2pi sqrt(h/g) where h is the height of the column in each arm at equilibrium = 0.15 m. T = 2pi sqrt(0.15/9.8) = about 0.78 s.

mcqs.q: In SHM, acceleration is maximum at:
mcqs.why: a = -omega^2 x is largest in magnitude where |x| = A, at the extremes.

mcqs.q: The time period of a simple pendulum depends on:
options: Amplitude (for large angles only in this option set)
Length of the pendulum and g
mcqs.why: T = 2pi sqrt(l/g) for small oscillations, independent of mass and amplitude.

mcqs.q: In SHM, kinetic and potential energies are equal when displacement is:
mcqs.why: Setting (1/2)m omega^2(A^2-x^2) = (1/2)m omega^2 x^2 gives x = A/sqrt(2).

mcqs.q: Resonance occurs when the frequency of the driving force:
options: Is much larger than natural frequency
Equals the natural frequency of the oscillator
Is much smaller than natural frequency
mcqs.why: At matching frequencies energy transfer per cycle is maximum, giving large amplitude.

mcqs.q: If the length of a simple pendulum is increased by 4 times, its period becomes:
mcqs.why: T proportional to sqrt(l), so 4 times length gives 2 times period.

mcqs.q: Damped oscillations are those in which:
options: Amplitude decreases with time due to friction/resistance
mcqs.why: Dissipative forces remove energy, so amplitude decays gradually.

chapters.title: Waves
points: **Wave speed** v = **nu x lambda**. **Transverse waves** (light, strings) vibrate perpendicular to propagation; **longitudinal waves** (sound) vibrate parallel, forming compressions and rarefactions.
**Progressive wave equation**: **y = A sin(omega t - kx + phi)**, where **k = 2pi/lambda** is the propagation constant.
**Speed of a transverse wave** on a stretched string **v = sqrt(T/mu)**, where T is **tension** and mu is **mass per unit length**.
**Speed of sound** in a gas (**Newton-Laplace**): **v = sqrt(gamma P / rho)** = sqrt(gamma RT / M). Sound speed in air is about 332 m/s at 0 deg C and increases about 0.61 m/s per degree C rise.

**Standing waves**: **nodes** (zero amplitude) and **antinodes** (maximum amplitude) form. String fixed at both ends: harmonics **nu_n = n v/(2L)**, all harmonics present. **Open organ pipe**: all harmonics; **closed pipe**: only odd harmonics, fundamental nu = v/(4L).
**Beats**: when two sounds of close frequencies nu1 and nu2 play together, **beat frequency = |nu1 - nu2|**.
**Doppler effect**: **apparent frequency** changes when source and observer move relative to each other; frequency increases on **approach**, decreases on **recession**.

**Superposition principle**: net displacement is the **vector sum** of individual displacements; **intensity** is proportional to **amplitude squared**, I proportional to A^2, and to frequency squared for a wave on a string.

questions.q: You have learnt that a travelling wave in one dimension is represented by y = f(x +- vt). Is the converse true? Examine whether these can possibly represent a travelling wave: (a) (x - vt)^2, (b) log[(x + vt)/x0], (c) 1/(x + vt).
questions.a: Yes to all three. Any function of (x +- vt) keeps its shape while moving with speed v, so each can represent a travelling wave.

questions.q: A steel wire has a length of 12.0 m and a mass of 2.10 kg. What should be the tension in the wire so that the speed of a transverse wave on the wire equals the speed of sound in dry air at 20 deg C (343 m/s)?

A hospital uses an ultrasonic scanner to locate tumours in a tissue. What is the wavelength of sound in the tissue in which the speed of sound is 1.7 km/s? The operating frequency of the scanner is 4.2 MHz.
questions.a: lambda = v/f = 1700/4.2 x 10^6 = about 4.0 x 10^-4 m, i.e. about 0.4 mm.

questions.q: With the propagation of longitudinal waves through a medium, the quantity transmitted is: (a) matter, (b) energy, (c) energy and matter, (d) energy, matter and momentum.
questions.a: (b) Energy. The particles of the medium only oscillate about their mean positions; they are not carried along with the wave.

questions.q: A transverse harmonic wave on a string is described by y = 3.0 sin(36t + 0.018x + pi/4), with x and y in cm and t in seconds. (a) Find the frequency and speed of the wave. (b) If the linear mass density of the string is as in the NCERT problem giving a speed consistent with the equation, state the direction of propagation.
questions.a: omega = 36 rad/s gives nu = 36/(2pi) = 5.73 Hz. k = 0.018 cm^-1 gives lambda = 2pi/k = 349 cm = 3.49 m. Speed v = nu x lambda = 5.73 x 3.49 = about 20 m/s. The + sign in (omega t + kx) means the wave travels in the negative x-direction.

questions.q: For the wave y = 2.0 cos 2pi(10t - 0.0080x + 0.035), with x and y in cm, calculate the displacement at position x = 100 cm and time t = 11 s.
questions.a: Phase = 2pi(10 x 11 - 0.0080 x 100 + 0.035) = 2pi(110 - 0.80 + 0.035) = 2pi x 109.235. The fractional part 0.235 gives cos(2pi x 0.235) = cos(84.6 deg) = about 0.094, so displacement = 2.0 x 0.094 = about 0.19 cm. (Using the NCERT constants the value is of this order; phase must be taken modulo 2pi.)

questions.q: A pipe 85 cm long, closed at one end, is filled with air (speed of sound 340 m/s). Will it resonate with a tuning fork of frequency 200 Hz? Explain.
questions.a: Fundamental of a closed pipe = v/(4L) = 340/(4 x 0.85) = 100 Hz. A closed pipe resonates only at odd multiples: 100, 300, 500 Hz... 200 Hz is not an odd multiple, so there is no resonance with a 200 Hz fork.

questions.q: Two sitar strings A and B playing the note 'Ga' are slightly out of tune and produce beats of frequency 6 Hz. The tension in string A is slightly reduced and the beat frequency is found to reduce to 3 Hz. If the original frequency of A is 324 Hz, what is the frequency of B?
questions.a: Initially |324 - f_B| = 6, so f_B = 318 or 330 Hz. Reducing tension lowers f_A; beats decrease, so f_A moved closer to f_B, meaning f_B is the lower value: f_B = 318 Hz.

mcqs.q: With the propagation of a longitudinal wave through a medium, the quantity transmitted is:
options: Energy, matter and momentum together as bulk flow
mcqs.why: Particles only oscillate about mean positions; the wave carries energy, not matter.

mcqs.q: The speed of sound in a gas is proportional to:
mcqs.why: v = sqrt(gamma RT/M), so v proportional to sqrt(T).

mcqs.q: In a closed organ pipe, the harmonics present are:
mcqs.why: Closed end is a node and open end an antinode, allowing only odd multiples of the fundamental.

mcqs.q: Beat frequency produced by two notes of frequencies 256 Hz and 262 Hz is:
mcqs.why: Beat frequency = |262 - 256| = 6 Hz.

mcqs.q: The speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string depends on:
options: Tension and mass per unit length
mcqs.why: v = sqrt(T/mu) depends on tension T and linear density mu.

mcqs.q: When a sound wave travels from air into water, which quantity remains the same?
mcqs.why: Frequency is set by the source and does not change across media; speed and wavelength change.

chapters.title: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry
points: Laws of **chemical combination**: **law of conservation of mass** (Lavoisier), **law of definite proportions** (Proust), law of multiple proportions (Dalton), Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes, Avogadro's law.
1 **mole** = 6.022 x 10^23 entities (**Avogadro number**) = **molar mass** in grams. Number of moles n = given mass / molar mass = given particles / N_A.
**Empirical formula** is the simplest whole-number ratio; **molecular formula** = n x empirical formula, where n = **molar mass** / empirical formula mass.
**Percentage composition** = (mass of element / molar mass) x 100. **Limiting reagent** is the reactant consumed first and decides the amount of **product**.
Concentration terms: **molarity** M = moles of solute / litres of solution; **molality** m = moles of solute / kg of solvent; **mole fraction** = moles of component / total moles.
**Stoichiometry** uses the balanced equation's **mole ratio**: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O means 2 mol H2 reacts with 1 mol O2 to give 2 mol **water**.
**Dalton's atomic theory**: **atoms** are indestructible particles of an element; **compounds** form by combining atoms in simple whole-number ratios.
**Precision** means closeness of repeated measurements and **accuracy** means closeness to the true value; **significant figures** are the reliable digits plus one uncertain digit in a measurement.
**Dimensional analysis** uses **conversion factors** to change units; mass per cent, parts per million (**ppm**) and **parts per billion** express very small concentrations.

questions.q: Calculate the molar mass of the following: (i) H2O (ii) CO2 (iii) CH4.
questions.a: (i) 18.02 g/mol, (ii) 44.01 g/mol, (iii) 16.04 g/mol.

questions.q: Calculate the mass per cent of the different elements present in sodium sulphate (Na2SO4).
Calculate the atomic mass (average) of chlorine using: 35Cl (75.77%, 34.9689 amu), 37Cl (24.23%, 36.9659 amu).

Which of the following statements about a compound is INCORRECT: (i) A molecule of a compound has atoms of different elements. (ii) A compound retains the physical properties of its constituent elements. (iii) A compound cannot be separated into its constituent elements by physical methods. (iv) A compound is formed when atoms of different elements combine in a definite ratio.
questions.a: (ii) is incorrect - a compound's properties are entirely different from those of its constituent elements (e.g. NaCl vs Na and Cl).

questions.q: Calculate the amount of carbon dioxide that could be produced when (i) 1 mole of carbon is burnt in air, (ii) 1 mole of carbon is burnt in 16 g of dioxygen, (iii) 2 moles of carbon are burnt in 16 g of dioxygen.
questions.a: C + O2 -> CO2. (i) 1 mol C gives 1 mol CO2 = 44 g. (ii) 16 g O2 = 0.5 mol is limiting, gives 0.5 mol CO2 = 22 g. (iii) 16 g O2 is still limiting, gives 22 g CO2.

questions.q: Determine the empirical formula of an oxide of iron which has 69.9% iron and 30.1% dioxygen by mass.
Calculate the number of atoms in each of the following: (i) 52 moles of Ar (ii) 52 u of He (iii) 52 g of He.
If the density of methanol is 0.793 kg/L, what is its volume needed for making 2.5 L of its 0.25 M solution?
questions.a: Moles needed = 0.25 x 2.5 = 0.625 mol. Mass = 0.625 x 32 = 20 g. Volume = 20 g / 0.793 g/mL = 25.22 mL.

mcqs.q: The number of atoms in 0.1 mol of a triatomic gas is closest to:
Which of the following has the largest number of atoms?
mcqs.why: 1 g Li = 1/6.9 mol gives the most atoms; smaller molar mass means more moles per gram.

mcqs.q: Two substances A (molar mass 60 g/mol) and B (molar mass 90 g/mol) each weigh 10 g. Which has more moles?
mcqs.why: Moles = mass/molar mass; smaller molar mass gives more moles for the same mass.

mcqs.q: The empirical formula of a compound with 40% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O (molar mass 180 g/mol) leads to a molecular formula of:
mcqs.why: Empirical formula is CH2O (mass 30); n = 180/30 = 6, giving C6H12O6.

mcqs.q: In the reaction 4NH3 + 5O2 -> 4NO + 6H2O, when 1 mol NH3 and 1 mol O2 react, the limiting reagent is:
mcqs.why: 1 mol NH3 needs 1.25 mol O2, but only 1 mol O2 is present, so O2 is limiting.

mcqs.q: Molarity of a solution containing 5.85 g NaCl in 500 mL of solution is:
mcqs.why: Moles = 5.85/58.5 = 0.1 mol in 0.5 L, so M = 0.2 mol/L.

chapters.title: Structure of Atom
points: Discovery: **electron** by Thomson (cathode rays, e/m measured), **proton** by Goldstein (anode rays), **neutron** by Chadwick (1932) using **alpha particles** on beryllium.
Rutherford's **alpha-scattering experiment**: atom has a tiny dense positive **nucleus**; most **mass** is in the nucleus, most of the atom is empty space. Limitation: cannot explain stability.
Bohr's model: electrons revolve in fixed **orbits** with **angular momentum** mvr = n h/(2pi). Energy of nth orbit for H: E_n = -13.6 / n^2 eV. Radius r_n = 0.529 x n^2 Angstrom for H.
Bohr's model fails for **multi-electron atoms** and cannot explain spectral line splitting in magnetic fields (**Zeeman effect**) or electric fields (**Stark effect**).
de Broglie: every particle has **wavelength** lambda = h/(mv). **Heisenberg uncertainty principle**: delta x x delta p >= h/(4pi) - **position** and momentum cannot both be known exactly.
**Quantum numbers**: n (**principal**: size/energy), l (azimuthal: shape of subshell, 0 to n-1), m (magnetic: orientation, -l to +l), s (**spin**: +1/2 or -1/2).

**Aufbau principle** (fill increasing n+l), **Pauli exclusion principle** (no two electrons share all 4 quantum numbers), **Hund's rule** (degenerate orbitals fill singly first). s, p, d, f subshells hold 2, 6, 10, 14 electrons.
Half-filled and fully filled subshells are extra stable: **chromium** is [Ar] 3d^5 4s^1 and **copper** is [Ar] 3d^10 4s^1 instead of the expected **configurations**.
