**Photoelectric effect**: light of frequency above the **threshold frequency** ejects electrons; **work function** W0 = h nu0 and Einstein's equation is h nu = W0 + (1/2)mv^2.

**Electromagnetic spectrum** runs from radio waves to gamma rays with c = nu x lambda; **Planck's quantum theory** gives photon energy E = h nu, and the **Rydberg formula** predicts hydrogen spectral lines.

questions.q: Calculate the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in the bromine isotope 80Br35.
questions.a: Protons = 35, electrons = 35 (neutral atom), neutrons = 80 - 35 = 45.

questions.q: The longest wavelength doublet absorption transition is observed at 589 and 589.6 nm. Calculate the frequency of each transition and the energy difference between the two excited states.
questions.a: nu1 = c/lambda1 = 5.093 x 10^14 s^-1; nu2 = 5.088 x 10^14 s^-1. Energy difference = h(nu1 - nu2) = about 3.3 x 10^-22 J.

questions.q: Electrons are emitted with zero velocity from a metal surface when it is exposed to radiation of wavelength 6800 Angstrom. Calculate the threshold frequency and the work function of the metal.
questions.a: Threshold frequency nu0 = c/lambda = 3 x 10^8/6800 x 10^-10 = 4.41 x 10^14 s^-1. Work function W0 = h nu0 = about 2.92 x 10^-19 J.

questions.q: Which of the following statements in relation to the hydrogen atom is correct: (i) 3s, 3p and 3d orbitals all have the same energy, (ii) 3s and 3p orbitals are of lower energy than 3d orbital, (iii) 3p orbital is lower in energy than 3d orbital, (iv) 3s orbital is lower in energy than 3p orbital.
questions.a: (i) In hydrogen, which has only one electron, the energy depends only on the principal quantum number n.

questions.q: Calculate the wavelength of an electron moving with a velocity of 2.05 x 10^7 m/s.
What is the total number of orbitals associated with the principal quantum number n = 3?
questions.a: Number of orbitals = n^2 = 9 (one 3s, three 3p and five 3d orbitals).

questions.q: Calculate the wavelength for the transition from n = 4 to n = 2 in the hydrogen atom (Rydberg constant = 1.09677 x 10^7 m^-1).
Calculate the energy of a photon of light of wavelength 400 nm.

mcqs.q: The total number of orbitals in a shell with principal quantum number n is:
mcqs.why: Orbitals per shell = n^2; electrons per shell = 2n^2.

mcqs.q: For an electron with l = 2, the possible values of m are:
mcqs.why: m takes 2l+1 values from -l to +l, i.e. 5 values for l = 2 (d subshell).

mcqs.q: The configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1 belongs to:
mcqs.why: Total electrons = 11, which is sodium.

mcqs.q: Which set of quantum numbers is NOT possible?
mcqs.why: l must be less than n; l = 2 is impossible for n = 2.

mcqs.q: The de Broglie wavelength of a particle doubles when its:
mcqs.why: lambda = h/(mv) = h/p, so halving momentum doubles the wavelength.

mcqs.q: In the hydrogen spectrum, the Balmer series lies in the:
mcqs.why: Balmer transitions end at n = 2 and fall in the visible region.

chapters.title: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
points: **Modern periodic law**: properties of elements are periodic functions of their **atomic numbers** (Moseley). **Periodicity** is the repetition of similar properties at regular intervals.
Long form of the **periodic table**: 7 **periods** (rows) and 18 **groups** (columns). Blocks: s (groups 1-2), p (13-18), d (transition metals), f (lanthanides/actinides).
**Atomic radius** decreases across a period (increasing **effective nuclear charge** pulls electrons in) and increases down a group (new **shells** are added).

**Ionisation enthalpy**: energy to remove an electron; increases across a period, decreases down a group. **Beryllium** and **nitrogen** are higher than expected due to stable filled/half-filled subshells.

**Electron gain enthalpy**: energy released on adding an electron; generally increases across a period; **chlorine** has the highest (more than **fluorine** because F is very small and electron repulsion offsets attraction).
**Electronegativity**: tendency to attract shared electrons; increases across a period, decreases down a group; **fluorine** is the most **electronegative** element.
**Diagonal relationship**: Li resembles Mg, Be resembles Al (similar **charge density**) because **trends** oppose each other across and down.

**Screening effect** of inner electrons reduces the **effective nuclear charge** Zeff felt by valence electrons; **valency** and oxidation states vary periodically, with maximum oxidation state often equal to group number for s and p block elements.

**Metallic character** decreases across a period and increases down a group, while **non-metallic character** shows the opposite trend; oxides change from **basic** through amphoteric to acidic across a period.

questions.q: What is the basic theme of organisation in the periodic table?
questions.a: To simplify and systematise the study of elements and their compounds: elements with similar properties recur at regular intervals, so the properties are periodic functions of atomic number.

questions.q: Write the atomic number of the element present in the third period and seventeenth group of the periodic table.
questions.a: 17 - it is chlorine.

questions.q: Among the second period elements the actual ionisation enthalpies are in the order Li < B < Be < C < O < N < F < Ne. Explain why (i) Be has higher ionisation enthalpy than B, and (ii) O has lower ionisation enthalpy than N and F.
questions.a: (i) Be loses its 2s electron, which penetrates closer to the nucleus; B loses a 2p electron, which is higher in energy. (ii) N has a stable half-filled 2p^3 configuration, so removing an electron costs more; O loses one electron to reach that stable half-filled arrangement. F has the highest effective nuclear charge of the three.

questions.q: Consider the isoelectronic species Na+, Mg2+, F- and O2-. The correct order of increasing radii is: (i) F- < O2- < Mg2+ < Na+ (ii) Mg2+ < Na+ < F- < O2- (iii) O2- < F- < Na+ < Mg2+ (iv) O2- < F- < Mg2+ < Na+
questions.a: (ii) Mg2+ < Na+ < F- < O2-. All have 10 electrons; higher nuclear charge pulls the same electron cloud in more strongly.

questions.q: Write the general outer electronic configuration of s, p, d and f block elements.
questions.a: s-block: ns^1-2, p-block: ns^2 np^1-6, d-block: (n-1)d^1-10 ns^0-2, f-block: (n-2)f^1-14 (n-1)d^0-1 ns^2.

questions.q: Write the group, period and block for the elements with atomic numbers 19, 29 and 33.
questions.a: 19 (K): group 1, period 4, s-block. 29 (Cu): group 11, period 4, d-block. 33 (As): group 15, period 4, p-block.

questions.q: Predict the formulas of the stable binary compounds formed by (i) silicon and oxygen, (ii) magnesium and fluorine.
questions.a: (i) Si is group 14 (valency 4) and O is divalent, giving SiO2. (ii) Mg is group 2 (+2) and F is group 17 (-1), giving MgF2.

questions.q: Would you expect the second electron gain enthalpy of oxygen to be positive, more negative or less negative than the first? Justify your answer.
questions.a: Positive (endothermic). Adding a second electron to the already negative O- ion faces strong repulsion, so energy must be supplied to overcome it.

mcqs.q: The element with atomic number 26 belongs to which block?
mcqs.why: Z = 26 is iron, [Ar] 3d6 4s2, a d-block transition element.

mcqs.q: Which of the following pairs has the same number of electrons in the outermost shell?
mcqs.why: C and Si are both group 14 elements with 4 valence electrons.

mcqs.q: Atomic radius generally increases down a group because:
options: New shells are added and shielding increases
mcqs.why: Each step down adds a shell and inner electrons shield the nuclear pull.

mcqs.q: The most electronegative element in the periodic table is:
mcqs.why: Fluorine has the highest electronegativity (4.0 on the Pauling scale).

mcqs.q: Which ion has the smallest radius among the isoelectronic series O2-, F-, Na+, Mg2+?
mcqs.why: All have 10 electrons; Mg2+ has the highest nuclear charge (12), pulling the cloud in most.

mcqs.q: Ionisation enthalpy across a period generally increases because:
mcqs.why: Zeff rises across a period while the shell stays the same, holding electrons tighter.

chapters.title: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
points: **Ionic bond**: complete **electron transfer** from metal to non-metal; **lattice energy** holds the crystal (e.g. NaCl). Conducts electricity only in molten/aqueous state.
**Covalent bond**: electron sharing; formed by **orbital overlap** - **sigma bonds** (axial overlap, stronger) and **pi bonds** (sideways overlap).

**VSEPR theory**: electron pairs arrange to minimise **repulsion**; lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bond pair > bond pair-bond pair repulsion. Shapes: linear (2 bp), trigonal planar (3), tetrahedral (4), e.g. NH3 is **pyramidal** and H2O is bent due to lone pairs.
**Hybridisation**: **sp** (linear, 180 deg, e.g. CO2), **sp2** (trigonal planar, 120 deg, e.g. BF3), **sp3** (tetrahedral, 109.5 deg, e.g. CH4).
**Molecular orbital theory**: **bonding MOs** lower energy, **antibonding MOs** raise it; **bond order** = (N_b - N_a)/2. Bond order zero means no stable molecule.

**Dipole moment** measures bond **polarity**; molecules with symmetric shapes (CO2, CCl4) have zero net dipole. **Hydrogen bonding** (H bonded to F, O, N) gives water and ice their special properties.
**Resonance**: delocalised electrons shown by multiple **Lewis structures** (e.g. benzene, O3); the true structure is a **resonance hybrid** with bond lengths between single and double.
**Octet rule** and its limitations: electron-deficient **BF3**, odd-electron NO, and expanded-octet **PCl5** and SF6 do not obey it; **formal charge** helps choose the best Lewis structure.

**Bond enthalpy**, **bond length** and **bond angle** describe a covalent bond: stronger bonds are shorter, and bond strength increases in the order single < double < triple for the same pair of atoms.

questions.q: Explain the formation of a chemical bond.
questions.a: A chemical bond is the attractive force that holds atoms together in a molecule. Atoms combine to form molecules because the energy of the system is lower (more stable) when they are bonded than when the atoms are far apart.

questions.q: Explain why the BeH2 molecule has a zero dipole moment although the Be-H bonds are polar.
questions.a: BeH2 is linear: the two equal and opposite Be-H bond dipoles cancel each other exactly, giving zero net dipole moment.

questions.q: Although both CO2 and H2O are triatomic molecules, the shape of H2O is bent while that of CO2 is linear. Explain this on the basis of dipole moment.
questions.a: CO2 has zero dipole moment, so its two bond moments cancel - the molecule must be linear. H2O has a net dipole moment of 1.85 D, so its bond moments do not cancel - the molecule is bent.

questions.q: Isostructural species are those which have the same shape and hybridisation. Among the given species, identify the isostructural pair: (a) NF3 and BF3 (b) BF4- and NH4+ (c) BCl3 and BrCl3 (d) NH3 and NO3-
questions.a: (b) BF4- and NH4+: both are tetrahedral.

questions.q: Write the Lewis structures for H2S and SiCl4.
questions.a: H2S: S at the centre with two S-H bonds and two lone pairs (bent shape). SiCl4: Si at the centre with four Si-Cl single bonds and no lone pair on Si (tetrahedral).

questions.q: Using Lewis symbols, show the formation of NaCl from sodium and chlorine atoms.
questions.a: Na (2,8,1) loses its valence electron to become Na+ (2,8) and Cl (2,8,7) gains it to become Cl- (2,8,8); the oppositely charged ions attract to form NaCl.

questions.q: Although the geometries of NH3 and H2O molecules are both distorted tetrahedral, the bond angle in water is less than that in ammonia. Discuss.
questions.a: NH3 has one lone pair (bond angle 107 deg) while H2O has two lone pairs (bond angle 104.5 deg). Lone pair-lone pair repulsion in water is stronger, pushing the O-H bonds closer together.

questions.q: Use molecular orbital theory to predict the bond order and magnetic behaviour of O2, O2+ and O2-.
questions.a: Bond order: O2 = 2, O2+ = 2.5, O2- = 1.5. All three have unpaired electrons in pi* orbitals and are paramagnetic; stability increases with bond order: O2+ > O2 > O2-.

mcqs.q: The shape and hybridisation of BF3 are:
mcqs.why: B has 3 bond pairs and no lone pair: trigonal planar, sp2.

mcqs.q: Which molecule has a net dipole moment of zero?
mcqs.why: BF3 is symmetric trigonal planar, so its three bond dipoles cancel.

mcqs.q: The bond order of the O2 molecule according to MOT is:
mcqs.why: Bond order = (10 - 6)/2 = 2 for O2.

mcqs.q: In NH3, the H-N-H bond angle is about:
mcqs.why: One lone pair compresses the tetrahedral angle to about 107 deg.

mcqs.q: Which of the following contains a coordinate (dative) bond?
mcqs.why: In NH4+, nitrogen donates its lone pair to H+ forming a coordinate bond.

mcqs.q: Hydrogen bonding is strongest in:
mcqs.why: F is the smallest and most electronegative, so HF shows the strongest H-bonding.

chapters.title: Thermodynamics
points: System types: **open** (exchanges matter and energy), **closed** (energy only), **isolated** (neither). **State functions** (U, H, S, G) depend only on the state, not the path; heat and work are path functions.
First law: **delta U** = q + w (chemistry sign convention: work done ON the system is positive). **Enthalpy** H = U + PV; at constant pressure **delta H** = q_p.
Enthalpy changes: **delta_f H** (formation), **delta_c H** (combustion), **Hess's law** (delta H of a reaction is the sum of delta H of its steps, independent of path).
**Bond enthalpies** estimate delta H: sum of (**bonds broken**) minus sum of (**bonds formed**).
**Entropy** S measures disorder; delta S = q_rev / T. **Spontaneous processes** increase total entropy of the **universe**.
**Gibbs free energy**: delta G = delta H - T delta S. Reaction is **spontaneous** when delta G < 0; at **equilibrium** delta G = 0 and delta G0 = -RT ln K.
A reaction is always spontaneous when **delta H** < 0 and **delta S** > 0; it becomes spontaneous at high temperature when delta H > 0 and delta S > 0 (T > delta H / delta S).

**Extensive properties** (mass, volume, U, H) depend on amount of matter, while **intensive properties** (temperature, pressure, density) do not; **reversible processes** proceed through equilibrium states, **irreversible processes** do not.

**Enthalpy of neutralisation** for a strong acid and strong base is about -57.1 kJ/mol; **lattice enthalpy** and **enthalpy of solution** are linked through a Born-Haber type cycle and **enthalpy of hydration**.

questions.q: Choose the correct answer. A thermodynamic state function is a quantity: (i) used to determine heat changes (ii) whose value is independent of path (iii) used to determine pressure-volume work (iv) whose value depends on temperature only.
questions.a: (ii) A state function depends only on the initial and final states, not on the path taken.

questions.q: For a process to occur under adiabatic conditions, the correct condition is: (i) delta T = 0 (ii) delta p = 0 (iii) q = 0 (iv) w = 0
questions.a: (iii) q = 0 - no heat enters or leaves the system.

questions.q: Enthalpies of formation of CO(g), CO2(g), N2O(g) and N2O4(g) are -110, -393, 81 and 9.7 kJ/mol respectively. Find the value of delta_rH for: N2O4(g) + 3CO(g) -> N2O(g) + 3CO2(g).

Thermodynamics is not concerned about: (i) energy changes involved in a chemical reaction, (ii) the extent to which a chemical reaction proceeds, (iii) the rate at which a reaction proceeds, (iv) the feasibility of a chemical reaction.
questions.a: (iii) Thermodynamics says nothing about how fast a reaction happens - that is the domain of chemical kinetics.

questions.q: The reaction of cyanamide, NH2CN(s) + 3/2 O2(g) -> N2(g) + CO2(g) + H2O(l), has delta U = -742.7 kJ/mol at 298 K. Calculate delta H for the reaction (R = 8.314 J/K/mol).
Calculate the enthalpy change for H2(g) + Cl2(g) -> 2HCl(g) using bond enthalpies: H-H = 435, Cl-Cl = 242, H-Cl = 431 kJ/mol.
Calculate the standard enthalpy of formation of CH4(g) from: delta_c H0 CH4 = -890.3, delta_f H0 CO2 = -393.5, delta_f H0 H2O = -285.8 kJ/mol.
For an isothermal free expansion of an ideal gas into vacuum, state the values of w, q and delta U.
questions.a: w = 0 (no external pressure to work against), q = 0 and delta U = 0, from the first law delta U = q + w for an isothermal change of an ideal gas.

mcqs.q: For a spontaneous process at constant T and P, delta G must be:
mcqs.why: delta G < 0 is the criterion for spontaneity at constant T and P.

mcqs.q: In an adiabatic process, which quantity is zero?
mcqs.why: Adiabatic means no heat exchange, so q = 0.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an intensive property?
mcqs.why: Density does not depend on the amount of substance.

mcqs.q: If delta H > 0 and delta S > 0, the reaction is spontaneous:
mcqs.why: delta G = delta H - T delta S becomes negative only when T is large enough.

mcqs.q: Hess's law is based on:
mcqs.why: Hess's law follows because enthalpy is a state function, a consequence of the first law.

mcqs.q: The enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state is taken as:
mcqs.why: By convention delta_f H0 of an element in its standard state is zero.

chapters.title: Equilibrium
points: **Dynamic equilibrium**: forward and reverse **rates** are equal; **concentrations** stay constant though reactions continue (e.g. in a closed vessel H2 + I2 <=> 2HI).
Law of **mass action**: for aA + bB <=> cC + dD, **K_c** = [C]^c [D]^d / ([A]^a [B]^b). K_p uses **partial pressures**; K_p = K_c (RT)^(delta n).
**Reaction quotient** Q compares with K: if **Q < K** the reaction moves forward; if **Q > K** it moves backward; Q = K at equilibrium.

**Le Chatelier's principle**: a system at equilibrium shifts to oppose any change - increasing reactant **concentration**, **pressure** (towards fewer gas moles), or lowering temperature for exothermic reactions favours products.
Acids donate H+ (**Bronsted-Lowry**) or accept electron pairs (**Lewis**); **conjugate acid-base pairs** differ by one H+. Water is **amphiprotic**.
**pH** = -log [H+]; **pOH** = -log [OH-]; at 25 deg C pH + pOH = 14 and **K_w** = 10^-14. Buffer solutions resist pH change (weak acid + its salt, or weak base + its salt).
**Solubility product** K_sp: for a sparingly soluble salt, **precipitation** occurs when the **ionic product** exceeds K_sp (common ion effect lowers solubility).

**Henderson-Hasselbalch equation**: pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]) for an **acidic buffer** and pOH = pKb + log([salt]/[base]) for a **basic buffer**; degree of ionisation of weak electrolytes follows **Ostwald's dilution law**.

**Hydrolysis** of salts: salts of weak acid and strong base give **alkaline** solutions, salts of strong acid and weak base give **acidic** solutions, and salts of strong acid and strong base are neutral.

questions.q: A liquid is in equilibrium with its vapour in a sealed container at a fixed temperature. The volume of the container is suddenly increased. (a) What is the initial effect on vapour pressure? (b) How do the rates of evaporation and condensation change initially? (c) What happens when equilibrium is restored finally, and what will be the final vapour pressure?
questions.a: (a) Vapour pressure falls initially as the same vapour spreads over a larger volume. (b) Evaporation increases and condensation decreases. (c) More liquid evaporates until equilibrium is restored; the final vapour pressure equals the original value, since it depends only on temperature.

questions.q: The pH of a sample of vinegar is 3.76. Calculate the concentration of hydrogen ions in it.
The ionisation constants of HF, HCOOH and HCN at 298 K are 6.8 x 10^-4, 1.8 x 10^-4 and 4.8 x 10^-9 respectively. Calculate the ionisation constants of their conjugate bases.
For the reaction H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g), the standard free energy change delta G0 is greater than zero. The equilibrium constant K would be: (i) K = 0 (ii) K > 1 (iii) K = 1 (iv) K < 1
questions.a: (iv) K < 1, since delta G0 = -RT ln K; a positive delta G0 means ln K is negative.

questions.q: At 450 K, Kp for 2SO2(g) + O2(g) <=> 2SO3(g) is 2.0 x 10^10 bar^-1. Calculate Kc at this temperature (R = 0.0831 L bar/K/mol).
questions.a: delta n = 2 - 3 = -1. Kc = Kp (RT)^(-delta n) in consistent form gives Kc = Kp x RT = 2.0 x 10^10 x 0.0831 x 450 = 7.48 x 10^11 M^-1.

questions.q: The ionisation constant of acetic acid is 1.74 x 10^-5. Calculate the degree of ionisation of 0.05 M acetic acid.
The solubility product of silver chloride, AgCl, is 1.6 x 10^-10 at 298 K. Calculate its solubility in mol/L and in g/L (molar mass AgCl = 143.5 g/mol).
Calculate the pH of a buffer solution containing 0.10 M acetic acid and 0.10 M sodium acetate (Ka of acetic acid = 1.8 x 10^-5).

mcqs.q: For the reaction N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3, Kp and Kc are related by:
mcqs.why: delta n = 2 - 4 = -2, so Kp = Kc (RT)^-2.

mcqs.q: Increasing pressure on the equilibrium N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3 (exothermic) at constant temperature shifts it:
mcqs.why: The forward direction has fewer gas moles (2 vs 4), so pressure favours NH3 formation.

mcqs.q: The pH of a 0.001 M HCl solution is:
mcqs.why: pH = -log(10^-3) = 3 for a fully dissociated strong acid.

mcqs.q: A buffer solution is made from a weak acid and:
options: Its salt with a strong base
Its salt with a weak base
mcqs.why: An acidic buffer is a weak acid plus its conjugate salt with a strong base.

mcqs.q: If Q > K for a reaction at a given temperature, the reaction proceeds:
mcqs.why: Q > K means products are in excess, so the net reaction runs in reverse.

mcqs.q: The conjugate base of H2PO4- is:
mcqs.why: Removing one H+ from H2PO4- gives its conjugate base HPO4^2-.

chapters.title: Redox Reactions
points: **Oxidation** = loss of electrons (increase in **oxidation number**); **reduction** = gain of electrons (decrease in oxidation number). They always occur together in a **redox reaction**.

**Oxidation number rules**: free elements 0; Group 1 metals +1; Group 2 +2; F -1; O usually -2 (except -1 in **peroxides**, +2 in OF2); H usually +1 (except -1 in metal **hydrides**). Sum of oxidation numbers equals the **charge** of the species.
**Oxidising agents** accept electrons (get reduced): e.g. KMnO4, K2Cr2O7. **Reducing agents** donate electrons (get oxidised): e.g. metals, H2, C as **electron donors**.

Balancing redox reactions: **ion-electron method** (**half-reaction method**) - split into oxidation and reduction halves, balance atoms (O with H2O, H with H+ in acidic medium), balance charge with electrons, then combine.
**Disproportionation**: the same element is both oxidised and reduced (e.g. Cl2 + 2NaOH -> NaCl + NaOCl + H2O; here **chlorine** goes from 0 to -1 and +1 in **products**).
**Electrochemical series**: metals above **hydrogen** displace H2 from acids; a metal higher in the series displaces one below it from its **salt solution** through a **displacement reaction**.

**Standard electrode potential** E0 measures tendency to be reduced; a more negative E0 means a stronger **reducing agent**, and **fluorine** is the strongest oxidising agent while lithium is the strongest reducing agent in aqueous solution.
Types of redox reactions: **combination**, **decomposition** and **disproportionation**; in a **metal displacement** reaction a more reactive metal replaces a less reactive one from its compound.

questions.q: Assign the oxidation number to Mn in K2MnO4.
questions.a: Let it be x: 2(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0 gives x = +6.

questions.q: Consider the elements Cs, Ne, I and F. (a) Identify the element that exhibits only negative oxidation state. (b) The element that exhibits only positive oxidation state. (c) The element that exhibits both positive and negative oxidation states. (d) The element which exhibits neither negative nor positive oxidation state.
questions.a: (a) F (b) Cs (c) I (d) Ne.

questions.q: The compound AgF2 is unstable. However, if formed, it acts as a very strong oxidising agent. Why?
questions.a: Ag(II) is unstable and readily gains one electron to become the stable Ag(I); the strong tendency to be reduced makes AgF2 a powerful oxidising agent.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an example of a redox reaction: (i) CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O (ii) Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2 (iii) 2K + F2 -> 2KF (iv) BaCl2 + H2SO4 -> BaSO4 + 2HCl
questions.a: (iv) - it is a double displacement (precipitation) reaction with no change in oxidation numbers.

questions.q: Assign oxidation numbers to the underlined elements: (i) S in H2S2O7 (ii) Os in OsO4 (iii) Cr in CrO5.
questions.a: (i) 2(+1) + 2x + 7(-2) = 0 gives S = +6. (ii) x + 4(-2) = 0 gives Os = +8. (iii) CrO5 has four peroxide oxygens (-1 each) and one oxo oxygen (-2), so x - 4 - 2 = 0 gives Cr = +6.

questions.q: Identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent in: 3Fe(s) + 4H2O(g) -> Fe3O4(s) + 4H2(g).
questions.a: Fe is oxidised (0 to about +8/3 in Fe3O4), so Fe is the reducing agent. H in H2O is reduced (+1 to 0), so H2O is the oxidising agent.

questions.q: Balance the redox reaction by the ion-electron method in acidic medium: MnO4- + I- -> Mn2+ + I2.
questions.a: 2MnO4- + 10I- + 16H+ -> 2Mn2+ + 8H2O + 5I2. Reduction: MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- -> Mn2+ + 4H2O (x2); oxidation: 2I- -> I2 + 2e- (x5).

questions.q: Given E0(Cu2+/Cu) = +0.34 V and E0(Ni2+/Ni) = -0.25 V, will nickel displace copper from a copper sulphate solution? Justify.
questions.a: Yes. E0cell = 0.34 - (-0.25) = +0.59 V, which is positive, so Ni + Cu2+ -> Ni2+ + Cu is spontaneous.

mcqs.q: The oxidation number of sulphur in Na2S4O6 (sodium tetrathionate) is:
mcqs.why: 2(+1) + 4x + 6(-2) = 0 gives 4x = 10, so the average oxidation number is +2.5.

mcqs.q: In the reaction Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu, the oxidising agent is:
mcqs.why: Cu2+ gains electrons (is reduced), so Cu2+ is the oxidising agent.

mcqs.q: Which reaction is a disproportionation?
mcqs.why: In H2O2, oxygen (-1) is both oxidised to 0 in O2 and reduced to -2 in H2O.

mcqs.q: The oxidation number of oxygen in KO2 (potassium superoxide) is:
mcqs.why: K is +1, so O2- overall is -1 and each oxygen is -1/2 in the superoxide ion.

mcqs.q: A reducing agent in a reaction:
mcqs.why: A reducing agent donates electrons and is itself oxidised.

chapters.title: Organic Chemistry - Some Basic Principles and Techniques
points: **Tetravalency** of carbon (Kekule) and **catenation**: carbon forms 4 **covalent bonds** and long chains, giving millions of organic compounds.
**Functional groups** decide a compound's chemistry: -OH (**alcohol**), -CHO (aldehyde), -CO- (ketone), -COOH (**carboxylic acid**), -NH2 (amine), -X (halide).

**IUPAC naming**: choose the longest chain containing the principal **functional group**, number to give it the lowest **locant**; prefixes for **substituents** in alphabetical order (e.g. 2-methylbutane).
**Structural isomerism**: chain (butane vs 2-methylpropane), position (1-propanol vs 2-propanol), functional (ethanol vs dimethyl ether), **metamerism**, **tautomerism** (keto-enol).
Electronic effects: **inductive effect** (electronegativity-based, permanent), **electromeric effect** (temporary, on attack), **resonance**/mesomeric effect (delocalisation), hyperconjugation.
**Carbocation stability**: 3 deg > 2 deg > 1 deg (**hyperconjugation** + inductive); **carbanion stability** is the reverse. Free radicals follow carbocation order.
**Purification**: **distillation** (liquids), fractional distillation, **crystallisation** (solids), chromatography, sublimation (e.g. camphor), steam distillation for steam-volatile compounds.
Qualitative analysis: **Lassaigne's test** - N gives Prussian blue, S gives violet with nitroprusside, halogens give AgX precipitate. Quantitative: **Kjeldahl** (N), **Carius** (halogen/S).

**Homolytic fission** gives free radicals and **heterolytic fission** gives carbocations or carbanions; **electrophiles** are electron-seeking reagents and **nucleophiles** are nucleus-seeking (electron-rich) reagents.

**Steric hindrance** and **stereoisomerism**: geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism arises from restricted rotation about C=C, and **optical isomerism** arises from a chiral carbon with four different groups.

questions.q: What are the hybridisation states of each carbon atom in CH2=C=O?
questions.a: The CH2 carbon is sp2 hybridised (two sigma bonds + one pi); the central carbon joined to C and O is sp hybridised.

questions.q: Indicate the sigma and pi bonds in CH2=C=CH2 (allene).
questions.a: 4 C-H sigma + 2 C-C sigma = 6 sigma bonds; 2 pi bonds (one on each C=C).

questions.q: Explain the terms inductive and electromeric effects. Which electron displacement effect explains the correct acidity order: Cl3CCOOH > Cl2CHCOOH > ClCH2COOH?
questions.a: The inductive effect is the permanent polarisation of sigma bonds by electronegative atoms; the electromeric effect is a temporary shift of pi electrons under attack by a reagent. The -I effect of the Cl atoms explains the acidity order - more Cl atoms pull electron density away and stabilise the carboxylate ion.

questions.q: The principle involved in paper chromatography is: (i) adsorption (ii) partition (iii) solubility (iv) volatility
questions.a: (ii) Partition - the components distribute between the stationary (water held on paper) and mobile phases.

questions.q: Draw the resonance structures of the acetate ion, CH3COO-, and explain why both C-O bond lengths are equal.
questions.a: Two equivalent structures with the negative charge and double bond exchanged between the two oxygens. The true structure is the resonance hybrid, so both C-O bonds are identical, intermediate between single and double.

questions.q: Classify the following as electrophiles or nucleophiles: CH3+, NH3, NO2+, OH-.
questions.a: Electrophiles (electron-deficient): CH3+ and NO2+. Nucleophiles (electron-rich): NH3 (lone pair on N) and OH-.

questions.q: Write the IUPAC name of the compound (CH3)2CH-CH2-C(CH3)3.
questions.a: The longest chain has 5 carbons with methyl groups at positions 2, 2 and 4: 2,2,4-trimethylpentane.

questions.q: Explain hyperconjugation and use it to explain the stability order of ethyl, isopropyl and tert-butyl carbocations.
questions.a: Hyperconjugation is delocalisation of sigma electrons of a C-H bond (on the carbon adjacent to the positive centre) into the empty p orbital. More alpha-hydrogens give more hyperconjugative structures: tert-butyl (9) > isopropyl (6) > ethyl (3), so stability increases in that order.

mcqs.q: The IUPAC name of CH3-CH(OH)-CH3 is:
mcqs.why: Three-carbon chain with -OH on carbon 2: propan-2-ol.

mcqs.q: Which carbocation is the most stable?
mcqs.why: Maximum hyperconjugation and +I effect stabilise the tertiary carbocation most.

mcqs.q: Lassaigne's test for nitrogen gives which colour on adding FeSO4 and FeCl3 followed by acid?
mcqs.why: Sodium cyanide formed in the extract gives ferric ferrocyanide, Prussian blue.

mcqs.q: The -I effect (electron-withdrawing inductive effect) is strongest for:
mcqs.why: Fluorine is the most electronegative, so -F exerts the strongest -I effect.

mcqs.q: Paper chromatography is based on the principle of:
mcqs.why: Components partition between the stationary water phase on paper and the mobile phase.

mcqs.why: Kjeldahl's method converts organic nitrogen to ammonia, which is measured volumetrically.

chapters.title: Hydrocarbons
points: **Alkanes** (CnH2n+2): saturated, sp3. Preparation: hydrogenation of alkenes/alkynes, **Wurtz reaction** (2RX + 2Na -> R-R), **decarboxylation** of sodium salts (soda lime: RCOONa + NaOH -> RH). Reactions: free-radical halogenation, combustion, pyrolysis/cracking.

**Alkenes** (CnH2n): contain C=C, sp2. Preparation: dehydration of alcohols (conc. H2SO4, **Saytzeff product** major), dehydrohalogenation of alkyl halides. Reactions: **electrophilic addition** - H2, X2, HX (Markovnikov), hydration, ozonolysis.

**Alkynes** (CnH2n-2): C triple C, sp. **Acetylene** from CaC2 + H2O. Terminal alkynes are **acidic** (pKa about 25): RC triple CH + NaNH2 -> salt; gives red precipitate with ammoniacal Cu2Cl2 and white with AgNO3. Hydration gives methyl ketones (Hg2+/H2SO4).

**Benzene**: aromatic, planar hexagon with delocalised pi electrons; **Huckel rule** (4n+2 pi electrons) explains stability. **Electrophilic substitution**: nitration, halogenation (FeX3), sulphonation, Friedel-Crafts alkylation/acylation (AlCl3).
Directing effects: -OH, -NH2, -CH3 are **ortho/para directors** and **activators**; -NO2, -CHO, -COOH are **meta directors** and deactivators (halogens are ortho/para but deactivating).
**Conformations** of ethane: **staggered** is more stable than **eclipsed** (torsional strain); energy difference about 12.5 kJ/mol. Sawhorse and Newman projections show them.
**Markovnikov's rule** explained by the most stable **carbocation intermediate**; **peroxide effect** (Kharasch) reverses it only for HBr addition to alkenes.
**Aromatisation**: n-hexane on heating with **Cr2O3** or MoO3 catalyst gives benzene; **catalytic reforming** converts alkanes to arenes, and coal tar is a major source of **aromatic compounds**.
**Carcinogenicity**: many **polynuclear hydrocarbons** containing fused benzene rings (e.g. benzopyrene in tobacco smoke and coal tar) are **toxic** and carcinogenic.

questions.q: How will you convert ethyne into benzene?
questions.a: Pass ethyne (acetylene) through a red-hot iron tube at 873 K: 3 HC triple-bond CH -> C6H6 (cyclic polymerisation).

questions.q: Write the IUPAC names of the products obtained by the ozonolysis of pent-2-ene.
questions.a: Ethanal (CH3CHO) and propanal (CH3CH2CHO) - the double bond breaks to give one aldehyde from each side.

questions.q: Draw the cis and trans structures of hex-2-ene. Which isomer has the higher boiling point, and why?
questions.a: The cis isomer has the higher boiling point: its dipole moment is larger, giving stronger dipole-dipole attraction than in the nearly non-polar trans form.

questions.q: Arrange the following hydrogen halides in order of their decreasing reactivity with propene: (i) HCl > HBr > HI (ii) HBr > HI > HCl (iii) HI > HBr > HCl (iv) HCl > HI > HBr
questions.a: (iii) HI > HBr > HCl - as the halogen size increases, the H-X bond weakens, so the proton is donated more easily in electrophilic addition.

questions.q: How will you convert propene into (i) propan-2-ol and (ii) propan-1-ol?
questions.a: (i) Acid-catalysed hydration (H2O/H+) follows Markovnikov's rule to give propan-2-ol. (ii) Hydroboration-oxidation (B2H6, then H2O2/OH-) gives the anti-Markovnikov product propan-1-ol.

questions.q: Arrange n-pentane, isopentane (2-methylbutane) and neopentane (2,2-dimethylpropane) in order of decreasing boiling point and explain.
questions.a: n-pentane > isopentane > neopentane. Branching reduces surface area and weakens van der Waals forces, so the straight-chain isomer with the largest contact area boils highest.

questions.q: What happens when benzene is treated with methyl chloride in the presence of anhydrous AlCl3? Name the reaction and the electrophile involved.
questions.a: Friedel-Crafts alkylation: benzene gives toluene (methylbenzene). The electrophile is the methyl carbocation equivalent, CH3+, generated from CH3Cl and AlCl3.

questions.q: Addition of HBr to propene gives 2-bromopropane in the absence of peroxide but 1-bromopropane in its presence. Explain both outcomes.
questions.a: Without peroxide, electrophilic addition through the more stable secondary carbocation gives the Markovnikov product 2-bromopropane. With peroxide, a free-radical chain (Kharasch effect) adds Br first to give the more stable radical at the terminal carbon, yielding 1-bromopropane.

mcqs.why: 2CH3Br + 2Na -> CH3-CH3 + 2NaBr; coupling of two methyl groups gives ethane.

chapters.title: Sets
points: A set is a **well-defined collection** of **distinct objects**. **Roster form** lists elements: A = {1, 2, 3}; **set-builder form** describes them: A = {x : x is a natural number less than 4}.
**Subsets**: A is a **subset** of B if every element of A is in B. A set with n elements has **2^n subsets** and 2^n - 1 **proper subsets**. **Power set** P(A) is the set of all subsets of A.
**Operations**: **union** A u B, **intersection** A n B, **difference** A - B, **complement** A' (elements of the universal set not in A).
**De Morgan's laws**: the complement of a **union** is the intersection of complements: (A u B)' = A' n B'; the complement of an **intersection** is the union of complements: (A n B)' = A' u B'.
**Counting rule**: for **finite sets**, n(A u B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A n B); and n(A u B u C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - n(A n B) - n(B n C) - n(C n A) + n(A n B n C).
**Intervals**: open (a, b), closed [a, b], half-open [a, b). **Empty set** phi has zero elements and is a **subset of every set**.
**Equal sets** have exactly the same elements: {1, 2, 3} = {3, 2, 2, 1} since **order** and **repetition** don't matter. A **singleton set** has exactly one element.
The **universal set** U contains every object under discussion; the **complement** is always taken w.r.t. U. Sets with A n B = phi are **disjoint sets**.

**Symmetric difference** A d B = (A - B) u (B - A) collects elements in exactly one of A, B. **Venn diagrams** draw sets as **overlapping regions** to picture union, intersection and counting arguments.

questions.q: Whether the following is a set or not: (i) The collection of all months of a year beginning with the letter J. (ii) The collection of the ten most talented writers of India.
questions.a: (i) It is a set: January, June, July are well defined. (ii) It is not a set: 'most talented' is not well defined.

questions.q: Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5, 6}. Find A union B.
Let X and Y be sets such that n(X) = 17, n(Y) = 23 and n(X union Y) = 38. Find n(X intersection Y).
questions.a: n(X intersection Y) = 17 + 23 - 38 = 2.

questions.q: Let A and B be two sets. Then A intersection (A union B) is equal to: (A) A (B) B (C) null set (D) A intersection B
questions.a: (A) A. Absorption law: A is a subset of A union B, so the intersection with A is A itself.

questions.q: Which of the following are sets? (i) The collection of all even integers. (ii) The collection of all beautiful flowers in a garden.
questions.a: (i) It is a set: even integers are well defined. (ii) It is not a set: 'beautiful' is subjective, not well defined.

questions.a: A - B = {1, 3, 5}; B - A = {8}. They are not equal: set difference is not commutative.

chapters.title: Relations and Functions
points: An **ordered pair** (a, b) keeps order: (1, 2) != (2, 1). The **Cartesian product** A x B = {(a, b) : a in A, b in B}; if n(A) = p and n(B) = q, then n(A x B) = **pq**.
A **relation** R from A to B is a **subset** of A x B. Its **domain** is the set of first elements; its **range** is the set of second elements.
A **function** f: A -> B assigns each element of A **exactly one** element of B. The **co-domain** is the whole target set B; the **range** is the set of images, a subset of the co-domain.
**Types**: **one-one** (injective: distinct inputs give distinct outputs), **onto** (surjective: range = co-domain), **bijective** (one-one and onto).
**Standard functions**: **identity** f(x) = x; **constant** f(x) = c; **polynomial**; **rational**; **modulus** f(x) = |x|; **signum**; **greatest integer** f(x) = [x].
**Algebra of functions**: (f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x) (**sum**); (fg)(x) = f(x)g(x) (**product**); (f/g)(x) = f(x)/g(x) (**quotient**) where g(x) != 0.
For **finite sets** with n(A) = p and n(B) = q, the number of **relations** from A to B is **2^(pq)** and the number of **functions** is **q^p**.
**Domain restrictions** come from division and roots: f(x) = 1/(x - 2) needs x != 2; f(x) = sqrt(x) needs x >= 0. The **vertical line test** checks whether a graph represents a function.
The **greatest integer function** [x] has **domain** R and **range** Z; its graph is a **step graph**: [2.3] = 2 and [-1.2] = -2.

questions.q: If (x + 1, y - 2) = (3, 1), find the values of x and y.

questions.a: No. P x Q = {(a,r), (b,r), (c,r)} while Q x P = {(r,a), (r,b), (r,c)}; the ordered pairs differ.

questions.q: Find the domain and range of the real function f(x) = sqrt(9 - x^2).
questions.a: Domain: -3 <= x <= 3, i.e. [-3, 3]. Range: [0, 3], since sqrt preserves non-negative values and 9 - x^2 is at most 9.
(D) x can take -2, -1, 0, 1, 2 (x^2 must be at most 8); e.g. x = 2 works with y = +/-1.

questions.a: The polynomial is defined for every real x, so the domain is R (all real numbers).

questions.a: Domain: R - {5}, since the denominator cannot be zero. Range: R - {0}, since 1/(x - 5) can be any non-zero real number.

questions.q: The real function f is defined by f(x) = x^2 for all real x. Is f one-one? Justify.
questions.a: No. f(2) = 4 = f(-2): distinct inputs give the same output, so f is many-one.

chapters.title: Trigonometric Functions
points: An angle in **radians** = arc length / radius; 1 **radian** is approx 57.3 **degrees**. 360 deg = 2pi radians; convert with radians = degrees x pi/180.
**ASTC rule** by quadrant: I (all positive), II (sin positive), III (tan positive), IV (cos positive). **Odd/even**: sin(-x) = -sin x; cos(-x) = cos x; tan(-x) = -tan x.
**Key identities**: sin^2 x + cos^2 x = 1; 1 + tan^2 x = sec^2 x; 1 + cot^2 x = cosec^2 x. These **Pythagorean identities** all follow from the first by dividing by **cos^2 x** or sin^2 x.
**Compound angles**: the **sum formulas** sin(A+B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B; cos(A+B) = cos A cos B - sin A sin B; tan(A+B) = (tan A + tan B)/(1 - tan A tan B).
**Double angles**: sin 2A = 2 sin A cos A; cos 2A = cos^2 A - sin^2 A = 2cos^2 A - 1 = 1 - 2sin^2 A; tan 2A = 2 tan A/(1 - tan^2 A) - these are the **compound-angle** formulas with B = A.
**Product to sum**: these convert **products** of sines and cosines into **sums**: 2 sin A cos B = sin(A+B) + sin(A-B); 2 cos A sin B = sin(A+B) - sin(A-B); also cos^2 A = (1 + cos 2A)/2.
**Sum to product**: these convert **sums** into **products**: sin C + sin D = 2 sin((C+D)/2) cos((C-D)/2); cos C + cos D = 2 cos((C+D)/2) cos((C-D)/2).
**Triple angles**: sin 3A = 3 sin A - 4 sin^3 A; cos 3A = 4 cos^3 A - 3 cos A. **Half-angle** formulas come from the double-angle ones with A replaced by A/2.
sin and cos are **periodic** with **period** 2pi; tan and cot with period pi. Memorise the **standard angles**: sin(pi/6) = 1/2, cos(pi/3) = 1/2, tan(pi/4) = 1.
**Bounds**: a sin x + b cos x lies between -sqrt(a^2 + b^2) and +sqrt(a^2 + b^2) - the **maximum** and **minimum** of the expression.

chapters.title: Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations
points: i = sqrt(-1), with i^2 = -1, i^3 = -i, i^4 = 1. A **complex number** z = a + ib has **real part** a and **imaginary part** b; its **modulus** |z| = sqrt(a^2 + b^2).
The **conjugate** of a + ib is a - ib; z x conjugate(z) = |z|^2. To **divide**, multiply numerator and denominator by the **conjugate** of the denominator.
**Argand plane**: the **real axis** (x) and **imaginary axis** (y); z = a + ib is the point (a, b); |z| is its **distance from the origin**.
**Argument** theta = tan^-1(b/a), adjusted by **quadrant** for the correct angle. **Polar form**: z = r(cos theta + i sin theta), where r = |z|.
**Algebra**: **addition** (a+ib) + (c+id) = (a+c) + i(b+d); **multiplication** (a+ib)(c+id) = (ac - bd) + i(ad + bc).
**Quadratic** ax^2 + bx + c = 0 has roots x = (-b +- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac))/(2a). **Discriminant** D = b^2 - 4ac: D > 0 gives two **real roots**; D = 0 **equal roots**; D < 0 **complex conjugate roots**.
**Sum of roots** = -b/a, **product of roots** = c/a. A quadratic with roots alpha, beta is x^2 - (**sum**)x + (**product**) = 0.
**Modulus rules**: |z1 z2| = |z1| |z2| and |z1/z2| = |z1|/|z2|. **Triangle inequality**: |z1 + z2| <= |z1| + |z2|.
**Square roots of negatives**: sqrt(-a) = i sqrt(a) for a > 0; so x^2 + 1 = 0 gives x = **+-i**. Powers of i repeat every 4: i^(4n+k) = i^k.
z is **purely real** iff z = conjugate(z); z is **purely imaginary** iff z + conjugate(z) = 0.

chapters.title: Linear Inequalities
points: **Inequality rules**: adding/subtracting the same number keeps the **sense**; multiplying/dividing by a **positive number** keeps it, by a **negative number** reverses it.
**Solving** ax + b > 0: e.g. 2x - 6 > 0 gives x > 3. **Solution sets** are **intervals** on the **number line**.
**Quadratic inequalities**: factor and use a **sign chart**. x^2 - 4 > 0 gives x < -2 or x > 2.
**Absolute value**: |x| < a means -a < x < a (x lies **between** -a and a); |x| > a means x < -a or x > a (x lies **outside** that interval).
**Two-variable inequalities** ax + by > c: the **boundary line** ax + by = c divides the plane; **test the origin** to find the **solution half-plane**.
**System of inequalities**: the solution is the **intersection** (common region) of all individual solution sets, found **graphically**.
A **linear inequality in one variable** has the form ax + b > 0 (or <, >=, <=). Its **solution set** is all x satisfying it, drawn on a **number line**.
**Graphical method**: draw the boundary as a **solid line** for >= / <= and a **dotted line** for > / <, then shade the **feasible region** on the correct side.
If the boundary line passes through the origin, the **origin test** fails - test another point like (1, 0) instead. For **strict inequalities** the boundary itself is excluded.

chapters.title: Permutations and Combinations
points: **Fundamental principle of counting**: if one task has m ways and another has n ways, both together have **m x n ways**.
**Factorial**: n! = n(n-1)...2x1; 0! = 1. **Permutations** (order matters): nPr = n!/(n-r)!; **combinations** (order irrelevant): nCr = n!/(r!(n-r)!).
nPr counts **arrangements** (seating, passwords); nCr counts **selections** (committees, teams).
**Key results**: nCr = nC(n-r); nC0 = nCn = 1; nC1 = n; nCr + nC(r-1) = (n+1)Cr (**Pascal's rule**).
**Permutations with repetitions**: n objects with p, q identical among them give n!/(p! q!) distinct **arrangements**.
**Circular arrangements**: (n-1)! ways to seat n distinct objects around a **circle**, since **rotations** are identical.
**Permutations with repetition allowed**: filling r positions from n choices gives **n^r ways**. Note nPr = 0 when r > n.
**Combinations with repetition**: choosing r objects from n types with repeats allowed gives **(n+r-1)Cr ways**.
**Standard models**: the number of **diagonals** of an n-sided polygon = nC2 - n = n(n-3)/2; **handshakes** among n people = nC2.

chapters.title: Binomial Theorem
points: **Binomial theorem**: (a + b)^n = sum over r of nCr a^(n-r) b^r, for r = 0 to n. There are **n+1 terms**.
**General term**: T_(r+1) = nCr a^(n-r) b^r. **Middle term(s)**: if n is even, the ((n/2)+1)th term; if n is odd, two middle terms.
**Coefficients are symmetric**: nCr = nC(n-r). **Sum of all binomial coefficients** = 2^n.
(1 + x)^n = 1 + nx + nC2 x^2 + ...; putting x = 1 and x = -1 gives useful **coefficient sums** and **alternating sums**.
**Greatest binomial coefficient**: for even n it is nC(n/2), the **middle coefficient**; for odd n both nC((n-1)/2) and nC((n+1)/2) tie as the largest.
Putting x = 1 in (1 + x)^n gives nC0 + nC1 + ... + nCn = **2^n**; putting x = -1 gives the **alternating sum** nC0 - nC1 + nC2 - ... = **0**.
The **constant term** (term **independent of x**) is found by setting the **exponent of x** in the general term to zero and solving for r.
(x + a)^n + (x - a)^n keeps only **even-powered** terms; (x + a)^n - (x - a)^n keeps only **odd-powered** terms.

chapters.title: Sequences and Series
points: **Arithmetic progression**: a, a+d, a+2d...; **nth term** a_n = a + (n-1)d; **sum** S_n = (n/2)(2a + (n-1)d) = (n/2)(first + last).
**Geometric progression**: a, ar, ar^2...; **nth term** a_n = a r^(n-1); **sum** S_n = a(r^n - 1)/(r - 1). For |r| < 1, **infinite sum** S_inf = a/(1 - r).
**Arithmetic mean** of a and b: (a+b)/2. **Geometric mean**: sqrt(ab). **AM >= GM** for positive numbers.
**Relation between AM, GM, HM**: AM >= GM >= HM; **GM^2 = AM x HM**.
**Special sums**: sum k = n(n+1)/2 (**first n naturals**); sum k^2 = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 (**squares**); sum k^3 = [n(n+1)/2]^2 (**cubes**).
A series can converge only if its **terms tend to zero** (necessary but not sufficient); the **infinite GP** sum formula needs |r| < 1.
**nth term from sum**: a_n = S_n - S_(n-1), with a_1 = S_1 - recovers terms when only the **partial sums** are known.
**Harmonic progression**: a sequence whose **reciprocals** form an AP. The **harmonic mean** of a and b is 2ab/(a+b).
**Method of differences**: write the general term as a **telescoping difference**; e.g. sum of k(k+1) up to n terms is n(n+1)(n+2)/3.
The **geometric mean** of n numbers is (product)^(1/n). An **infinite GP** with |r| >= 1 **diverges**.

chapters.title: Straight Lines
points: **Slope** m = tan theta = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1), where theta is the angle with the positive x-axis. **Parallel lines** have equal slopes; **perpendicular lines** have m1 x m2 = -1.
**Forms**: **point-slope** y - y1 = m(x - x1); **slope-intercept** y = mx + c; **two-point** form; **intercept form** x/a + y/b = 1; **normal form** x cos alpha + y sin alpha = p.
**General equation**: Ax + By + C = 0 has slope **-A/B** and intercepts **(-C/A, -C/B)**.
**Angle between lines** with slopes m1, m2: tan theta = |(m1 - m2)/(1 + m1 m2)|; theta is taken as the **acute angle** between them.
**Distance** of point (x1, y1) from line Ax + By + C = 0: d = |Ax1 + By1 + C|/sqrt(A^2 + B^2). **Parallel lines** differ only in C.
**Concurrency**: three lines are **concurrent** if they pass through one point; check via **determinants** or by solving two and substituting in the third.
**Intercept form** x/a + y/b = 1 cuts the axes at (a, 0) and (0, b). **Two-point form**: (y - y1) = ((y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1))(x - x1).
**Family of lines** through the intersection of L1 = 0 and L2 = 0 is **L1 + kL2 = 0**. Lines **parallel** to Ax + By + C = 0 are Ax + By + k = 0.

The **foot of the perpendicular** and the **image of a point** in a line are found using the perpendicular slope. **Distance between parallel lines** Ax + By + C1 = 0 and Ax + By + C2 = 0 is |C1 - C2|/sqrt(A^2 + B^2).

chapters.title: Conic Sections
points: **Circle**: (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2. **General form** x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has **centre** (-g, -f) and **radius** sqrt(g^2 + f^2 - c).
**Parabola**: set of points **equidistant** from **focus** and **directrix**; standard form y^2 = 4ax (focus (a, 0), directrix x = -a).
**Ellipse**: x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1 (a > b); **foci** at (+-c, 0) with c^2 = a^2 - b^2; **eccentricity** e = c/a < 1; **latus rectum** = 2b^2/a.
**Hyperbola**: x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1; **foci** at (+-c, 0) with c^2 = a^2 + b^2; e > 1; **asymptotes** y = +- (b/a)x.
**Eccentricity identifies the conic**: e = 0 **circle**, e = 1 **parabola**, 0 < e < 1 **ellipse**, e > 1 **hyperbola**.
**Parametric points**: circle (r cos theta, r sin theta) with **parameter** theta; ellipse (a cos theta, b sin theta) where theta is the **eccentric angle**.
The four **standard parabolas**: y^2 = 4ax (opens right), y^2 = -4ax (left), x^2 = 4ay (up), x^2 = -4ay (down) - **focus** and **directrix** follow the direction of opening.
**Latus rectum** length: 4a for a **parabola**, 2b^2/a for **ellipse** and **hyperbola**. Its endpoints form the **focal chord** perpendicular to the axis.
The **auxiliary circle** of the ellipse x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1 is x^2 + y^2 = a^2. The **eccentric angle** theta gives the point (a cos theta, b sin theta).

chapters.title: Introduction to Three Dimensional Geometry
points: A point in 3D is (x, y, z): x, y, z are **distances** from the YZ, XZ, XY **planes** respectively. The eight **octants** are the 3D analogue of quadrants.
**Distance** between (x1, y1, z1) and (x2, y2, z2): sqrt((x2-x1)^2 + (y2-y1)^2 + (z2-z1)^2) - the 3D **Pythagoras** extension of the **distance formula**.
**Distance from origin** of (x, y, z): sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2). Distance from **coordinate planes**: |x| from YZ, |y| from XZ, |z| from XY.
**Section formula**: the point dividing the join of (x1,y1,z1) and (x2,y2,z2) in ratio m:n is ((mx2+nx1)/(m+n), (my2+ny1)/(m+n), (mz2+nz1)/(m+n)); the **midpoint** uses m = n = 1.
**Centroid** of a triangle with vertices (x1,y1,z1), (x2,y2,z2), (x3,y3,z3) is the **average of the coordinates**.
**Standard points**: the **origin** is (0, 0, 0); a point in the **XY-plane** has z = 0; a point on the **x-axis** has y = z = 0.
The **x-axis** is the intersection of the XZ and XY **planes**. The three **coordinate planes** divide space into 8 **octants**.
**Collinearity test**: three points are **collinear** if the sum of the two smaller **segment distances** equals the largest one.

chapters.title: Limits and Derivatives
points: **Limit**: lim x->a f(x) = L means f(x) approaches L as x approaches a. **Direct substitution** works when the function is **continuous** there.

**Standard limits**: lim x->0 sin x/x = 1; lim x->0 (e^x - 1)/x = 1 (**exponential**); lim x->0 (a^x - 1)/x = ln a (**logarithmic**); lim x->0 (1+x)^(1/x) = e; lim x->a (x^n - a^n)/(x - a) = n a^(n-1).
**Algebra of limits**: the limit of a sum/product/quotient is the sum/product/quotient of the **limits** (denominator not zero). **Factorise** or **rationalise** to remove 0/0 forms.
**Derivative**: f'(x) = lim h->0 [f(x+h) - f(x)]/h (**first principle**). Geometrically it is the **slope of the tangent** at that point.
**Rules**: (x^n)' = n x^(n-1); (u+v)' = u' + v'; (uv)' = u'v + uv' (**product rule**); (u/v)' = (u'v - uv')/v^2 (**quotient rule**); **chain rule** dy/dx = dy/du x du/dx.
**Derivatives of trig functions**: (sin x)' = cos x; (cos x)' = -sin x (note the **minus sign**); (tan x)' = sec^2 x.
**Indeterminate forms**: 0/0 is resolved by **factorisation**, **rationalisation**, or **standard limits**: lim x->0 (1 - cos x)/x = 0 and lim x->0 (1 - cos x)/x^2 = 1/2.
**One-sided limits**: the limit exists only if the **left-hand** and **right-hand** limits are equal. lim x->0 |x|/x does not exist.
More **trig derivatives**: (sec x)' = sec x tan x; (cosec x)' = -cosec x cot x; (cot x)' = -**cosec^2 x**.
The **second derivative** f''(x) measures **concavity**. The derivative of a **constant** is 0, and (ln x)' = **1/x**.

chapters.title: Statistics
points: **Measures of central tendency**: mean, median, mode. **Measures of dispersion**: range, **mean deviation**, variance, **standard deviation**.
**Mean deviation about mean** = (sum |x_i - xbar|)/n; about **median** uses the median in place of the mean.
**Variance** sigma^2 = (sum (x_i - xbar)^2)/n = (sum x_i^2)/n - (xbar)^2. **Standard deviation** sigma = sqrt(variance).
For **grouped data**: mean = sum f_i x_i / sum f_i; **variance** = (sum f_i x_i^2 / N) - (mean)^2.
**Coefficient of variation** CV = (sigma/xbar) x 100: smaller CV means more **consistent** data - used to **compare two series**.
**Standard deviation** is independent of **origin** (shifting data doesn't change it) but scales with **change of scale**: if y = ax + b, sigma_y = |a| sigma_x.
**Median**: for odd n the **middle value**; for even n the average of the two **middle values**. **Mode** is the most frequent value - data may have **no mode** or several.
**Step deviation method**: for grouped data with equal **class width** h, use u_i = (x_i - A)/h about an **assumed mean** A to simplify mean and variance.
**Correcting a wrong observation** changes both **mean** and **variance** - recompute from sum x_i and sum x_i^2 rather than from the old statistics.

questions.q: Find the mean deviation about the mean for the numbers 4, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 17.
questions.a: Mean = 10. Sum of absolute deviations = 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 + 2 + 3 + 7 = 24; mean deviation = 24/8 = 3.

questions.a: (B) 2.57. Mean = 7; absolute deviations 4, 3, 3, 3, 0, 3, 2 sum to 18, and 18/7 = 2.57.

questions.a: Total sum = 7 x 8 = 56; the five sum to 42, so the remaining two sum to 14. Sum of squares = 7(16 + 64) = 560; the five give 460, so the remaining squares sum to 100. With a + b = 14 and a^2 + b^2 = 100, ab = 48, so the observations are 6 and 8.

questions.a: Mean = (n + 1)/2 and variance = (n^2 - 1)/12, so SD = sqrt((n^2 - 1)/12).

chapters.title: Probability
points: **Random experiment**: outcome not predictable in advance. **Sample space** S = set of all possible outcomes; an **event** is a subset of S.
**Probability** of event E: P(E) = n(E)/n(S) for **equally likely outcomes**; 0 <= P(E) <= 1; P(**impossible**) = 0, P(**sure event**) = 1.
**Complement**: P(not E) = 1 - P(E). **Addition rule**: P(A u B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A n B); for **mutually exclusive** events P(A u B) = P(A) + P(B).
**Mutually exclusive** events cannot occur together (A n B = phi); **exhaustive** events cover the whole sample space.
For **two dice**: the sample space has 36 outcomes; P(sum = 7) = 6/36 = 1/6; P(**doublet**) = 6/36 = 1/6.
P(**at least one**) = 1 - P(none) is often the fastest route in '**at least**' problems.
**Types of events**: a **simple event** is a single outcome; a **compound event** combines several; **complementary events** have probabilities summing to 1.
**Odds in favour** = P(E)/P(not E); **odds against** = P(not E)/P(E) - a common phrasing in **card** and **dice** word problems.
**Exhaustive cases** to memorise: one die 6, two dice 36, a **deck** 52 cards in 4 **suits** of 13, with 12 **face cards**, 26 red and 26 black.

questions.q: A coin is tossed twice. What is the probability that at least one tail occurs?
questions.a: Sample space {HH, HT, TH, TT}; favourable outcomes = 3, so P = 3/4.

questions.q: A die is thrown. Find the probability of getting (i) a prime number, (ii) a number greater than 6.
questions.a: (i) Primes are 2, 3, 5, so P = 3/6 = 1/2. (ii) 0 - no face exceeds 6.

questions.q: One card is drawn from a well-shuffled deck of 52 cards. Calculate the probability that the card will (i) be an ace of spades, (ii) be an ace, (iii) be a black card.
If P(A union B) = P(A intersection B) then: (A) P(A) = P(B) (B) P(A) > P(B) (C) P(A) < P(B) (D) none of these
questions.a: (A) P(A) = P(B). Since P(A union B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A intersection B), equality forces P(A) + P(B) = 2P(A intersection B), which (with P(A intersect B) <= each) gives P(A) = P(B).

questions.q: Three coins are tossed once. Find the probability of getting exactly two heads.
questions.a: Sample space has 8 outcomes; favourable are HHT, HTH, THH (3 outcomes). P = 3/8.

If E and F are events such that P(E) = 1/4, P(F) = 1/2 and P(E and F) = 1/8, find (i) P(E or F), (ii) P(not E and not F).
questions.a: (i) P(E or F) = 1/4 + 1/2 - 1/8 = 5/8. (ii) P(not E and not F) = P(not (E or F)) = 1 - 5/8 = 3/8.

questions.q: A letter is chosen at random from the word ASSASSINATION. Find the probability that it is (i) a vowel, (ii) a consonant.
questions.a: The word has 13 letters. Vowels: A, A, A, I, I, O = 6, so P = 6/13. Consonants = 7, so P = 7/13.

chapters.title: The Living World
points: Defining properties of living beings: **growth**, **reproduction**, **metabolism**, **cellular organisation** and **consciousness** (ability to sense the environment).
**Biodiversity**: about **1.7-1.8 million species** have been identified and described so far; many more await discovery.
Taxonomy is the **classification**, **identification** and **nomenclature** of organisms. Systematics also includes evolutionary relationships (**Linnaeus** is called the father of taxonomy).

Binomial nomenclature (**Carolus Linnaeus**): each name has two parts - **genus** (capital first letter) and **specific epithet** (lowercase). Names are in **Latin**, written in italics (or underlined when handwritten).

Taxonomic hierarchy (broad to narrow): **Kingdom** > **Phylum/Division** > **Class** > **Order** > **Family** > **Genus** > **Species**. **Species** is the basic unit; taxa with fewer ranks share more common features.
Example: mango - Kingdom **Plantae**, Division **Angiospermae**, Class **Dicotyledonae**, Order **Sapindales**, Family **Anacardiaceae**, Genus **Mangifera**, Species **indica**.

Herbarium is a storehouse of **dried, pressed and preserved** plant specimens mounted on sheets, each carrying a label with **date**, **place of collection** and collector's name - the quickest aid for **taxonomic study**.

Botanical gardens (e.g. **Kew, England**; **Indian Botanical Garden, Howrah**) keep living plants, **museums** preserve specimens, and **zoological parks** keep wild animals in protected environments; **keys** (contrasting character pairs) are the standard taxonomic aids for **identification**.

questions.q: Why are living organisms classified?
questions.a: Classification makes it convenient to study the enormous diversity of living beings: it groups organisms with common characteristics so their study becomes systematic.

questions.q: Why do classification systems continue to change over time?
questions.a: Because new organisms are discovered and new techniques (cytotaxonomy, chemotaxonomy, DNA studies) keep revealing new relationships, so the criteria and systems keep being refined.

questions.q: If you were to identify and classify the people you meet often, what criteria would you use (say, at least ten)?
questions.a: Age, sex, height, weight, skin colour, education, profession, income and marital status - any set of useful, observable characters serves for a workable classification.

questions.q: As we go from species to kingdom in a taxonomic hierarchy, the number of common characteristics: (a) will decrease (b) will increase (c) remain the same (d) may increase or decrease, depending on the number of taxa used.
questions.a: (a) Will decrease. Lower categories share more characters; higher taxa are united on fewer, broader characteristics.

questions.q: Define a taxon. Give some examples of taxa at different hierarchical levels.
questions.a: A taxon (plural taxa) is a unit of classification representing a rank - species, genus, family, order, class, phylum/division or kingdom. E.g., Mangifera is a genus, Anacardiaceae a family, Sapindales an order.

questions.q: Given below is the scientific name of Mango. Write the rules you follow to write the scientific names.
questions.a: Mangifera indica - rules: the genus name begins with a capital letter and the specific epithet with a small letter; names are in Latin, printed in italics (or underlined separately when handwritten); the author's name is abbreviated after the specific epithet (e.g. Linn.).

questions.q: Define and understand the following terms: (i) Phylum (ii) Class (iii) Family (iv) Order (v) Genus.
questions.a: (i) Phylum: a group of related classes (animals). (ii) Class: a group of related orders. (iii) Family: a group of related genera. (iv) Order: an assemblage of families with a few similar characters. (v) Genus: a group of closely related species.

questions.q: Illustrate the taxonomical hierarchy with suitable examples of a plant and an animal.
questions.a: Plant (wheat): Kingdom Plantae > Division Angiospermae > Class Monocotyledonae > Order Poales > Family Poaceae > Genus Triticum > Species aestivum. Animal (man): Kingdom Animalia > Phylum Chordata > Class Mammalia > Order Primata > Family Hominidae > Genus Homo > Species sapiens.

mcqs.why: Systematics covers classification, nomenclature, identification and evolutionary relationships.

mcqs.why: A genus is a group of closely related species.

Collection of endemic and exotic living species
Collection of only local plants and animals

chapters.title: Biological Classification
points: R. Whittaker (1969) proposed the **five-kingdom system**: **Monera**, **Protista**, **Fungi**, **Plantae**, **Animalia** - based on **cell structure**, **body organisation**, **nutrition** and **phylogeny**.

Monera: **prokaryotic bacteria**; cell wall has **peptidoglycan**. Includes **archaebacteria** (extreme habitats), **eubacteria** (true bacteria), **cyanobacteria** (photosynthetic, e. Nostoc, Anabaena - nitrogen fixers).

Protista: single-celled **eukaryotes** - **Chrysophytes** (diatoms, golden algae; chief ocean producers), **Dinoflagellates** (e. Gonyaulax causes red tides), **Euglenoids** (Euglena - mixotroph), **Slime moulds**, **Protozoans** (Amoeba, Paramoecium, Plasmodium - malarial parasite).

Fungi: eukaryotic, **heterotrophic**, cell wall of **chitin**. Classes: **Phycomycetes** (Mucor), **Ascomycetes** (yeast, Penicillium), **Basidiomycetes** (Agaricus mushroom), **Deuteromycetes** (Alternaria).

Viruses are **non-cellular**, **obligate intracellular parasites** with protein coat (**capsid**); they are inert outside a host - not placed in the five-kingdom system. **Viroids** (Diener) are naked RNA; **prions** are infectious proteins; **lichens** are symbiosis of alga + fungus.

Diatomaceous earth - the **silica**-rich deposits of diatom cell walls - is used in polishing and filtration; **red tides** form when dinoflagellates like **Gonyaulax** multiply rapidly and release toxins.

Mycelium is the network of **hyphae** forming the fungal body; **mycorrhiza** is the mutualistic association of fungus with plant roots (e.g. **Pinus**), improving mineral uptake; fungi reproduce by spores - **zoospores**, **conidia**, **ascospores** and **basidiospores**.
Archaebacteria survive extremes - **halophiles** in salt, **thermoacidophiles** in hot springs, **methanogens** in marshes and the **rumen** of cattle, where they produce methane (**biogas**).

questions.q: How have classification systems of organisms changed over time?
questions.a: They expanded from two kingdoms (Linnaeus) to three, four and finally Whittaker's five kingdoms, as study criteria broadened from morphology to cell structure, mode of nutrition and evolutionary relationships.

questions.q: Give two economically important uses of (i) heterotrophic bacteria and (ii) archaebacteria.
questions.a: (i) Heterotrophic bacteria: making curd and antibiotics, and Rhizobium fixing nitrogen in legume fields. (ii) Archaebacteria: methanogens in gobar gas (biogas) plants and in the rumen of ruminants, helping cellulose digestion.

questions.q: State the structure and genetic material present in viruses. Name four viruses and the diseases they cause.
questions.a: A virus has a protein capsid surrounding nucleic acid (DNA or RNA), sometimes with a lipid envelope. Examples: TMV (tobacco mosaic), HIV (AIDS), Variola virus (smallpox), Influenza virus (flu).

questions.q: All eukaryotic unicellular organisms belong to: (a) Monera (b) Protista (c) Fungi (d) Bacteria
questions.a: (b) Protista.

questions.q: What is the nature of cell walls in diatoms?
questions.a: Diatom cell walls are embedded with silica, making them indestructible. Their two overlapping shells fit together like a soap box (epitheca over hypotheca); the deposits left behind form diatomaceous earth.

questions.q: How are viroids different from viruses?
questions.a: Viroids are infectious naked (capsid-less) RNA molecules discovered by T.O. Diener, whereas viruses have a protein capsid enclosing their nucleic acid (DNA or RNA).

questions.q: Find out what the terms 'algal bloom' and 'red tides' signify.
questions.a: Algal bloom: excessive growth of algae in water bodies, depleting oxygen. Red tides: rapid multiplication of red dinoflagellates like Gonyaulax, giving the sea a red colour and releasing toxins that kill marine animals.

questions.q: What do the terms phycobiont and mycobiont signify?
questions.a: In lichens, the algal partner is the phycobiont (photosynthetic, provides food) and the fungal partner is the mycobiont (provides shelter and absorbs minerals and water).

mcqs.why: Whittaker proposed the five-kingdom system in 1969.

mcqs.why: Halophiles are archaebacteria that thrive in salty habitats.

mcqs.why: Slime moulds are saprophytic protists with naked multinucleate cytoplasm (plasmodium).

mcqs.why: Mycorrhiza is the mutualistic root-fungus association.

mcqs.why: In plasmogamy without immediate karyogamy, two haploid nuclei coexist as a dikaryon.

chapters.title: Plant Kingdom
points: Algae: **chlorophyllous** simple plants, mostly aquatic. **Green algae** (Chlamydomonas, Spirogyra), **brown algae** (Laminaria, Fucus - contain fucoxanthin), **red algae** (Polysiphonia, Gelidium - source of agar).
Algae provide at least half of the Earth's total **CO2 fixation** through **photosynthesis**.

Bryophytes: **amphibians of the plant kingdom** (need water for fertilisation); no true **vascular tissue**; main plant body is **haploid gametophyte**. Examples: **Funaria** (moss), **Marchantia** (liverwort), **Sphagnum** (peat moss).

Pteridophytes: first terrestrial plants with **vascular tissue** (**xylem** and **phloem**); main body is **diploid sporophyte**; seedless. Examples: **Selaginella**, **Equisetum** (horsetail), ferns like **Dryopteris**.
Gymnosperms: **naked seeds** (ovules not enclosed in an ovary). Examples: **Pinus**, **Cycas** (living fossil), **Ginkgo**. Male and female **cones** are borne on the same or different plants.
Angiosperms: seeds enclosed in **fruits**; divided into **dicots** (two cotyledons, reticulate venation) and **monocots** (one cotyledon, parallel venation). **Flowers** are the reproductive units.
Life cycles: **haplontic** (e. Volvox), **diplontic** (e. Fucus, seed plants), **haplo-diplontic** (bryophytes, pteridophytes, e. Ectocarpus); all show **alternation of generations**.

Double fertilisation is unique to **angiosperms**: **syngamy** (one male gamete + egg -> diploid zygote) plus **triple fusion** (second male gamete + two polar nuclei -> triploid **primary endosperm nucleus**).
Heterospory - production of **megaspores** and **microspores** (e.g. **Selaginella**, **Salvinia**) - is considered the precursor of the **seed habit**.

questions.q: Why are bryophytes called amphibians of the plant kingdom?
questions.a: They can live on land, but depend on water for sexual reproduction, since their male gametes are flagellated and swim to the egg. They also need a thin film of water for growth. Like amphibians of the animal world, they need both land and water - hence the title.

questions.q: On what basis are algae primarily classified?
questions.a: On the nature of their photosynthetic pigments, the type of stored food reserve and the flagellation pattern.

questions.q: Mention the group names in which archegonia (the female sex organ) is present.
questions.a: Bryophyta, Pteridophyta and Gymnosperms.

questions.q: Cyanobacteria are classified under: (a) Protista (b) Plantae (c) Monera (d) Algae
questions.a: (c) Monera, as they are prokaryotic.

questions.q: Both gymnosperms and angiosperms bear seeds, then why are they classified separately?
questions.a: In gymnosperms the seeds are naked (ovules are not enclosed in an ovary), while in angiosperms the ovules are enclosed in an ovary and the seeds develop inside a fruit.

questions.q: What is heterospory? Briefly comment on its significance. Give two examples.
questions.a: Heterospory is the production of two kinds of spores - megaspores (female) and microspores (male). It is considered a precursor of the seed habit. Examples: Selaginella and Salvinia.

questions.q: Write a note on the economic importance of algae and gymnosperms.
questions.a: Algae: food (Porphyra, Laminaria), agar from Gelidium/Gracilaria for culture media, carrageenan, iodine from kelps, and half of global CO2 fixation. Gymnosperms: timber, resins, turpentine, drugs like ephedrine from Ephedra, and ornamental plants.

questions.q: Explain briefly the following terms with suitable examples: (i) protonema (ii) antheridium (iii) archegonium (iv) diplontic (v) sporophyll (vi) isogamy.
questions.a: (i) Protonema: creeping, green, branched filamentous stage in the moss life cycle. (ii) Antheridium: male sex organ. (iii) Archegonium: flask-shaped female sex organ. (iv) Diplontic: diploid sporophyte dominant life cycle (e.g. Fucus). (v) Sporophyll: leaf bearing sporangia. (vi) Isogamy: fusion of two morphologically similar gametes.

mcqs.why: Anisogamy is the fusion of two dissimilar motile gametes.

mcqs.why: The differentiated plant body of brown algae (kelps) has holdfast, stipe and frond.

mcqs.why: Bryophytes are haploid thalloid plants needing water for fertilisation.

mcqs.q: A prothallus is:
options: A structure in pteridophytes formed before the thallus develops
A sporophytic free-living structure formed in pteridophytes
A gametophytic free-living structure formed in pteridophytes
A primitive structure formed after fertilisation in pteridophytes
mcqs.why: The prothallus is the free-living haploid gametophyte of pteridophytes.

mcqs.q: Plants of this group are diploid and well adapted to extreme conditions. They grow bearing sporophylls in compact structures called cones. The group in reference is:
mcqs.why: Gymnosperms are diploid plants bearing cones with sporophylls.

mcqs.q: The embryo sac of an angiosperm is made up of:
mcqs.why: The mature embryo sac has 7 cells (egg, 2 synergids, 3 antipodals, 1 central cell) and 8 nuclei.

chapters.title: Animal Kingdom
points: Basis of classification: **level of organisation**, **body symmetry**, **germ layers**, **coelom**, **segmentation**, **notochord**.
Symmetry: **asymmetrical** (sponges), **radial** (coelenterates, ctenophores, adult echinoderms), **bilateral** (most animals from Platyhelminthes onwards).
Body cavity (**coelom**): **acoelomates** (Platyhelminthes), **pseudocoelomates** (Aschelminthes, e. Ascaris), **coelomates** (Annelida onwards).

Key phyla with NCERT examples: **Porifera** (Sycon, Spongilla), **Coelenterata/Cnidaria** (Hydra, Aurelia - jellyfish), **Ctenophora** (Pleurobrachia), **Platyhelminthes** (Taenia - tapeworm, Planaria), **Aschelminthes** (Ascaris, Wuchereria - filarial worm), **Annelida** (Pheretima - earthworm, Hirudinaria - leech), **Arthropoda** (largest phylum; Apis, Bombyx), **Mollusca** (Pila, Octopus), **Echinodermata** (Asterias - starfish), **Hemichordata** (Balanoglossus), **Chordata**.
Chordate features: **notochord**, **dorsal hollow nerve cord**, **pharyngeal gill slits**, **post-anal tail** (at some stage). Vertebrates have the notochord replaced by a **vertebral column**.
Arthropoda is the **largest animal phylum** (over 2/3 of named species); **jointed appendages** and **chitinous exoskeleton** are its features.

Chordates divide into **Urochordata** (tunicates - notochord only in the larval tail), **Cephalochordata** (**Branchiostoma** - notochord lifelong) and **Vertebrata** (notochord replaced by the vertebral column).

Vertebrate classes: **Cyclostomata** (jawless, e.g. Petromyzon), **Chondrichthyes** (cartilaginous fishes, e.g. Scoliodon, Trygon), **Osteichthyes** (bony fishes), **Amphibia**, **Reptilia** (dry cornified skin), **Aves** (feathers, **pneumatic bones**), **Mammalia** (**mammary glands**, hair, **diaphragm**; Ornithorhynchus and Echidna lay eggs).

questions.q: What difficulties would you have come across in classifying the animals, if common fundamental features are not taken into account?
questions.a: Without common fundamental features, every animal would have to be described and classified separately, making the study chaotic and nearly impossible.

questions.q: If you are given a specimen, what are the steps you would follow to classify it?
questions.a: Study its level of organisation, symmetry, germ layers, coelom, segmentation and notochord, then assign it to phylum, class, order, family, genus and species.

questions.q: How is the body cavity (coelom) useful in classification?
questions.a: The presence/absence and nature of the coelom separates acoelomates, pseudocoelomates and eucoelomates - a fundamental step in animal classification.

questions.q: Serial repetition of organs or segments in animals is known as: (a) segmentation (b) metamerism (c) metagenesis (d) metamorphosis
questions.a: (b) Metamerism.

questions.q: Distinguish between intracellular and extracellular digestion.
questions.a: Intracellular digestion takes place inside food vacuoles within cells (e.g. sponges, coelenterates), while extracellular digestion occurs outside cells in a digestive cavity or gut (e.g. higher animals).

questions.q: What is the difference between direct and indirect development?
questions.a: In direct development the young resembles the adult on hatching or birth; in indirect development there is a larval stage that metamorphoses into the adult (e.g. tadpole to frog).

questions.q: What are the peculiar features that you find in parasitic platyhelminthes?
questions.a: Hooks and suckers for attachment, loss of digestive organs (food absorbed through the body surface), high reproductive capacity, and hermaphroditism.

questions.q: What are the reasons that you can think of for the arthropods to constitute the largest group of the animal kingdom?
questions.a: Chitinous exoskeleton, jointed appendages, efficient locomotion, diverse feeding habits, high reproductive rate and adaptability to every habitat.

mcqs.q: The excretory organ in Annelida are:
mcqs.why: Annelids excrete through segmental nephridia.

mcqs.q: In which one of the following organisms are its excretory organs correctly stated?
options: Humans - kidneys, sebaceous glands and tear glands
Earthworm - pharyngeal, integumentary and septal nephridia
Cockroach - malpighian tubules and enteric caeca
Frog - kidneys, skin and buccal epithelium
mcqs.why: Earthworm has pharyngeal, integumentary and septal nephridia.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following pairs of animals comprises 'jawless fishes'?
mcqs.why: Lampreys and hag fishes are jawless cyclostomes.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following is a matching pair of an animal and a certain phenomenon it exhibits?
mcqs.why: Housefly (Musca) undergoes complete metamorphosis.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following is oviparous?
mcqs.why: Platypus is an egg-laying monotreme mammal.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following statements is incorrect?
options: In cockroaches and prawns excretion of waste material is through malpighian tubules
In ctenophores, locomotion is mediated by comb plates
In Fasciola, flame cells help in excretion
Earthworms are hermaphrodites and yet cross fertilisation takes place among them
mcqs.why: Prawns (crustaceans) excrete through green/antennal glands, not Malpighian tubules.

chapters.title: Morphology of Flowering Plants
points: Root systems: **tap root** (from radicle, e. mustard, dicots) vs **fibrous root** (from base of stem, e. wheat, monocots). Modifications: **storage** (carrot, turnip), **prop roots** (banyan), **stilt roots** (maize, sugarcane), **pneumatophores** for breathing (Rhizophora).

Stem modifications: **tendrils** (cucumber), **thorns** (Citrus, Bougainvillea), **underground storage** (potato - tuber, ginger - rhizome, onion - bulb, Colocasia - corm), **runner** (grass), **stolon** (jasmine), **offset** (Eichhornia), **sucker** (banana).

Leaf: parts - **leaf base**, **petiole**, **lamina**. Venation: **reticulate** (dicots) vs **parallel** (monocots). Phyllotaxy: **alternate**, **opposite**, **whorled**. Modifications: **tendril** (pea), **spines** (cactus), **storage** (onion), **insect capture** (pitcher plant).
Inflorescence: **racemose** (main axis keeps growing, younger flowers at top) vs **cymose** (main axis ends in a flower, older at top).

Flower: **bisexual**/**unisexual**; **actinomorphic** (radial symmetry, mustard) vs **zygomorphic** (bilateral, pea, gulmohur); ovary position: **hypogynous** (superior ovary, mustard), **perigynous** (plum, rose), **epigynous** (inferior ovary, guava, cucumber).
