Aestivation: **valvate** (Calotropis), **twisted** (china rose), **imbricate** (Cassia), **vexillary** (pea). Placentation: **marginal** (pea), **axile** (tomato, lemon), **parietal** (mustard, Argemone), **basal** (sunflower), **free central** (Primrose).
Floral formula uses symbols: **Br** (bracteate), **K** (calyx), **C** (corolla), **A** (androecium), **G** (gynoecium); **floral diagrams** represent flower structure.

Seed structure: a **dicot seed** (e.g. gram) has a **seed coat** (**testa** + **tegmen**), **hilum**, two food-storing **cotyledons**, and an embryo with **radicle** and **plumule**; a **monocot seed** (e.g. maize) has **endosperm** plus a single shield-shaped cotyledon called the **scutellum**.

Gynoecium: **apocarpous** (carpels free, e.g. lotus, rose) vs **syncarpous** (carpels fused, e.g. mustard, tomato); after fertilisation the ovules become **seeds** and the ovary wall becomes the **pericarp**.

questions.q: What modification of root is found in the (a) banyan tree, (b) turnip, (c) mangroves?
questions.a: (a) Prop roots for support. (b) The tap root is swollen for food storage. (c) Pneumatophores (breathing roots) that grow vertically upward out of the mud.

questions.q: Differentiate between racemose and cymose inflorescence.
questions.a: In racemose inflorescence, the main axis continues to grow and flowers open in acropetal succession (oldest at the base). In cymose, the main axis ends in a flower, so growth is limited and flowers open in basipetal order (oldest at the top).

questions.q: What is a flower? Describe the parts of a typical angiosperm flower.
questions.a: A flower is a modified, condensed shoot specialised for sexual reproduction. Its parts are calyx (sepals), corolla (petals), androecium (stamens) and gynoecium (carpels).

questions.q: Roots developed from parts of the plant other than the radicle are called: (a) tap roots (b) fibrous roots (c) adventitious roots (d) prop roots
questions.a: (c) Adventitious roots.

questions.q: How is a pinnately compound leaf different from a palmately compound leaf?
questions.a: In a pinnately compound leaf the leaflets arise along a common axis (rachis), as in neem; in a palmately compound leaf all leaflets arise from a single point at the tip of the petiole, as in silk cotton.

questions.q: Define the following terms: (i) aestivation (ii) placentation (iii) actinomorphic (iv) zygomorphic (v) superior ovary (vi) perigynous flower (vii) epipetalous stamen.
questions.a: (i) Arrangement of sepals/petals in a bud. (ii) Arrangement of ovules in the ovary. (iii) Flower divisible into two equal halves in any plane. (iv) Divisible into two equal halves in only one plane. (v) Ovary above other floral parts (hypogynous). (vi) Ovary half-inferior, at the same level as other parts. (vii) Stamens attached to petals.

questions.q: Describe the various types of placentations found in flowering plants.
questions.a: Marginal (pea), axile (tomato, lemon), parietal (mustard, Argemone), free central (Primrose) and basal (sunflower).

questions.q: How do the various leaf modifications help plants?
questions.a: Tendrils (pea) help climbing; spines (cactus) reduce water loss and protect; storage leaves (onion, garlic) store food; pitcher leaves trap insects to supplement nitrogen.

mcqs.q: Venation is a term used to describe the pattern of arrangement of:
options: Veins and veinlets in a lamina
mcqs.why: Venation is the arrangement of veins and veinlets in the leaf lamina.

mcqs.q: The placenta is attached to the developing seed near the:
mcqs.why: The placenta connects the seed near the hilum.

mcqs.q: Which of the following plants is used to extract the blue dye?
mcqs.why: Indigo dye is extracted from Indigofera.

mcqs.q: In a cymose inflorescence the main axis:
options: Has unlimited growth but lateral branches end in flowers
mcqs.why: In cymose inflorescence the main axis ends in a flower, limiting its growth.

mcqs.q: The mature seeds of plants such as gram and peas possess no endosperm, because:
options: There is no double fertilisation in them
Endosperm is not formed in them
Endosperm gets used up by the developing embryo during seed development
mcqs.why: In non-endospermic seeds the endosperm is consumed by the developing embryo.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following statements is correct?
options: In tomato, fruit is a capsule
Seeds of orchids have oil-rich endosperm
Flower of tulip is a modified shoot
mcqs.why: A flower is a modified shoot, as in tulip.

chapters.title: Anatomy of Flowering Plants
points: Tissue systems: **epidermal** (protection), **ground tissue system** (**cortex**, **pith**, **pericycle**), **vascular tissue system** (**xylem** + **phloem** in vascular bundles).
Simple tissues: **parenchyma** (living, thin walls, storage/photosynthesis), **collenchyma** (living, thickened corners, flexibility), **sclerenchyma** (dead, lignified walls, mechanical strength).

Complex tissues: **xylem** (**tracheids**, **vessels**, xylem parenchyma, xylem fibres - conducts water, mostly dead) and **phloem** (**sieve tube elements**, **companion cells**, phloem parenchyma, phloem fibres - translocates food).

Dicot stem: vascular bundles are **conjoint**, **collateral** and **open** (**cambium** present), arranged in a **ring**. Monocot stem: bundles are **closed** (no cambium) and **scattered** in ground tissue.
Dicot root: **xylem** and **phloem** in separate **radial** bundles (2-4 xylem arms). Monocot root: **polyarch** (many xylem bundles) with a large **pith**.

Dorsiventral (dicot) leaf: **palisade mesophyll** near upper surface, stomata mostly on lower surface, **bundle sheath** cells. Isobilateral (monocot) leaf: mesophyll not differentiated, **bulliform cells** in upper epidermis help leaf rolling.
Anomalous secondary growth aside, dicots show **secondary growth** by **vascular cambium** and **cork cambium**; monocots generally lack secondary growth.

Stomata: each stoma has two **guard cells** (dumb-bell shaped in grasses, kidney-shaped in dicots) flanking the **stomatal pore**; together with **subsidiary cells** they form the **stomatal apparatus**.

Annual rings: **spring wood** (early wood, wide vessels) and **autumn wood** (late wood, narrow vessels) alternate each year - counting these **growth rings** estimates a tree's age (**dendrochronology**).

questions.q: State the location and function of the different types of meristems in plant tissue.
questions.a: Apical meristems at root/shoot tips cause primary growth (length). Lateral meristems (vascular and cork cambium) cause secondary growth (girth). Intercalary meristems at nodes cause elongation of internodes.

questions.q: 'Cork cambium forms tissues that form the cork.' Do you agree with this statement? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. The cork cambium (phellogen) cuts off cells: those towards the outside become cork (phellem), and those towards the inside become secondary cortex (phelloderm).

questions.q: What is periderm? How does periderm develop in dicot stems?
questions.a: Periderm is the protective tissue that replaces the epidermis in older stems; it consists of phellem (cork), phellogen (cork cambium) and phelloderm, formed by the activity of the cork cambium.

questions.q: A transverse section of the stem is stained first with safranin and then fast green following the usual schedule of double staining. What would be the colour of the stained xylem and phloem? (a) Red and green (b) Green and red (c) Orange and yellow (d) Purple and orange
questions.a: (a) Red and green - lignified xylem takes safranin (red), non-lignified phloem takes fast green.

questions.q: Why are xylem and phloem called complex tissues?
questions.a: Because each is made of more than one type of cell working together as a unit - xylem has tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and fibres; phloem has sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and fibres.

questions.q: What is stomatal apparatus? Explain the structure of stomata with a labelled diagram.
questions.a: The stomatal apparatus consists of two guard cells (dumb-bell shaped in grasses, kidney-shaped in dicots), the stomatal pore between them, and subsidiary cells. Guard cells regulate opening and closing of the pore for gas exchange and transpiration.

questions.q: Name the three basic tissue systems in the flowering plants. Give the tissue names under each system.
questions.a: Epidermal tissue system (epidermis, stomata, trichomes); ground tissue system (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma in cortex, pith, pericycle); vascular tissue system (xylem and phloem in vascular bundles).

questions.q: How is the study of plant anatomy useful to us?
questions.a: It helps identify plants, understand adaptations, improve crops, distinguish timber, and solve taxonomic and physiological problems.

mcqs.q: Cells of this tissue are living and show angular wall thickening. They also provide mechanical support. The tissue is:
mcqs.why: Collenchyma cells are living with thickened corners and give mechanical support.

mcqs.q: Epiblema of roots is equivalent to:
mcqs.why: Epiblema is the outermost layer of the root, equivalent to the epidermis.

mcqs.q: A conjoint and open vascular bundle will be observed in the transverse section of:
mcqs.why: Dicot stems have conjoint, collateral, open vascular bundles in a ring.

mcqs.q: Interfascicular cambium and intrafascicular cambium join to form:
mcqs.why: Together they form the continuous cambium ring for secondary growth.

mcqs.q: What is the fate of primary xylem in a dicot root showing extensive secondary growth?
options: It is retained in the centre of the axis
May or may not get crushed
It gets surrounded by primary phloem
mcqs.why: In roots the primary xylem stays at the centre as secondary growth proceeds.

mcqs.q: Water containing cavities in vascular bundles are found in:
mcqs.why: Maize (monocot) vascular bundles have water-containing cavities (lysigenous cavities).

chapters.title: Structural Organisation in Animals
points: Four tissue types: **epithelial**, **connective**, **muscular**, **neural**.

Epithelial tissue lines surfaces: **squamous** (thin, in alveoli and blood vessels), **cuboidal** (kidney tubules, glands), **columnar** (stomach, intestine lining), **ciliated columnar** (fallopian tubes, bronchioles), **glandular** (secretion).

Connective tissues connect and support: **loose** (areolar, adipose), **dense** (**tendons** connect muscle to bone, **ligaments** connect bone to bone), **specialised** (cartilage, bone, blood - fluid connective tissue).

Muscular tissue: **skeletal**/striated (voluntary, attached to bones), **smooth** (involuntary, in digestive tract and blood vessels, spindle-shaped), **cardiac** (only in heart, striated but involuntary, with **intercalated discs**).
Neural tissue: **neurons** are the unit; **neuroglia** protect and support them. Neurons conduct impulses, but neuroglial cells make up more than half the volume of neural tissue.
Frog (**Rana tigrina**) is the NCERT model organism: **cold-blooded**, undergoes **metamorphosis**, males have **vocal sacs** and **copulatory pads**; heart is **3-chambered** (2 atria, 1 ventricle).
Cockroach (**Periplaneta americana**): body in **head**, **thorax** and **abdomen** (10 segments); **compound eyes**, chewing **mouthparts**; males have **anal styles** which females lack.

Earthworm (**Pheretima**): **hermaphrodite** with 4 pairs of **spermathecae** (segments 6-9) and **clitellum** (segments 14-16); closed circulation with 4 pairs of **hearts**; **segmental nephridia** excrete.

questions.q: Answer in one word or one line: (i) Give the common name of Periplaneta americana. (ii) How many pairs of spermathecae are found in the earthworm? (iii) What is the number of segments in the abdomen of a cockroach?
questions.a: (i) American cockroach. (ii) Four pairs. (iii) 10 segments.

questions.q: Mention briefly the role of (a) ureters in a frog, (b) Malpighian tubules, (c) the body wall in an earthworm.
questions.a: (a) Transport urine from kidneys to the cloaca. (b) Excretion in insects - they remove nitrogenous wastes into the gut. (c) Protection, locomotion (with setae and muscles) and moist surface for cutaneous respiration.

questions.q: Cells present in the inner lining of large blood vessels are: (a) cuboidal epithelium (b) columnar epithelium (c) squamous epithelium (d) stratified epithelium
questions.a: (c) Squamous epithelium (endothelium).

questions.q: Adipose tissue is a type of: (a) epithelial tissue (b) connective tissue (c) muscular tissue (d) neural tissue
questions.a: (b) Connective tissue - its cells store fat in large globules.

questions.q: What are the cellular components of blood?
questions.a: RBCs (erythrocytes), WBCs (leucocytes - granulocytes like neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, and agranulocytes like lymphocytes and monocytes) and platelets (thrombocytes).

questions.q: Distinguish between (a) simple epithelium and compound epithelium, (b) cardiac muscle and striated muscle.
questions.a: (a) Simple epithelium is one cell thick (absorption/secretion); compound epithelium is multilayered (protection). (b) Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart, involuntary with intercalated discs; striated (skeletal) muscle is attached to bones and voluntary.

questions.q: What are the following and where do you find them in animal body: (a) chondrocytes (b) axons (c) ciliated epithelium?
questions.a: (a) Cartilage cells, found in cartilage. (b) Long processes of neurons carrying impulses away from the cell body. (c) Epithelium with cilia, lining the fallopian tubes and bronchioles.

questions.q: Mention briefly about the circulatory system of earthworm.
questions.a: Earthworm has a closed circulatory system: blood flows in vessels; four pairs of hearts (7th-9th segments) pump blood; haemoglobin is dissolved in plasma, so blood is red.

mcqs.q: The clitellum is a distinct part in the body of earthworm, it is found in:
mcqs.why: The clitellum is present in segments 14-16 of earthworm.

mcqs.q: Setae help in locomotion in earthworm but are not uniformly present in all the segments. They are present in:
mcqs.why: Setae are absent from the first, last and clitellar segments; they occur in segments like 20-22.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following statements is true for cockroach?
options: The number of ovarioles in each ovary are ten
The larval stage is called caterpillar
Anal styles are absent in females
mcqs.why: Anal styles are present only in male cockroaches; females lack them.

mcqs.q: Match the following and choose the correct option: A. Adipose tissue - i. Nose; B. Stratified epithelium - ii. Blood; C. Hyaline cartilage - iii. Skin; D. Fluid connective tissue - iv. Fat cell.
mcqs.why: Adipose-fat cell, stratified epithelium-skin, hyaline cartilage-nose, fluid connective tissue-blood.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following is not a characteristic of phylum Annelida?
mcqs.why: Annelids are true coelomates; pseudocoelom belongs to Aschelminthes.

mcqs.q: Which of the following happens in the common cockroach?
options: Malpighian tubules are excretory organs projecting out from the colon
Oxygen is transported by haemoglobin in blood
The food is ground by mandibles and gizzard
mcqs.why: Cockroach grinds food in the gizzard; its blood carries no respiratory pigment.

chapters.title: Cell: The Unit of Life
points: Cell theory (**Schleiden** and **Schwann**, later refined by **Virchow**): all organisms are made of cells, the cell is the **basic unit of life**, and new cells arise from **pre-existing cells** (**omnis cellula e cellula**).
Prokaryotic cells (bacteria): no **membrane-bound nucleus** or organelles; DNA is a single **circular molecule** in the **nucleoid**; ribosomes are **70S**; **mesosomes** are membrane infoldings.

Eukaryotic cells: true **nucleus** and organelles. Plant cells have a **cell wall** (cellulose), **chloroplasts** and a large **central vacuole**; animal cells lack walls and plastids but have **centrioles**.

Endomembrane system: **ER** (rough ER - protein synthesis with ribosomes; smooth ER - lipid synthesis), **Golgi apparatus** (packaging, modification, lysosome formation), **lysosomes** (suicidal bags with hydrolytic enzymes), **vacuoles**.

Mitochondria: **double membrane**, own DNA and **70S ribosomes**, site of **aerobic respiration** (powerhouse of the cell). Chloroplast: double membrane with **thylakoids** stacked as **grana**, site of **photosynthesis**.

Cytoskeleton (**microfilaments**, **microtubules**, **intermediate filaments**) gives shape and movement. Nucleus contains **chromatin** (DNA + histones); **nucleolus** makes rRNA. Ribosomes (**80S** in eukaryotes = 60S + 40S) synthesise proteins.
Plasma membrane follows the **fluid mosaic model** (Singer and Nicolson, 1972): a **phospholipid bilayer** with proteins - it is **selectively permeable**, and neutral solutes cross by **diffusion**.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts carry **70S ribosomes** and their own **circular DNA** - strong evidence for their **endosymbiotic origin** from free-living bacteria.
Inclusion bodies (**phosphate granules**, **cyanophycean granules**, **glycogen granules**) store reserve material free in the **cytoplasm** - they are **not membrane-bound**.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT correct? (a) Robert Brown discovered the cell. (b) Schleiden and Schwann formulated the cell theory. (c) Virchow explained that cells are formed from pre-existing cells. (d) A unicellular organism carries out its life activities within a single cell.
questions.a: (a) is not correct: Brown discovered the nucleus (1831); cells were first seen and named earlier (Hooke, Leeuwenhoek).

questions.q: New cells generate from: (a) bacterial fermentation (b) regeneration of old cells (c) pre-existing cells by division (d) abiotic materials
questions.a: (c) Pre-existing cells by division (Virchow: Omnis cellula-e cellula).

questions.q: Both lysosomes and vacuoles are endomembrane structures, yet they differ in terms of their functions. Comment.
questions.a: Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes and carry out intracellular digestion. Vacuoles mainly store substances (food, sap, waste) and maintain turgor in plant cells.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a eukaryote: (a) Euglena (b) Anabaena (c) Spirogyra (d) Agaricus
questions.a: (b) Anabaena - a cyanobacterium, hence prokaryotic.

questions.q: What is a mesosome in a prokaryotic cell? Mention the functions that it performs.
questions.a: Mesosomes are infoldings of the bacterial plasma membrane. They help in cell wall formation, DNA replication and distribution to daughter cells, respiration, secretion and increasing surface area.

questions.q: Which is the important site of formation of glycoproteins and glycolipids in eukaryotic cells?
questions.a: The Golgi apparatus (Golgi complex).

questions.q: What is a centromere? How does the position of centromere form the basis of classification of chromosomes?
questions.a: The centromere is the primary constriction where sister chromatids are held together and spindle fibres attach. Its position classifies chromosomes as metacentric (middle), sub-metacentric (sub-middle), acrocentric (sub-terminal) or telocentric (terminal).

questions.q: Name two cell-organelles that are double membrane bound. What are the characteristics of these two organelles? State their functions.
questions.a: Mitochondria and chloroplasts. Both are double-membraned, have their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, divide by fission (semi-autonomous), and are sites of energy conversion - mitochondria for aerobic respiration, chloroplasts for photosynthesis.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following is not an inclusion body found in prokaryotes?
mcqs.why: Prokaryotic inclusion bodies include phosphate, cyanophycean and glycogen granules, not glucan granules.

mcqs.q: Which of the following stains is not used for staining chromosomes?
mcqs.why: Safranin is used for plant tissues, not chromosome staining.

mcqs.q: The stain used to visualise mitochondria is:
mcqs.why: Janus green is the vital stain for mitochondria.

mcqs.q: The size of Pleuropneumonia-like Organism (PPLO) is:
mcqs.why: PPLO are the smallest cells, about 0.1 micrometer in diameter.

mcqs.q: A common characteristic feature of plant sieve tube cells and most of mammalian erythrocytes is:
mcqs.why: Both mature sieve tubes and mammalian RBCs lack a nucleus.

mcqs.q: Select one which is not true for ribosome:
options: Have no role in protein synthesis
mcqs.why: Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis.

chapters.title: Biomolecules
points: Primary metabolites (**proteins**, **carbohydrates**, **lipids**, **nucleic acids**) have identifiable functions; **secondary metabolites** (alkaloids like **morphine**, **codeine**; pigments; drugs like **vinblastin**; **essential oils**) have no direct role in growth but many are useful to humans.

Carbohydrates: **monosaccharides** (glucose, fructose, ribose), **disaccharides** (sucrose = glucose + fructose; lactose = glucose + galactose; maltose = glucose + glucose), **polysaccharides** (starch - energy storage in plants, glycogen - animal starch, cellulose - structural, beta-1,4 links, gives no colour with iodine).

Proteins: polymers of **amino acids** joined by **peptide bonds**; 20 standard amino acids. Structure levels: **primary** (sequence), **secondary** (alpha helix, beta pleated sheet), **tertiary** (3D folding), **quaternary** (multiple chains, e. haemoglobin with 4 subunits). **Collagen** is the most abundant animal protein; **RuBisCO** is the most abundant protein in the biosphere.
Lipids: **fatty acids** + **glycerol**; **saturated** (no double bonds, solid) vs **unsaturated** (double bonds, liquid oils). **Phospholipids** form cell membranes.
Nucleic acids: **nucleotides** = nitrogenous base + pentose sugar + phosphate. DNA: **2'-deoxyribose**, bases **A, G, C, T**. RNA: **ribose** (extra 2'-OH), **U** instead of T.

Enzymes are **protein catalysts**: lower **activation energy**, speed reactions without being consumed. Activity depends on **temperature** (optimum ~37 deg C) and **pH**; **competitive inhibitors** resemble the substrate (e. sulpha drugs, statins), **non-competitive** bind elsewhere. **Apoenzyme** + **cofactor** = holoenzyme.

Amino acids: **essential amino acids** (e.g. lysine, methionine) must come from the **diet**; **non-essential** ones are synthesised in the body; amino acids join by **peptide bonds** with loss of water.
DNA's two strands are held by **hydrogen bonds** - **A=T** with two bonds, G=C with three - while **phosphodiester bonds** link nucleotides along each strand of the **Watson-Crick double helix**.

Isozymes are multiple forms of the same **enzyme** (e.g. **lactate dehydrogenase**); **cofactors** help catalysis - **coenzymes** (NAD, FAD, from vitamins), **prosthetic groups** (tightly bound, e.g. haem) and **metal ions** (Zn2+, Mg2+).

questions.q: What are macromolecules? Give examples.
questions.a: Very large molecules formed by the polymerisation of many small units. Examples: proteins, nucleic acids and polysaccharides.

questions.q: What is meant by the tertiary structure of proteins?
questions.a: The overall three-dimensional folding of a single polypeptide chain, stabilised by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulphide bonds and hydrophobic interactions.

questions.q: What is the difference between a nucleotide and a nucleoside? Give two examples of each.
questions.a: A nucleoside = nitrogenous base + pentose sugar (e.g. adenosine, cytidine). A nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate group (e.g. AMP, ATP).

questions.q: The chemical composition of living and inanimate matter differs mainly in that, per unit mass, living matter has more of: (a) gold (b) water (c) carbon, oxygen and hydrogen (d) calcium
questions.a: (c) Carbon, oxygen and hydrogen.

questions.q: Explain the composition of a triglyceride.
questions.a: A triglyceride is an ester of one glycerol molecule with three fatty acids.

questions.q: Find out how long each DNA molecule in a human cell is. What does this length indicate?
questions.a: About 2.2 metres per cell (6.6 x 10^9 base pairs x 0.34 nm). It indicates that DNA must be highly coiled and compacted (with histone proteins) to fit inside the tiny nucleus.

questions.q: Describe the important properties of enzymes.
questions.a: Enzymes are protein catalysts that lower activation energy; they are highly specific, work best at an optimum temperature and pH, are affected by inhibitors, and remain unchanged after the reaction.

questions.q: Illustrate a glycosidic, peptide and a phospho-diester bond.
questions.a: Glycosidic bond joins two monosaccharides (e.g. in disaccharides). Peptide bond joins two amino acids (-CO-NH-). Phospho-diester bond joins two nucleotides (3'-5' linkage in the DNA/RNA backbone).

mcqs.q: Many elements are found in living organisms either free or in the form of compounds. One of the following is not found in living organisms:
mcqs.why: Silicon is not a constituent element of living organisms.

mcqs.q: Amino acids, as the name suggests, have both an amino group and a carboxyl group in their structure. Which one of the following will not be found in an amino acid?
mcqs.why: Amino acids have -COOH, -NH2, -H and an R group; -COCH3 is not part of them.

mcqs.q: Which of the following sugars has the same number of carbons as that of glucose?
mcqs.why: Fructose, like glucose, is a 6-carbon hexose sugar.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a polysaccharide?
mcqs.why: Starch is a polymer of many glucose units; the others are disaccharides.

mcqs.q: Maltose is formed by:
mcqs.why: Maltose is a disaccharide of two glucose units.

mcqs.q: The most abundant chemical in living organisms could be:
mcqs.why: Water makes up 70-90% of living matter.

chapters.title: Cell Cycle and Cell Division
points: Cell cycle: **interphase** (**G1** - growth, **S** - DNA synthesis, **G2** - preparation) + **M phase** (division). **G0** is the quiescent exit phase (e. nerve cells, heart cells). Duration: about **24 h** in human cells; yeast ~90 min.
DNA content doubles in the **S phase** but chromosome number stays the same. Cell cycle is about **95% interphase**.

Mitosis stages: **prophase** (chromatin condenses, spindle forms), **metaphase** (chromosomes align at equator/metaphase plate), **anaphase** (sister chromatids separate to poles), **telophase** (nuclear envelope re-forms). Followed by **cytokinesis** (**cell plate** in plants, **furrow** in animals).
Significance of mitosis: **growth**, **repair**, **cell replacement**, maintaining **chromosome number**; basis of **asexual reproduction**.

Meiosis: two divisions - **meiosis I** (reductional: homologues separate, **crossing over** in prophase I) and **meiosis II** (equational: chromatids separate). Prophase I stages: **leptotene**, **zygotene** (synapsis, bivalents form), **pachytene** (crossing over at chiasmata), **diplotene**, **diakinesis**.

Crossing over between **non-sister chromatids** of homologous chromosomes creates new **gene combinations** (**variation**) - the raw material for **evolution**. Meiosis produces **4 haploid cells** from one diploid cell.
Karyokinesis is **nuclear division**; **cytokinesis** is cytoplasmic division - by **furrowing** in animal cells and **cell plate** formation (growing outward from the centre) in plant cells.
Meiosis I is **reductional** (chromosome number halves); meiosis II is **equational** (like mitosis) - the two together produce **four haploid cells** from one diploid cell.
Significance of meiosis: **gamete formation** conserves the **chromosome number** generation after generation, while **crossing over** creates **genetic variation** - the basis of evolution.

questions.q: What is the average cell cycle span for a mammalian cell?
questions.a: About 24 hours; the actual cell division (M phase) takes only about 1 hour of it.

questions.q: Distinguish anaphase of mitosis from anaphase I of meiosis. Also state: (i) at what stage do chromosomes move to spindle equator, (ii) during what stage does centromere split, (iii) during what stage does pairing of homologous chromosomes occur, (iv) during what stage does crossing over occur?
questions.a: In mitotic anaphase sister chromatids separate; in anaphase I homologous chromosomes (not chromatids) separate. (i) Metaphase. (ii) Anaphase. (iii) Zygotene. (iv) Pachytene.

questions.q: Describe the events taking place during interphase.
questions.a: G1: cell grows and prepares for DNA synthesis. S: DNA replicates, chromosome number of DNA doubles. G2: proteins are synthesised in preparation for mitosis, and cell growth continues.

questions.q: The process of meiosis results in: (a) production of gametes (b) reduction in chromosome number (c) introducing variation (d) all of the above
questions.a: (d) All of the above.

questions.q: Why is mitosis called equational division?
questions.a: Because the two daughter cells receive exactly the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell - the chromosome number is maintained (equated).

questions.q: How does cytokinesis in plant cells differ from that in animal cells?
questions.a: In plant cells a cell plate forms from vesicles at the centre and grows outward; in animal cells the cell membrane constricts inward forming a furrow.

questions.q: Describe the following: (a) synapsis (b) bivalent (c) chiasmata.
questions.a: (a) Synapsis: pairing of homologous chromosomes in zygotene. (b) Bivalent: the paired structure of two homologous chromosomes. (c) Chiasmata: X-shaped points where crossing over occurs, visible in diplotene.

questions.q: What is G0 (quiescent phase) of cell cycle?
questions.a: Cells that exit the cell cycle and stop dividing (e.g. nerve and heart cells) enter the inactive G0 phase, remaining metabolically active but not proliferating.

mcqs.q: At which stage of meiosis is the genetic constitution of gametes finally decided?
mcqs.why: Independent assortment at anaphase I decides the genetic constitution of gametes.

mcqs.q: Meiosis occurs in organisms during:
mcqs.why: Meiosis occurs for gamete formation in sexual reproduction.

mcqs.q: During anaphase-I of meiosis:
mcqs.why: Homologous chromosomes separate in anaphase I; chromatids stay together.

mcqs.q: Mitosis is characterised by:
mcqs.why: Mitosis is an equational (equal) division.

mcqs.q: A bivalent of meiosis-I consists of:
mcqs.why: A bivalent has two homologous chromosomes = four chromatids and two centromeres.

mcqs.q: Cells which are not dividing are likely to be at:
mcqs.why: Non-dividing cells rest in the quiescent G0 phase.

chapters.title: Photosynthesis in Higher Plants
points: Photosynthesis: 6CO2 + 12H2O --(light, chlorophyll)--> C6H12O6 + 6O2 + 6H2O. Oxygen released comes from **water**, not CO2 (proved by **isotope experiments**).

Site: **chloroplast**. **Light reactions** (in thylakoid membrane/grana) need light: **photolysis of water**, **ATP** and **NADPH** produced. **Dark reactions** (**Calvin cycle**, in stroma) use ATP and NADPH to fix CO2.

Pigments: **chlorophyll a** (chief pigment, blue-green), **chlorophyll b**, **xanthophylls**, **carotenoids** (accessory pigments that widen the absorption spectrum and protect against photo-oxidation).
Photosystems: **PS II** (P680) and **PS I** (P700). **Non-cyclic photophosphorylation** involves both and releases O2; **cyclic flow** involves only PS I (only ATP formed).
Calvin cycle (**C3**): CO2 acceptor is **RuBP** (5C); first stable product is **3-PGA** (3C); cycle needs **18 ATP** and **12 NADPH** per glucose.

C4 plants (maize, sugarcane): first product **oxaloacetic acid** (4C); **Kranz anatomy** (large bundle sheath cells); **PEP carboxylase** fixes CO2 in mesophyll; avoids photorespiration, shows high productivity. **CAM** plants (pineapple, desert plants) open stomata at night.
Factors affecting photosynthesis: **light intensity** and quality, **CO2 concentration** (limiting factor per Blackman's law of limiting factors), **temperature**, **water**.

The **action spectrum** of photosynthesis (peaks in blue and red) closely matches the **absorption spectrum** of **chlorophyll a** - Engelmann's experiment with **Cladophora** and aerobic bacteria proved chlorophyll's central role.
Chemiosmosis in the **thylakoid**: the **proton gradient** across the thylakoid membrane drives **ATP synthesis** via **ATP synthase** - the same principle as in mitochondria.

Photorespiration: in C3 plants **RuBisCO** binds O2 instead of CO2 under hot, dry conditions, wasting energy without making **ATP** or **NADPH** - C4 plants avoid it with their **CO2-concentrating mechanism**.

questions.q: By looking at a plant externally can you tell whether a plant is C3 or C4? Why or why not?
questions.a: No - C3 and C4 plants do not differ in any external feature; the difference is internal and physiological.

questions.q: Which organelle/structure inside the leaf tells you whether a plant is C3 or C4? Explain.
questions.a: The bundle sheath cells: C4 leaves show Kranz anatomy - large bundle sheath cells packed with chloroplasts, where the Calvin cycle runs, while the mesophyll only fixes CO2 into a 4-carbon acid.

questions.q: Compare C3 and C4 pathways of photosynthesis.
questions.a: C3: CO2 acceptor is RuBP, first stable product is 3-PGA, photosynthesis occurs in mesophyll cells. C4: CO2 acceptor is PEP, first product is oxaloacetic acid (4C), Calvin cycle occurs in the bundle sheath, and photorespiration is suppressed.

questions.q: Chlorophyll contains which metal ion at its centre: (a) Fe (b) Cu (c) Mg (d) Zn
questions.a: (c) Mg.

questions.q: RuBisCO is an enzyme that acts both as a carboxylase and oxygenase. Why do you think RuBisCO carries out more carboxylation in C4 plants?
questions.a: In C4 plants, the CO2 concentration mechanism delivers a high CO2 concentration at the RuBisCO site in bundle sheath cells, so carboxylation is favoured and photorespiration is suppressed.

questions.q: Suppose there were plants that had a high concentration of chlorophyll b, but lacked chlorophyll a, would they carry out photosynthesis? Then why do plants have chlorophyll b and other accessory pigments?
questions.a: No - only chlorophyll a (P680/P700 reaction centres) can directly convert light energy to chemical energy. Chlorophyll b and carotenoids are accessory pigments that absorb light of other wavelengths and pass the energy to chlorophyll a, widening the usable spectrum and protecting against photo-oxidation.

questions.q: Why is the colour of a leaf kept in the dark frequently yellow or pale green? Which pigment do you think is more stable?
questions.a: Chlorophyll breaks down faster in darkness while carotenoids/xanthophylls persist, revealing the yellow colour - so the carotenoid pigments are more stable.

questions.q: Give a comparison between cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation.
questions.a: Non-cyclic involves both PS I and PS II, splits water releasing O2, and produces ATP + NADPH. Cyclic involves only PS I, no O2 release, and produces only ATP.

mcqs.q: Which range of wavelength (in nm) is called photosynthetically active radiation (PAR)?
mcqs.why: PAR is the visible range 400-700 nm used in photosynthesis.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following is not true about the light reactions of photosynthesis?
options: Light energy provides energy for the photolysis of water through excitation of PS II
The flow of electrons from water to NADP in non-cyclic electron transport produces ATP
Reactions of the two photosystems are needed for the reduction of NADP
P680 and P700 are the reaction centres of PS I and PS II respectively
mcqs.why: P680 is the reaction centre of PS II and P700 of PS I - the pairing is reversed.

mcqs.q: Dark reactions of photosynthesis occur in:
mcqs.why: The Calvin cycle (dark reactions) takes place in the stroma.

mcqs.q: The correct sequence of flow of electrons in the light reaction is:
mcqs.why: Electrons flow from PSII through plastoquinone and cytochromes to PSI and ferredoxin.

mcqs.q: The enzyme that is not found in a C3 plant is:
mcqs.why: PEP carboxylase is the C4-fixing enzyme, not used for CO2 fixation in C3 plants.

mcqs.q: The reaction that is responsible for the primary fixation of CO2 is catalysed by:
mcqs.why: Primary fixation is by RuBP carboxylase in C3 and PEP carboxylase in C4 plants.

chapters.title: Respiration in Plants
points: Cellular respiration breaks glucose to release energy stored as **ATP**. **Respiratory quotient** RQ = volume of CO2 released / volume of O2 consumed (**1** for glucose, **< 1** for fats ~0.7, **> 1** for organic acids).
Glycolysis (**cytoplasm**, common to aerobic and anaerobic respiration): glucose -> 2 pyruvate, net gain **2 ATP** + **2 NADH**. **EMP pathway** (Embden, Meyerhof, Parnas).
Fermentation (**anaerobic**, cytoplasm): pyruvate -> **ethanol + CO2** (yeast) or **lactic acid** (muscles/bacteria); net gain only 2 ATP; dangerous in large amounts due to acid/alcohol accumulation.

Aerobic respiration: pyruvate enters **mitochondria**; **oxidative decarboxylation** gives **acetyl CoA** (2C) + NADH + CO2. **Krebs cycle** (in mitochondrial matrix): per acetyl CoA - **3 NADH**, **1 FADH2**, **1 GTP(ATP)**, **2 CO2** released.
Electron transport system (**inner mitochondrial membrane**): NADH and FADH2 pass electrons to **O2** (final acceptor); **proton gradient** drives ATP synthesis (**oxidative phosphorylation**).

ATP tally per glucose (NCERT): glycolysis gives a net gain of **8 ATP** when its cytoplasmic NADH is oxidised inside the mitochondria (only 6 ATP if the glycerol phosphate shuttle is used); the overall net gain in aerobic respiration is about **36 ATP** (38 by the other shuttle count) - NCERT notes these figures rest on idealised assumptions about transport into mitochondria. Respiration is an **amphibolic pathway**: its intermediates link carbohydrate, fat and protein metabolism.

Krebs cycle (**tricarboxylic acid cycle**): **acetyl CoA** (2C) condenses with **oxaloacetate** (4C) to form **citrate** (6C) via **citrate synthase**; each turn releases **2 CO2** with **3 NADH**, **1 FADH2** and **1 GTP**.
Fermentation regenerates **NAD+** so **glycolysis** can continue without oxygen - yeast makes **ethanol**, animal muscle makes **lactic acid**; both yield only 2 ATP per glucose.

Compensation point: the **light intensity** at which **photosynthesis** exactly balances **respiration**, so there is no net gas exchange; **RQ** of succulents is near zero as they release no CO2 at night.

questions.q: Explain the term RQ. What is its value for fats?
questions.a: RQ = volume of CO2 evolved / volume of O2 consumed. For glucose RQ = 1; for fats RQ is about 0.7, because fats are poorer in oxygen, so relatively more O2 is consumed than CO2 released.

questions.q: What are respiratory substrates? Name the most common one.
questions.a: Compounds oxidised during respiration to release energy. The most common is glucose (carbohydrates).

questions.q: What is the significance of step-wise release of energy in respiration?
questions.a: Energy released in small steps can be captured efficiently as ATP and does not damage the cell or escape as sudden heat; intermediates can also be drawn off for other pathways.

questions.q: The ultimate electron acceptor in aerobic respiration is: (a) the final cytochrome oxidase (b) oxygen (c) hydrogen (d) glucose
questions.a: (b) Oxygen - it accepts electrons and protons to form water.

questions.q: What is oxidative phosphorylation?
questions.a: The synthesis of ATP from ADP using the energy released as electrons pass through the electron transport chain and protons flow back through ATP synthase, with oxygen as the final electron acceptor.

questions.q: Discuss 'The respiratory pathway is an amphibolic pathway.'
questions.a: Respiration involves both breakdown (catabolism, e.g. glucose to CO2) and synthesis (anabolism - fatty acids synthesised from acetyl CoA, amino acids from alpha-ketoglutarate), so it is amphibolic rather than purely catabolic.

questions.q: What are the main steps in aerobic respiration? Where does each take place?
questions.a: Glycolysis in the cytoplasm; pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs (TCA) cycle in the mitochondrial matrix; electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation on the inner mitochondrial membrane.

questions.q: What are the assumptions made during the calculation of net gain of ATP?
questions.a: There is a sequential, orderly pathway with one substrate forming the next; NADH made in glycolysis enters mitochondria and is oxidised; no intermediate leaves the pathway; only glucose is being respired - no alternative substrate enters at intermediate stages.

mcqs.q: Phosphorylation of glucose during glycolysis is catalysed by:
mcqs.why: Hexokinase phosphorylates glucose to glucose-6-phosphate in glycolysis.

mcqs.q: Pyruvic acid, the key product of glycolysis, can have many metabolic fates. Under aerobic conditions it forms:
mcqs.why: Under aerobic conditions pyruvate is converted to acetyl CoA + CO2.

mcqs.q: Electron Transport System (ETS) is located in mitochondrial:
mcqs.why: The ETS complexes sit on the inner mitochondrial membrane.

mcqs.q: Which of the following exhibits the highest rate of respiration?
mcqs.why: Germinating seeds respire most actively to fuel rapid growth.

mcqs.q: Mitochondria are called powerhouses of the cell. Which of the following observations support this statement?
options: The enzymes of the Krebs cycle and the cytochromes are found in mitochondria
Mitochondria are found in almost all plant and animal cells
mcqs.why: ATP synthesis in mitochondria justifies the 'powerhouse' label.

mcqs.q: The end product of oxidative phosphorylation is:
mcqs.why: Oxidative phosphorylation ends with ATP and water formation.

chapters.title: Plant Growth and Development
points: Growth is **irreversible** permanent increase in size; plant growth is **indeterminate** (meristems keep dividing). **Primary growth** (length) by **apical meristems**; **secondary growth** (girth) by **lateral meristems** (**vascular cambium**, **cork cambium**).

Growth curve is **sigmoid** (S-shaped): **lag phase**, **log/exponential phase**, **steady** (stationary) phase. **Absolute** and **relative growth rates** differ - a small leaf can have a higher relative growth rate.

Plant growth regulators: **auxins** (cell elongation, apical dominance, root initiation - IAA, synthetic 2,4-D is a weedicide), **gibberellins** (stem elongation, bolting, breaks seed dormancy, malting in brewing), **cytokinins** (cell division, delay senescence, overcome apical dominance).

Abscisic acid (**ABA**): **stress hormone**; closes **stomata** during water stress, promotes **seed dormancy** and **abscission** of leaves/fruits. **Ethylene**: gaseous hormone, **fruit ripening**, **triple response**, breaks seed dormancy, used as **Ethephon** in agriculture.

Photoperiodism: response to relative length of **day/night** - **short day** plants (chrysanthemum, Xanthium), **long day** plants (spinach, radish), **day neutral** (tomato, maize). The critical photoperiod is sensed by leaves via **phytochrome** (**Pr**/**Pfr**).
**Vernalisation**: **low-temperature** promotion of flowering (e. winter wheat, biennials like carrot and cabbage); prevents **precocious reproductive development** in autumn.

Differentiation: **meristematic** cells mature into specialised **permanent tissues**; **dedifferentiation** regains division capacity (e.g. **cork cambium** from parenchyma); **redifferentiation** matures them again (e.g. secondary xylem).

Seed dormancy: internal inhibition of **germination**; broken by **chilling** (**stratification**), light or **gibberellins**, while **ABA** maintains it - dormancy lets seeds survive unfavourable periods.

Arithmetic growth: one daughter cell divides, the other differentiates (constant rate, e.g. **root elongation**); **geometric growth**: both daughters keep dividing (exponential) - together they give the **sigmoid curve**.

questions.q: Why is abscisic acid (ABA) also known as the stress hormone?
questions.a: ABA production shoots up under water stress and other harsh conditions. It closes the stomata (cutting water loss), promotes seed and bud dormancy, and helps the plant tolerate stress - hence, stress hormone.

questions.q: Define growth in plants.
questions.a: Growth is an irreversible, permanent increase in size (length, area, volume, mass or cell number) of an organ or its parts, accompanied by an increase in dry weight.

questions.q: Why is not any one parameter good enough to demonstrate growth throughout the life of a flowering plant?
questions.a: Different stages and organs grow differently: true growth at different times is better shown by pollen tube length, leaf area, root length, number of lateral roots or cell number - no single parameter works throughout life.

questions.q: The term 'auxin bioassay' refers to: (a) measurement using a potometer (b) lettuce hypocotyl elongation test (c) Avena coleoptile curvature test (d) hydroponics
questions.a: (c) Avena (oat) coleoptile curvature test.

questions.q: What do you understand by photoperiodism and vernalisation? Describe their significance.
questions.a: Photoperiodism: the response to day/night length controlling flowering - short-day plants flower below a critical photoperiod, long-day plants above it. Vernalisation: low-temperature treatment promoting flowering in biennials and winter cereals. Both ensure flowering in the favourable season.

questions.q: Which plant growth regulator would you use if you are asked to: (a) induce rooting in a twig (b) quickly ripen a fruit (c) delay leaf senescence (d) induce growth in axillary buds (e) 'bolt' a rosette plant (f) induce immediate stomatal closure in leaves.
questions.a: (a) Auxin (b) Ethylene (c) Cytokinin (d) Cytokinin (e) Gibberellin (f) Abscisic acid.

questions.q: Would a defoliated plant respond to the photoperiodic cycle? Why?
questions.a: No - the photoperiodic stimulus is perceived by the leaves (via phytochrome); without leaves the plant cannot detect day length.

questions.q: List the five main groups of natural plant growth regulators.
questions.a: Auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid and ethylene.

mcqs.q: Ethylene is used for:
mcqs.why: Ethylene hastens fruit ripening.

mcqs.q: Coconut water contains:
mcqs.why: Coconut water is a rich source of cytokinin (kinetin-like activity).

mcqs.q: The effect of apical dominance can be overcome by which of the following hormones:
mcqs.why: Cytokinins promote lateral bud growth and overcome apical dominance.

mcqs.q: Match the following: A. IAA - i. Herring sperm DNA; B. ABA - ii. Bolting; C. Ethylene - iii. Stomatal closure; D. GA - iv. Weed-free lawns; E. Cytokinins - v. Ripening of fruits.
mcqs.why: IAA-weed-free lawns, ABA-stomatal closure, ethylene-ripening, GA-bolting, cytokinins-herring sperm DNA (kinetin source).

mcqs.q: Apples are generally wrapped in waxed paper to:
options: Prevent aerobic respiration by checking the entry of O2
Prevent ethylene formation due to injury
mcqs.why: Wax paper restricts O2 entry, slowing respiration and ripening in storage.

mcqs.q: Growth can be measured in various ways. Which of these can be used as parameters to measure growth?
mcqs.why: Growth can be measured by cell number, cell size, length and weight.

chapters.title: Breathing and Exchange of Gases
points: Human respiratory system: nostrils -> **pharynx** -> **larynx** (voice box) -> **trachea** (incomplete C-shaped cartilage rings) -> **bronchi** -> **bronchioles** -> **alveoli** (site of gas exchange, ~300 million, enormous surface area). **Conducting part** vs **respiratory part**.

Breathing mechanism: **inspiration** - **diaphragm** contracts and flattens, ribs move up/out (**external intercostals**), thoracic volume rises, pressure falls, air flows in. **Expiration** is largely passive - diaphragm relaxes and domes up.

Volumes and capacities: **tidal volume** TV ~500 mL; **inspiratory reserve** IRV 2500-3000 mL; **expiratory reserve** ERV 1000-1100 mL; **residual volume** RV 1100-1200 mL; **vital capacity** = ERV + TV + IRV (~4600 mL); **total lung capacity** = VC + RV.
Exchange: gases diffuse from high to low **partial pressure**. **pO2** in alveoli 104 mmHg vs 40 in deoxygenated blood; **pCO2** in blood 45 vs 40 in alveoli - so O2 enters blood and CO2 leaves.

Transport of O2: ~97% as **oxyhaemoglobin** in RBCs, ~3% dissolved in plasma. One **Hb** binds 4 O2. Oxyhaemoglobin **dissociation curve** is sigmoid; **Bohr effect**: high CO2/low pH (exercising tissues) shifts the curve right, releasing more O2.

Transport of CO2: ~70% as **bicarbonate ions** (via **carbonic anhydrase** in RBCs), ~20-25% as **carbamino-haemoglobin**, ~7% dissolved. Regulation: **respiratory rhythm centre** in medulla with **pneumotaxic centre** in pons; chemosensitive area senses CO2 and H+.

Emphysema: chronic disorder where **alveolar walls** are damaged, reducing the respiratory surface - a major cause is **cigarette smoking**; **asthma** involves inflammation of **bronchi** and **bronchioles**, causing wheezing.
Frog respiration: **cutaneous** (through moist skin), **buccopharyngeal** (buccal cavity) and **pulmonary** (lungs); tadpoles breathe through **gills**.

Myoglobin in muscles stores **oxygen** and colours red muscle fibres; **foetal haemoglobin** has higher **oxygen affinity** than adult haemoglobin, helping the foetus draw oxygen across the **placenta**.

questions.q: Define vital capacity. What is its significance?
questions.a: Vital capacity is the maximum volume of air a person can breathe out after a forced inspiration (VC = ERV + TV + IRV, about 4600 mL). It indicates the strength of the respiratory muscles and the efficiency of the lungs.

questions.q: What is the effect of pCO2 on oxygen transport?
questions.a: High pCO2 (and low pH) reduces haemoglobin's affinity for O2 (Bohr effect), shifting the dissociation curve right, so tissues receive more oxygen where they need it most.

questions.q: What happens to the respiratory process in a man going up a hill?
questions.a: As altitude rises, pO2 falls; breathing rate and depth increase, and over days the RBC count rises to compensate for lower oxygen availability.

questions.q: Respiration in insects is called direct because: (a) the tissues exchange O2/CO2 directly with the air in the tubes (b) the tissues exchange O2/CO2 directly with the coelomic fluid (c) the tissues exchange O2/CO2 directly with the air outside through the body surface (d) the tissues exchange O2/CO2 directly with the air through internal tubes
questions.a: (a) Insects deliver air directly to tissues through tracheae, without blood as intermediary.

questions.q: Diffusion of gases occurs in the alveolar region only and not in the other parts of the respiratory system. Why?
questions.a: Only the alveoli have the thin, moist, richly vascularised surface and the enormous surface area with a short diffusion distance needed for gas exchange; the conducting parts have thick walls.

questions.q: How is respiration regulated?
questions.a: The respiratory rhythm centre in the medulla sets the basic rhythm; the pneumotaxic centre in the pons moderates it; a chemosensitive area near the rhythm centre senses CO2 and H+ and adjusts breathing rate and depth.

questions.q: What are the major transport mechanisms for CO2? Explain.
questions.a: About 70% as bicarbonate ions in plasma (via carbonic anhydrase in RBCs), 20-25% bound to haemoglobin as carbamino-haemoglobin, and about 7% dissolved in plasma.

questions.q: Define the oxygen dissociation curve. Can you suggest any reason for its sigmoidal pattern?
questions.a: It is a plot of percentage saturation of haemoglobin against pO2. It is sigmoid because haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen increases as more O2 molecules bind (cooperative binding).

mcqs.q: A person suffers punctures in his chest cavity in an accident, without any damage to the lungs. Its effect could be:
mcqs.why: Punctured chest cavity destroys the pressure gradient needed for breathing.

mcqs.q: It is known that exposure to carbon monoxide is harmful to animals because:
options: It destroys the chemical constitution of alveolus
mcqs.why: CO binds haemoglobin strongly, reducing oxygen transport.

mcqs.q: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding respiratory system?
options: Each terminal bronchiole gives rise to a network of bronchi
The lungs are covered by a double-layered membrane
The pleural fluid reduces friction on the lung surface
mcqs.why: Terminal bronchioles give rise to alveolar ducts and alveoli, not bronchi.

mcqs.q: Incidence of Emphysema - a respiratory disorder is high in cigarette smokers. In such cases:
options: The alveolar walls are found damaged
The plasma membrane is found damaged
The respiratory muscles are found damaged
mcqs.why: In emphysema the alveolar walls break down, reducing surface area.

mcqs.q: The oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve will show a right shift in case of:
mcqs.why: High pCO2 (Bohr effect) shifts the curve right, releasing more O2 to tissues.

mcqs.q: Respiratory process is regulated by certain specialised centres in the brain-stem which are known to reduce the inspiration duration. Such centres are:
mcqs.why: The pneumotaxic centre in the pons limits inspiration duration.

chapters.title: Body Fluids and Circulation
points: Blood: **plasma** (~55%, 90-92% water, 6-8% proteins like fibrinogen, albumin, globulins) + **formed elements** (~45%): **RBCs** (5-5.5 million/mm3, no nucleus, lifespan ~120 days, made in **red bone marrow**, destroyed in **spleen** 'graveyard of RBCs'), **WBCs** (6000-8000/mm3: neutrophils most abundant 60-65%, lymphocytes make antibodies), **platelets** (1.5-3.5 lakh/mm3, from megakaryocytes, blood clotting).

Blood groups: **ABO system** - A, B, AB (**universal recipient**), O (**universal donor**); **Rh factor** - Rh+ (~80% humans), Rh-; mismatch in pregnancy causes **erythroblastosis foetalis** (prevented by anti-Rh antibodies given to Rh- mother after first delivery).

Clotting: **platelets** + damaged tissue release **thrombokinase** -> **prothrombin** --(Ca2+)--> **thrombin** -> **fibrinogen** -> **fibrin** mesh traps cells. **Heparin** and **citrate** are natural/commercial anticoagulants.

Human heart: **4 chambers** (2 atria, 2 ventricles), **double circulation** (pulmonary + systemic), so oxygenated and deoxygenated blood never mix. Valves: **tricuspid** (right AV), **bicuspid**/**mitral** (left AV), **semilunar** at aorta and pulmonary artery.

Cardiac cycle **0.8 s**: **joint diastole** 0.4 s, **atrial systole** 0.1 s, **ventricular systole** 0.3 s. Heart sounds: **'lub'** (AV valves close) and **'dub'** (semilunar valves close). **Stroke volume** ~70 mL; **cardiac output** = SV x heart rate ~5000 mL/min.

SA node (**pacemaker**, right atrium) generates impulses -> **AV node** -> **Bundle of His** -> **Purkinje fibres**. ECG waves: **P** (atrial depolarisation), **QRS complex** (ventricular depolarisation), **T** (ventricular repolarisation).

Lymph (**tissue fluid**): drains into lymphatic capillaries; rich in **lymphocytes**, poor in proteins; returns **interstitial fluid** to blood and carries absorbed fats via **lacteals** in the intestinal villi.

Coronary circulation: the heart's own supply via **coronary arteries**; blockage causes **angina** (chest pain) or **myocardial infarction** (heart attack) - death of heart muscle from lack of **oxygen**.

Double circulation: **pulmonary circulation** (right ventricle -> lungs -> left atrium) oxygenates blood; **systemic circulation** (left ventricle -> body -> right atrium) delivers it; the **hepatic portal system** carries gut blood to the **liver** first.

questions.q: Name the formed elements of the blood and mention one function of each.
questions.a: RBCs (erythrocytes): transport O2 and CO2. WBCs (leucocytes): defence against infection. Platelets (thrombocytes): blood clotting.

questions.q: What is the importance of plasma proteins?
questions.a: Fibrinogen is needed for clotting, globulins are involved in defence, and albumins help maintain the osmotic balance of blood.

questions.q: Match column I with column II: (a) Eosinophils, (b) RBC, (c) AB group, (d) Platelets, (e) Systole - with (i) Coagulation, (ii) Universal recipient, (iii) Resist infections, (iv) Contraction of heart, (v) Gas transport.
questions.a: a - iii, b - v, c - ii, d - i, e - iv.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is correct: (a) Serum = blood + fibrinogen (b) Lymph = plasma + RBC + WBC (c) Blood = plasma + RBC + WBC (d) Plasma = blood - lymphocytes
questions.a: (c) Blood = plasma + RBC + WBC (and platelets are also formed elements).

questions.q: Why do we call our heart myogenic?
questions.a: Because the heartbeat originates in the heart muscle itself (the SA node generates the impulse), not from a nervous signal outside the heart.

questions.q: Sino-atrial node is called the pacemaker of our heart. Why?
questions.a: The SA node generates the maximum number of action potentials (70-75 per minute) and sets the rhythm of the heartbeat.

questions.q: Define a cardiac cycle and the cardiac output.
questions.a: Cardiac cycle: the sequence of systole and diastole of atria and ventricles in one heartbeat (~0.8 s). Cardiac output: the volume of blood pumped by each ventricle per minute (stroke volume x heart rate, about 5000 mL).

questions.q: Draw a standard ECG and explain the different segments in it.
questions.a: P wave: atrial depolarisation (contraction). QRS complex: ventricular depolarisation. T wave: ventricular repolarisation (recovery). The intervals help diagnose heart conditions.

mcqs.q: What would be the cardiac output of a person having 72 heart beats per minute and a stroke volume of 50 mL?
mcqs.why: Cardiac output = 72 x 50 = 3600 mL/min.

mcqs.q: The second heart sound (dub) is associated with the closure of:
mcqs.why: 'Dub' is produced by closure of the semilunar valves.

mcqs.q: Which of the following correctly explains a phase/event in cardiac cycle in a standard electrocardiogram?
options: Time between S and T represents atrial systole
P-wave indicates beginning of ventricular contraction
mcqs.why: The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarisation/contraction.

mcqs.q: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
options: A person of 'O' blood group has anti 'A' and anti 'B' antibodies in his blood plasma
A person of 'B' blood group can't donate blood to a person of 'A' blood group
Blood group is designated on the basis of the presence of antibodies in the blood plasma
A person of AB blood group is universal recipient
mcqs.why: Blood groups are designated by antigens on RBCs, not antibodies in plasma.

mcqs.q: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
options: Dup - sudden opening of semilunar valves at the beginning of ventricular diastole
Lubb - sharp closure of AV valves at the beginning of ventricular systole
Pulsation of radial artery - valves in the blood vessels
mcqs.why: 'Lubb' is the sharp closure of AV valves at the start of ventricular systole.

mcqs.q: The wall of the human heart is made of:
mcqs.why: The heart wall has epicardium, myocardium and endocardium.

chapters.title: Excretory Products and their Elimination
points: Excretion modes: **ammonotelic** (ammonia - most toxic, needs lots of water; aquatic animals like bony fishes), **ureotelic** (urea - mammals, frogs, sharks; made in liver by **ornithine cycle**), **uricotelic** (uric acid - birds, reptiles, insects; least toxic, minimal water loss).

Human kidney: ~**1-1.2 million nephrons** each. Nephron = **glomerulus** + **Bowman's capsule** (**Malpighian body**) + **PCT** + **Loop of Henle** + **DCT** + **collecting duct**. **Juxtamedullary** nephrons have long loops; **cortical** nephrons have short loops.

Urine formation: (1) **Glomerular filtration** - ~180 L/day filtered through glomerular capillaries (**GFR** ~125 mL/min) under pressure; (2) **selective reabsorption** (~99% in PCT mostly: all glucose, amino acids, most Na+, water); (3) **tubular secretion** (K+, H+, drugs into filtrate, mainly DCT).

Loop of Henle + **vasa recta** form the **counter-current mechanism** concentrating urine (up to 4x plasma). **ADH** (**vasopressin**) increases water reabsorption in DCT/collecting duct when blood is concentrated; its absence causes **diabetes insipidus**.

Regulation: **RAAS** - low pressure in afferent arteriole makes **JG cells** release **renin** -> **angiotensin II** (vasoconstriction + **aldosterone** release -> Na+ and water reabsorption). **ANF** from heart walls opposes RAAS.

Accessory excretion: **lungs** remove CO2 and water; **liver** converts ammonia to urea and excretes bilirubin/bile pigments; **skin** removes sweat (water, NaCl, some urea) and sebum; saliva. **Dialysis** (**haemodialysis**) is used in kidney failure.
Micturition: the **neural reflex** emptying the urinary bladder - **stretch receptors** signal the CNS, which relaxes the **urethral sphincter** and contracts the **detrusor muscle**.
Kidney disorders: **uremia** (excess urea in blood - treated by **haemodialysis**), **renal calculi** (kidney stones of **calcium oxalate**), **glomerulonephritis** (inflammation of glomeruli).
Sweat glands excrete **water**, **NaCl** and small amounts of **urea** and **lactic acid**; **sebaceous glands** eliminate sterols, hydrocarbons and waxes through **sebum**.

questions.q: Define GFR (glomerular filtration rate).
questions.a: The amount of filtrate formed by both kidneys per minute - about 125 mL/min (180 litres per day).

questions.q: Explain the autoregulatory mechanism by which the kidney controls GFR.
questions.a: The juxtaglomerular (JG) apparatus senses falling GFR and releases renin, which activates the renin-angiotensin mechanism to constrict vessels and raise glomerular pressure and GFR back to normal.

questions.q: Explain the counter-current mechanism in the kidney.
questions.a: The flow of filtrate in the two limbs of Henle's loop (and blood in vasa recta) in opposite directions creates and maintains a salt gradient in the medulla, allowing water reabsorption and concentrated urine.

questions.q: Which one of the following is the least toxic excretory product: (a) urea (b) uric acid (c) ammonia (d) CO2
questions.a: (b) Uric acid - it can be excreted almost dry, conserving water.

questions.q: Give a brief account of the mechanism of urine formation.
questions.a: Glomerular filtration (180 L/day through the Malpighian body), selective reabsorption (PCT reabsorbs all glucose, amino acids, most Na+ and water), and tubular secretion (K+, H+, drugs into DCT) concentrate the filtrate into about 1.5 L of urine.

questions.q: Describe the role of liver, lungs and skin in excretion.
questions.a: Liver: converts ammonia to urea (ornithine cycle) and excretes bile pigments, cholesterol and degraded drugs. Lungs: remove CO2 and water vapour. Skin: sweat glands excrete water, NaCl and small amounts of urea; sebaceous glands remove sterols and waxes.

questions.q: Terrestrial animals are generally either ureotelic or uricotelic, not ammonotelic. Why?
questions.a: Ammonia is highly toxic and needs large amounts of water for elimination; land animals conserve water, so they convert ammonia to less toxic urea or uric acid.

questions.q: What is meant by the term osmoregulation?
questions.a: The maintenance of the body's water and salt balance (osmotic concentration of blood and tissue fluids) despite changes in the environment.

mcqs.q: The condition of accumulation of urea in the blood is termed as:
mcqs.why: Uremia is the accumulation of urea in blood due to kidney failure.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following statements is incorrect?
options: The medullary zone of kidney is divided into a few conical masses called medullary pyramids projecting into the calyces
Inside the kidney the cortical region extends in between the medullary pyramids as renal pelvis
Glomerulus along with Bowman's capsule is called the renal corpuscle
Nephron is the structural and functional unit of kidney
mcqs.why: Cortical tissue between medullary pyramids forms renal columns (columns of Bertini), not the renal pelvis.

mcqs.q: The net pressure gradient that causes the fluid to filter out of the glomeruli into the capsule is:
mcqs.why: The effective filtration pressure in the glomerulus is about 20 mm Hg (10-20 mm Hg range in NCERT).

mcqs.q: Different types of excretory structures and animals are given below. Match them appropriately: A. Protonephridia - i. Prawn; B. Nephridia - ii. Cockroach; C. Malpighian tubules - iii. Earthworm; D. Green gland or Antennal gland - iv. Flatworms.
mcqs.why: Protonephridia-flatworms, nephridia-earthworm, Malpighian tubules-cockroach, green gland-prawn.

mcqs.q: Which of the following parts of mammalian nephron is involved in the active reabsorption of sodium?
mcqs.why: Most active Na+ reabsorption occurs in the PCT.

mcqs.q: Which of the following causes an increase in sodium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule?
mcqs.why: Aldosterone increases Na+ reabsorption in the DCT and collecting duct.

chapters.title: Locomotion and Movement
points: Types of movement: **amoeboid** (pseudopodia - macrophages, WBCs), **ciliary** (trachea, fallopian tubes - move mucus/ova), **muscular** (limbs, tongue, jaw).

Muscle fibre structure: **sarcolemma**, **sarcoplasm**, **myofibrils** with alternating dark **A bands** (myosin + actin overlap) and light **I bands** (actin only). **Sarcomere** = distance between two **Z lines** - the functional unit of contraction.

Thick filaments: **myosin** (head has **ATPase** and actin-binding sites; **meromyosin**). Thin filaments: **actin** + **troponin** + **tropomyosin**; **Ca2+** binds troponin to uncover actin binding sites.

Sliding filament theory: **Ca2+** from **sarcoplasmic reticulum** exposes actin sites; **myosin heads** form **cross-bridges**, pull actin to the centre using **ATP**; **A band** length stays constant while **I band** and **H zone** shrink; Z lines come closer.

Neuromuscular junction: **motor neuron** releases **acetylcholine**; **red fibres** (myoglobin-rich, aerobic, slow) vs **white fibres** (fast, anaerobic, fatigue quickly). **Muscle fatigue** is due to **lactic acid** accumulation during anaerobic respiration.

Skeletal system: **206 bones** (**axial** 80: skull 22, vertebral column 26, ribs 24 + sternum, hyoid; **appendicular** 126). Joints: **fibrous** (fixed - skull sutures), **cartilaginous** (slightly movable - between vertebrae), **synovial** (freely movable - **ball and socket**: shoulder/hip; **hinge**: knee/elbow; **pivot**: atlas-axis; **gliding**: carpals; **saddle**: thumb). Disorders: **myasthenia gravis** (autoimmune, junction affected), **tetany** (low Ca2+ spasms), **muscular dystrophy**, **osteoporosis**, **arthritis**, **gout** (uric acid crystals).
Cori's cycle: **lactic acid** from anaerobic muscle activity travels by blood to the **liver**, is reconverted to **glucose**, and returns to muscles - linking **muscle fatigue** to liver metabolism.

Locomotion needs coordinated **muscular**, **skeletal** and **neural** systems; muscles work in **antagonistic pairs** (biceps contracts while **triceps** relaxes); all movement uses **ATP** from cellular respiration.
Rigor mortis: after death no **ATP** is made, so **cross-bridges** between **actin** and **myosin** cannot break - muscles stiffen; it is a forensic sign of **death**.

questions.q: Define sliding filament theory of muscle contraction.
questions.a: During contraction, the thin actin filaments slide over the thick myosin filaments towards the centre of the sarcomere: the H-zone and I-bands shorten while the A-band length stays constant; the process is driven by ATP and regulated by Ca2+.

questions.q: Describe the important steps in muscle contraction.
questions.a: Neural signal reaches the neuromuscular junction -> acetylcholine triggers an action potential -> Ca2+ released from sarcoplasmic reticulum binds troponin -> myosin heads form cross-bridges with actin -> power stroke pulls actin filaments -> ATP breaks the bridges and the cycle repeats; on relaxation Ca2+ is pumped back.

questions.q: What are the different types of movements exhibited by the cells of the human body?
questions.a: Amoeboid movement (e.g. macrophages and WBCs), ciliary movement (e.g. in the trachea and oviducts) and muscular movement (by muscle cells).

questions.q: Match: (a) Fast muscles, (b) Slow muscles, (c) Actin filament, (d) Sarcomere - with (i) Myoglobin, (ii) Lactic acid accumulation, (iii) Contractile unit, (iv) I-band.
questions.a: a - ii, b - i, c - iv, d - iii.

questions.q: Write true or false. If false, correct the statement: (a) Actin is present in thin filament. (b) The H-zone of a striated muscle fibre represents both thick and thin filaments. (c) The human skeleton has 206 bones. (d) There are 11 pairs of ribs in man. (e) The sternum is present on the ventral side of the body.
questions.a: (a) True. (b) False - the H-zone has only thick filaments. (c) True. (d) False - 12 pairs. (e) True.

questions.q: How do you distinguish between a skeletal muscle and a cardiac muscle?
questions.a: Skeletal muscle: voluntary, multinucleate, unbranched fibres with clear striations. Cardiac muscle: involuntary, usually uninucleate, branched fibres joined by intercalated discs, never fatigues.

questions.q: Name the type of joint between the following: (a) atlas/axis (b) carpal/metacarpal of thumb (c) between phalanges (d) femur/acetabulum (e) between cranial bones (f) between pubic bones.
questions.a: (a) Pivot (b) Saddle (c) Hinge (d) Ball and socket (e) Fibrous/fixed (f) Cartilaginous.

questions.q: Write the difference between: (a) actin and myosin (b) red and white muscles (c) pectoral and pelvic girdles.
questions.a: (a) Actin forms thin filaments (with troponin/tropomyosin); myosin forms thick filaments with ATPase heads. (b) Red fibres are myoglobin-rich, aerobic, fatigue-resistant; white fibres are myoglobin-poor, anaerobic, fatigue fast. (c) Pectoral girdle (clavicle + scapula) attaches forelimbs; pelvic girdle (two coxal bones) attaches hindlimbs and bears weight.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following is showing the correct sequential order of vertebrae in the vertebral column of human beings?
mcqs.why: Vertebral order is cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral, coccygeal.

mcqs.q: Rib bones are joined to the sternum by:
mcqs.why: Costal cartilages joining ribs to the sternum are hyaline cartilage.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following statements is true?
options: Head of humerus bone articulates with the acetabulum of pectoral girdle
Head of humerus bone articulates with the glenoid cavity of pectoral girdle
Head of humerus bone articulates with the acetabulum of pelvic girdle
Head of humerus bone articulates with the glenoid cavity of pelvic girdle
mcqs.why: The humerus head fits the glenoid cavity of the pectoral girdle (scapula).

mcqs.q: Muscles with characteristic striations and involuntary are:
options: Muscles in the wall of alimentary canal
mcqs.why: Cardiac muscles are striated but involuntary.

mcqs.q: Match the following and mark the correct option: A. Sternum - i. Synovial fluid; B. Glenoid cavity - ii. Vertebrae; C. Freely movable joint - iii. Pectoral girdle; D. Cartilaginous joint - iv. Flat bones.
mcqs.why: Sternum-flat bone, glenoid cavity-pectoral girdle, freely movable joint-synovial fluid, cartilaginous joint-vertebrae.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following is not a disorder of bone?
mcqs.why: Atherosclerosis is a disorder of arteries, not bone.

chapters.title: Neural Control and Coordination
points: Neuron: **cell body** (cyton with **Nissl granules**), **dendrites** (receive signals, towards cell body), **axon** (conducts away; long fibres; **myelin sheath** by Schwann cells in PNS, **nodes of Ranvier** between them).

Impulse conduction: **resting potential** ~-70 mV maintained by **Na+/K+ pump** (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in) and selective permeability. **Action potential**: Na+ influx depolarises the membrane (+40 mV), then K+ outflow repolarises. **Saltatory conduction** in myelinated fibres jumps node to node - much faster.

Synapse: **electrical** (rare, gap junctions, faster) vs **chemical** (most common; **synaptic vesicles** release **neurotransmitters** like acetylcholine into the **synaptic cleft**; impulse crosses only one way).

Human brain: **cerebrum** (largest part, two hemispheres joined by **corpus callosum**; frontal/parietal/temporal/occipital lobes; intelligence, memory, voluntary actions); **thalamus** (sensory relay); **hypothalamus** (temperature, hunger, thirst, hormones link to pituitary); **midbrain**; **cerebellum** (balance, posture, coordination); **pons** (relay); **medulla oblongata** (involuntary centres - respiration, heartbeat, swallowing, vomiting).

Reflex action: sudden **involuntary response** via **reflex arc** - receptor -> sensory neuron -> CNS (interneuron, often in spinal cord) -> motor neuron -> effector. It bypasses conscious thought for speed (e. knee jerk, withdrawing hand from hot object).

Eye: **sclera**, **choroid** (absorbs light), **iris** controls pupil size, **lens** focuses on retina; retina has **rods** (dim light, rhodopsin pigment) and **cones** (bright light, colour vision); **blind spot** (optic disc - no photoreceptors), **yellow spot**/**fovea** (sharpest vision). Ear: **pinna**, **auditory canal**, **tympanum**, **ossicles** (**malleus**, **incus**, **stapes** - smallest bone), **cochlea** with **organ of Corti** (hearing), **semicircular canals** and vestibular apparatus (balance).

Human neural system: **central neural system** (brain + **spinal cord**) and **peripheral neural system** - **12 pairs** of cranial nerves and **31 pairs** of spinal nerves; the **visceral/autonomic** division controls involuntary organs via **sympathetic** and **parasympathetic** paths.
Nissl's granules in the **cell body** and **dendrites** are **rough ER** with ribosomes - the neuron's protein factories; the **axon hillock** is where the **action potential** begins.

Mechanism of vision: light -> **cornea** -> **lens** focuses the image on the **retina** -> photochemical change in **rhodopsin** (rods) -> impulse via the **optic nerve** to the visual cortex in the **occipital lobe**; the **fovea** gives the sharpest vision.

questions.q: Briefly describe the structure of the brain.
questions.a: The brain has three parts: forebrain (cerebrum, thalamus, hypothalamus), midbrain, and hindbrain (cerebellum, pons and medulla oblongata). The cerebrum is the largest part, divided into two hemispheres.

questions.q: Compare resting potential and action potential.
questions.a: Resting potential: the axonal membrane is polarised at about -70 mV (outside positive). Action potential: on stimulation, Na+ rushes in, the inside becomes positive (depolarisation), followed by K+ outflow restoring the resting state (repolarisation).

questions.q: Explain the following processes: (a) polarisation of the membrane of a nerve fibre, (b) depolarisation of the membrane, (c) conduction of a nerve impulse along an axon, (d) transmission of a nerve impulse across a chemical synapse.
questions.a: (a) Resting state with Na+/K+ pump maintaining -70 mV. (b) Stimulus opens Na+ channels; inside becomes positive. (c) The local current ahead of the impulse depolarises the next segment, so the impulse self-propagates. (d) The impulse releases neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft, which binds receptors on the post-synaptic membrane and starts a new impulse.

questions.q: The chemicals involved in the transmission of impulses at the chemical synapse are called: (a) hormones (b) neurotransmitters (c) cerebrospinal fluid (d) lymph
questions.a: (b) Neurotransmitters (e.g. acetylcholine).

questions.q: Give a brief account of the mechanism of synaptic transmission.
questions.a: The impulse reaching the axon terminal opens Ca2+ channels; synaptic vesicles release neurotransmitter (e.g. acetylcholine) into the synaptic cleft; it binds receptors on the post-synaptic membrane, generating a new impulse.

questions.q: Differentiate between: (a) myelinated and non-myelinated axons (b) dendrites and axons (c) rods and cones.
questions.a: (a) Myelinated axons have a myelin sheath and conduct by fast saltatory conduction; non-myelinated are slower. (b) Dendrites receive impulses toward the cell body; axons carry them away. (c) Rods work in dim light (rhodopsin, no colour); cones work in bright light and give colour vision.

questions.q: Answer briefly: (a) How do you perceive the colour of an object? (b) Which part of our body helps us in maintaining body balance? (c) How does transmission of impulses take place across a chemical synapse?
questions.a: (a) Cones in the retina detect different wavelengths, giving colour vision. (b) The cerebellum, with the vestibular apparatus and semicircular canals of the inner ear. (c) Neurotransmitter released into the synaptic cleft binds post-synaptic receptors, starting a new impulse.

questions.q: Explain the role of Na+ in the generation of action potential.
questions.a: Stimulus opens voltage-gated Na+ channels; Na+ rushes in, making the inside positive (depolarisation to about +40 mV); then K+ channels open, K+ leaves, restoring the resting potential (repolarisation).

mcqs.q: Potential difference across resting membrane is negatively charged. This is due to differential distribution of the following ions:
mcqs.why: Unequal Na+ and K+ distribution maintains the resting potential.

mcqs.q: Resting membrane potential is maintained by:
mcqs.why: The Na+/K+ ATPase ion pump maintains the resting potential.

mcqs.q: The function of our visceral organs is controlled by:
mcqs.why: Visceral organs are controlled by the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is not involved in knee-jerk reflex?
mcqs.why: The knee-jerk reflex arc is spinal and does not involve the brain.

mcqs.q: An area in the brain which is associated with strong emotions is:
mcqs.why: The limbic system is associated with emotions.

mcqs.q: Mark the vitamin present in Rhodopsin:
mcqs.why: Rhodopsin contains retinal, derived from vitamin A.

chapters.title: Chemical Coordination and Integration
points: Endocrine glands are **ductless** and release **hormones** directly into blood. **Hypothalamus** (releasing/inhibiting hormones like **GnRH**, **somatostatin**) controls the **pituitary** - the master gland.

Pituitary hormones: anterior lobe - **GH** (growth; excess = **gigantism**/**acromegaly**, deficiency = **dwarfism**), **TSH**, **ACTH**, **FSH**, **LH**, **prolactin**; posterior lobe releases **ADH** (**vasopressin** - water reabsorption) and **oxytocin** (childbirth contractions, milk ejection) - actually made in the hypothalamus and stored here.

Thyroid gland: **thyroxine** (**T4**/**T3**) regulates **basal metabolic rate**; needs **iodine**; deficiency causes **goitre**, **cretinism** (children) and **myxoedema** (adults); excess = **exophthalmic goitre** (Graves disease). **Calcitonin** lowers blood Ca2+. **Parathormone** (**PTH**) from parathyroids raises blood Ca2+.

Pancreas (mixed gland): **Islets of Langerhans** - **beta cells** secrete **insulin** (lowers blood glucose; deficiency = **diabetes mellitus**), **alpha cells** secrete **glucagon** (raises glucose). Adrenal: **cortex** - **glucocorticoids** (cortisol), **mineralocorticoids** (aldosterone - Na+/water balance); **medulla** - **adrenaline**/**noradrenaline** (emergency '3F' hormones: fight, flight, fright).
